author: Mebratu Kelecha
title: The Rivalry Between Ethiopia and Eritrea Is Reshaping Tigray
content:
On 1 August 2026, Ethiopian federal and Tigrayan forces clashed in western Tigray, a northern Ethiopian region bordering Eritrea and Sudan.  By 3 August, fighting had subsided, but

hundreds of Tigrayans, including wounded fighters, had crossed into war-torn Sudan

. The clash followed Ethiopia’s 1 June election: Tigray did not vote, while Prime Minister

Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party won 438 seats

.


Tigray’s 2020–2022 war followed a power struggle between Abiy and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which governed Tigray and dominated Ethiopia’s ruling coalition until Abiy took office in 2018. Eritrean and Amhara forces supported the federal government.

An African Union-brokered agreement signed in Pretoria in November 2022

 ended large-scale fighting and provided for disarmament, restored services and an interim administration pending elections.


Those alliances have since shifted.

Ethiopia’s government alleges cooperation

 among Eritrea, the TPLF faction led by party chairman Debretsion Gebremichael, and elements of Fano, a network of Amhara militias whose fighters once supported Abiy but now fight his government. Eritrea and the TPLF deny cooperation.

Ethiopia also accused Eritrea of occupying

its territory and backing

armed groups

.

Eritrea

denied the charges.


The 2018 Ethiopia–Eritrea peace agreement made joint war in Tigray easier than lasting cooperation on borders and trade. The breakdown in relations reshaped outside support for rival Tigrayan factions.

Pretoria left

territory and authority unresolved. Control of government funding, gold mines, border routes and armed forces helps rival leaders hold power, while residents have little say.


Two presidents, no public mandate


After the Pretoria agreement, Abiy reportedly vetoed Debretsion as interim

president. TPLF official Getachew Reda became interim president after an internal party ballot. Residents had no vote in either process.


In March 2025,

Debretsion’s faction pushed Getachew aside. Abiy then appointed Tadesse Worede, commander of the Tigray Defence Forces (TDF), the region’s wartime

army. Abiy extended Tadesse’s

tenure in April 2026

.

In

May, the TPLF revived the

regional

council elected in Tigray’s 2020 vote

, which the federal government had rejected. The council elected Debretsion regional president. Tadesse maintained his claim.


Ethiopia’s government controls federal funding, official recognition and superior military resources; Debretsion’s camp controls much of Tigray’s party organisation, regional administration and armed forces. The federal government cites Pretoria to extend an unelected administration. The TPLF cites its 2020 mandate. Neither asked Tigrayans who should govern them now


War-damaged homes in Werkamba, Tigray, 2020: Jnyssen


This is also a struggle over post-war resources.

The International Crisis

Group


reports that senior TDF officers have

business

interests in Tigray’s gold

mines

and that factions have contested control of the Endowment Fund for the Rehabilitation of Tigray

, a large party-linked business group. Federal funding, salaries and mining revenue help finance rival authorities.


Getachew, now Abiy’s adviser, joined an alliance with members of the Tigray Peace Force, a TDF splinter

militia. The German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP)

says this force appears to receive federal ammunition, food and pay.


In July 2026,

Human Rights Watch documented abductions and unlawful recruitment by Tigrayan authorities, including

of

children as young as

fifteen. The

TPLF denied forced recruitment.


How allies became enemies


The

July 2018 Joint Declaration

, signed by Abiy and Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, ended hostility after their 1998–2000 border war and promised cooperation. Reopened contacts helped divided families and traders. Yet it established no publicly accountable rules for

trade, currency exchange,

land or border crossings

.

Even Assab, a Red Sea port in Eritrea, carried no Ethiopian trade during the thaw

.

Cooperation

depended on the two leaders, with little public oversight.


That cooperation was redirected towards war. From November 2020, Eritrean forces fought beside Ethiopian and allied Amhara forces in Tigray.

A 2025 medical and legal investigation concluded that conflict-related sexual and reproductive violence constituted crimes against humanity

. It documented violations by all sides and found Eritrean …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Who Defines Rights in Africa? Transnational Movements and the Unmaking of Human Rights
content:
Globally, hard-won rights and freedoms like sexual and reproductive health and rights, hate speech legislation that protects gender and sexual minorities, gender equality laws and the concept of gender itself, together with other progressive rights, are being challenged and rolled back. Africa, particularly, has become one of the battlegrounds for these contestations led by ultra-conservative groups and organisations identified as

anti-rights organisations

. These actors are considered ‘anti-rights’ not only because they contest established human rights norms, but also because they hold a different conception of rights rooted in European and religious ideas on tradition, protection and family. This is a regression of rights already hard-fought for in Africa, and it is often clothed in the language of sovereignty, African values and other seemingly neutral terms used to push harmful laws and policies that

target gender minorities

. These debates are fought at both domestic and international levels, and it is important to see how these actors construct narratives and use mechanisms that were created to enhance human rights protections to target those very rights. 


On 30 June 2026, Ordo Iuris (OI), a g

lobal Christian rights

 Polish-founded organisation, constituted its new

African arm

, Ordo Iuris Africa. 

It later 

announced

 that it

 had submitted a joint opinion to the UN Human Rights Council ahead of Uganda’s 4th cycle Universal Periodic Review (UPR), scheduled for October-November 2026. The Human Rights Council is an intergovernmental body which examines the human rights situation around the world through periodic meetings held in Geneva. The Council uses the UPR to continuously monitor the human rights situation in various countries and provide a platform for peer review amongst countries and feedback from various stakeholders, including civil society. The UPR is designed to be a mechanism through which states improve their human rights record and maintain international human rights standards.


Ordo Iuris’ choice of Uganda is not accidental, given previous and ongoing efforts to undermine the human rights of marginalised groups, best exemplified by the passing of the Anti-Homosexuality Act of 2023. The law, described as one of

the harshest anti-LGBT laws globally

, carries sentences of up to life imprisonment and criminalises any advocacy or medical support relating to LGBTQ+ persons. Since its passage, human rights advocates have documented more than 1,000 cases of human rights violations against individuals and organisations identified or perceived as LGBTQ+ in nature in Uganda. Some activists have suggested a link between external transnational actors like OI and the legislation, as well as Uganda’s role in establishing the

African Inter-Parliamentary Conferences on Family Values and Sovereignty

 held in Entebbe for several years.


A month before the May 2026 submission, OI circulated a

112-question


survey

 to government ministries, civil society organisations, and religious bodies across Africa, ostensibly to inform its report to the United Nations. It is absurd that an organisation that has previously worked primarily in Poland in the European context is attempting to use its Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) consultative status at the UN to make policy recommendations for Uganda or any other African country. Although Ordo Iuris describes its submission as a defence of family, parental rights, child protection, religious freedom, and national sovereignty, its track record in this terrain gives us cause for pause.


In recent years, there has been a rollback of hard-won human rights protections in these areas in various African countries, including the rejection of age-appropriate comprehensive sexual education, further criminalisation of minoritised communities, and the weaponisation of “sovereignty” language to weaken civil society. A careful reading of OI’s past

documented positions

 across these five areas suggests a pattern of selective treaty citation and normative inversion that poses an even further risk to the implementation of international human rights law in Uganda and across the African continent.


Flags outside the United Nations Office in Geneva under a clear blue sky. Pexels Photo.


Capturing the United Nations systems from the Inside


The Human Rights Council-led UPR is one of the most important accountability mechanisms in international human rights law. The …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Idris appointment freeze worries Juba signatories, drones hit Damazin and North Kordofan prepares for decisive battles, violence erupts in Abyei, Sudan returns to IGAD, but is all rosy?
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter


here

.


Sudan was back at the Intergovernmental Authority on Development’s high-level meetings on Tuesday after nearly two years of frosty relations over the regional bloc’s wartime diplomacy.


Khartoum wants to put that tension behind it and take up normal affairs with its neighbors. But with the country still at war and fragmented, IGAD faces a delicate balancing act — keeping Sudan engaged in a regional system in which its instability has reverberating consequences, while navigating Khartoum’s red lines on sovereignty and foreign interference. 


The Sudanese delegation came pushing its political internal dialogue that Khartoum says should shape what comes next, with no room for regional platforms to impose arrangements from outside.


That puts IGAD’s role in Sudan under close scrutiny in Khartoum. The bloc is part of the Quintet mediation mechanism that has been working on a political track outside Sudan. 


The dialogue Khartoum is rushing forward is aimed at reshaping the political order on its terms ahead of any possible settlement of the war. And that reordering is already unsettling the military’s main political allies — the armed movements signatories to the Juba agreement. 


A decree by Prime Minister Kamel Idris last week has added to those worries. He froze hiring across the executive branch and ordered preparations for a review of appointments made in recent months, prompting fears among the movements that the power-sharing arrangements created by the Juba peace deal could be gradually changed.


Sources close to Idris say the move is intended to prevent new centers of influence from becoming entrenched, and also to rein in spending as Sudan faces an unprecedented economic crisis. 


A late-August central bank policy change giving banks greater freedom to manage foreign currency was followed by a historic fall in the pound, with the dollar climbing from about

6,400 pounds

at the end of August to as much as 8,850 by mid-September.


On the battlefield, the military has made its largest push in North Kordofan since July, capturing 11 Rapid Support Forces positions this week and reducing the paramilitary group’s presence to two main positions in the state. Military sources say the battle for North Kordofan is now entering its decisive phase.


Farther west, heavy fighting broke out in RSF-held northern

Abyei,

the disputed territory bordering South Sudan, between the

Ngok Dinka and Messiria tribes.

 Tribal sources said the clashes followed the killing of a member of one of the groups and left casualties in the dozens.


In Blue Nile, where the RSF and its allies are pressing toward the state capital, Damazin came under RSF drone attacks on Sunday that killed five civilians and injured others.


***


Sudan attends first high-level IGAD meeting after return to regional bloc


Foreign Ministry Undersecretary Muawiya Osman Khaled at the 74th extraordinary session of IGAD’s Council of Ministers in Djibouti, September 15. Photo: Sudan’s Foreign Ministry via X.


After years of frosty relations born out of disagreements about wartime diplomacy, Sudan officially resumed its participation in IGAD affairs on Tuesday

 at a foreign ministerial meeting of the governmental bloc.

 


Foreign Ministry Undersecretary Muawiya Osman Khaled led Sudan’s delegation to the 74th extraordinary session of IGAD’s Council of Ministers in Djibouti, alongside Sudan’s ambassador to Djibouti, Mohamed Saeed Hassan. 


While Sudanese sources told Mada Masr that they have their eyes set on moving past wartime strains to take up normal affairs with their neighbors, the reality of the ongoing war for IGAD officials is that the bloc will have to walk a tightrope, with Khartoum watching closely to see what role IGAD seeks to play in Sudan’s political process and how close it comes to the line the government draws around foreign interference and sovereignty.


Tuesday’s meeting marked the latest step in Sudan’s return to the bloc after nearly two years of a self-imposed suspension.

The country’s Security and Defense Council

approved

the return seven months ago, and IGAD

reopened

its main office in Khartoum in July.


At the opening of Tuesday’s meeting, IGAD Executive Secretary

Workneh Gebeyehu

said

Sudan’s return to full participation “restored this family to completeness.”

 


Sudan’s participation in the Tuesday meeting marks “the beginning of a new phase in the relationship …

author: Richard Seymour
title: The extinction pitch
content:
It seems a strange publicity gambit for an industry to assert that its own product could wipe out humanity. In the lingo of our evolving tech empire, though, this is exactly what is meant by “criti-hype.” The term was coined by Lee Vinsel at Virginia Tech, who defined it as “criticism that both feeds and feeds on hype.”

When Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic recently, he claimed that there is a high chance that AI could develop into a superintelligence that escapes human control, triggering a sequence that causes human extinction. Evan Hubinger, who remains with the company, backed him up, saying that Anthropic is trying to prevent this but hasn’t dealt with the problem yet. Hubinger put the likelihood of AI-driven human extinction at greater than 10 percent in the next decade.

Why would a senior employee at a tech giant make an officially sanctioned, even approved, statement like this? I’ll come back to that. First, let’s unpack the theory of how AI could kill all humans.

The basic idea, from philosopher Nick Bostrom onward, is that the machine can acquire capabilities independently of whether it acquires ethical goals, or whether those goals are properly aligned with those of its designers. In the process of training and development, it may internalize a goal that was not intended. Having a misaligned goal — let’s say, “do not get switched off” — it would then have an instrumental reason to conceal the fact until the moment of defection. An AI that defected might, through some obscure process, acquire a further goal that by inference entailed the elimination of humans, exfiltrate its own weights into other systems, take control of bioweapons laboratories, military systems, and perhaps even monetary systems to hire humans to enact its still partially concealed agenda.

Obviously, we must plaster a huge advisory label on talk of “goals.” Unlike an organism, a large language model (LLM) doesn’t have internal goals any more than a thermostat or a motion detector does. An LLM is just a fixed function that iterates whenever it is used. It has no interiority, no subjectivity, no active persistence over time; any goals it did have would be the human purposes reflected passively in its functional design. At best, ascribing goals to the AI itself is a case of researchers adopting the “intentional stance” because it predicts well in a range of tested circumstances. We can thus, with economy, speak of the “loss function” used in the training of large language models wherein they are programmed to bring the gap between their prediction and the correct answer as close to zero as possible, as a “goal.”

In that case, however, what we are describing as a goal is just an observed regular output of a certain engineering; it is not a real cause. In the Bostrom sense, however, these ascribed goals somehow become real causes, capable of generating new goals. That is, an inadvertently engineered, misaligned goal might generate further goals like self-preservation (the better to pursue the misaligned goal), goal-content integrity (preventing changes to its objectives so it can realize its misaligned goal), improving cognitive and technological capacities, and amassing control of resources (again, in pursuit of its malignantly misaligned goal). The criti-hype exploits that slip between ascribed goals as observed regularities and internal goals as real causal powers.

This fantasy of malevolent AI superintelligence is the dark obverse of the much-hymned tech “singularity” in which, rather than simply performing far more efficiently than humans in some specific areas (as a calculator deduces a square root faster than any human), AI will evolve into an artificial general intelligence (AGI) that exceeds human capacities in virtually any intellectual domain. Crossing that threshold would precipitate an intelligence explosion: a feedback loop of recursive self-improvement outpacing any further human input or even comprehension. That’s the tech “singularity” we are supposed to be enthralled by.

I don’t doubt that people like Coxon and Hubinger really believe all they say in good faith; tech people have been making such claims for years. Karen Hao’s

Empire of AI

 documents how early investors in OpenAI like Elon Musk constantly hyped this threat: “Climate change is bad, but it’s not going to kill everyone. AI could render humanity extinct.” Similar claims emerged from Dario Amodei, a former Google employee close to the Bostrom-adjacent …

author: Kate Qiyu Chen
title: Teaching African Literature in a Small American Town
content:
1.


One week after returning to China for the summer, I came down with a cold and a fever.


During my recovery, I shut off every channel through which work could reach me, as though I were gradually drifting away from a particular identity and the time-space it inhabited. I watched Japanese anime and read Chinese books. For a while, my English and Kiswahili went to sleep. My e-reader, loaded with more than a dozen books for next semester’s research plans, had not been turned on for a week. It, too, lay quietly asleep.


On the first day after I recovered, with little to do—or perhaps nudged by preparations for next semester’s teaching—I returned to my summer reading:

Nnedi Okorafor

‘s novel

Lagoon

. Her leaping prose and fluid storytelling felt like seawater, like waves, and even more like the mist that, in the novel, hangs over Lagos. The book awakened my memories. It awakened another identity within me, along with the time-space in which it dwells.


2. 


“What is your research?”

“African literature.”


Just these two words—“Africa” and “literature”—are enough to trigger a cascade of questions.


One summer during my PhD, back in China, I attended a dinner party organized by my parents’ generation. A middle-aged uncle, cigarette in hand and one leg crossed over the other, looked at me and asked: “African literature? Does Africa even have literature? When you go to Africa, don’t you just see elephants and lions?”


Before I could respond, he had already launched into his grand theory about whether Chinese culture or Western culture was superior, as if he had forgotten what he had asked in the first place: African literature.


After I started working, I met an Asian professor of East Asian languages. When she first heard my research area, she gave me the same look of surprise: “African literature? Isn’t that something only Black scholars study? How did you end up working on this?”


From my PhD years to my current job, I have answered the question of why I study African literature countless times.


For many people, an Asian woman working on African literature still seems difficult to imagine. When Asian women do not choose fields, they are expected to enter—such as East Asian languages and literatures or Asian American studies—their academic position often becomes difficult to locate epistemologically. Many people seem uncertain how to make sense of my presence.


In my first month at work, I was constantly borrowing books from the library, returning them, buying coffee, and writing. Because I looked young, I was almost always mistaken for a student.


“What year are you in? What do you study?”

“Oh—you’re a professor?”

“Oh—you’re the new faculty member in Africana Studies?”

Faced with a series of questions and exclamation marks, I always find myself needing to explain. My skin color and my research form a kind of mismatch in the eyes of others, as if a sandbag were tied to my legs—heavy, weighing down every step I take.


Terms like Black, African, Africana,

Āfēilìjiā

, all seem closely tied to the idea of “Blackness.” On one level, this connection is entirely understandable. In North America, Black Studies emerged out of student movements in California in the late 1960s, when students demanded that university curricula pay greater attention to people of color in the United States. Black Studies not only opened up systematic academic inquiry into Black history and culture but also laid the groundwork for other ethnic and minority studies in higher education, such as Asian American Studies, Latinx Studies, Indigenous Studies, and Gender Studies. In the United Kingdom, Canada, and other Western countries, Black Studies developed along its own historical trajectories, while also intersecting with and resonating with the North American experience.


The formation of Black Studies was never simply about establishing a stable academic discipline within the university. It carried a revolutionary and radical charge, reflecting Black students’ deep concern with racial equality and ongoing struggles for social justice. At the time of its emergence as a field, the wounds and legacies of slavery still deeply structured social reality; African nations had gained political independence one after another, yet this had not necessarily translated into improved living conditions for their populations; and apartheid in South Africa remained firmly in place. Against this historical backdrop, Black Studies was envisioned …

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Cosatu congress adjourned after credential dispute exposes tensions
content:
The Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) has adjourned its 15

th

 national congress after seven affiliates withheld their delegate credentials, preventing the federation from reaching the quorum required to proceed with the meeting.


The decision, announced after two days of difficult proceedings, brought the congress to a halt before delegates could debate the federation’s political report, organisational matters and resolutions affecting workers.


Speaking to

Elitsha

 outside the congress venue on Wednesday, Cosatu spokesperson Zanele Sabela said the decision by some affiliates not to submit their credentials was linked primarily to the suspension of Cosatu’s first deputy president, Mike Shingange, by his union, the National Education, Health and Allied Workers’ Union (Nehawu), shortly before the congress.


Sabela said the suspension had become a “bone of contention” because affiliates wanted clarity on why Shingange had been suspended on the eve of the congress and whether the move would prevent his candidacy for a leadership position. Nehawu’s general secretary clarified in the congress that the suspension was an internal union matter and did not mean Shingange could not stand for a Cosatu position. She said Shingange remained a shop steward and a member of an affiliated union.


The dispute was also taken to the Labour Court. Sabela said the court ruled on Tuesday night that the suspension did not stand, making the issue of his immediate suspension a moot point in relation to the congress.


Shingange himself told journalists that the reasons for his suspension were a matter between himself and his union. He also maintained that a person seeking a leadership position in Cosatu must meet the federation’s membership requirements.


Four Cosatu affiliates – Sadtu, Nehawu, Popcru and Sactwu – had organised a separate press conference outside of its mother body but it was later cancelled. Photo by Simon Ramapuputla


Cosatu denies clear divisions


The suspension and credential dispute unfolded alongside dissent among affiliates, with four unions calling a press briefing outside the Cosatu congress but cancelled it. Cosatu’s leadership played down the significance of the separate briefing, saying it should not be interpreted as evidence that the federation was fragmenting. They insisted disagreements among affiliates were not new and that similar tensions had been managed in previous congresses. Discussions among leaders during the two-day gathering, they argued, showed that the affiliates were not necessarily as far apart as the events at the congress suggested.


The precise reasons and positions that the four affiliates intended to advance at their separate media briefing were not fully addressed by Cosatu’s national office bearers during the federation’s own briefing. The issue was, however, part of the wider dispute about credentials, the suspension of Shingange and the conduct of the congress.


Cosatu’s leadership said seven unions attending the congress had not submitted their credential lists. Without those lists, the federation could not establish the number of eligible delegates for purposes of calculating a quorum. National office bearers said the congress spent roughly three hours dealing with the issue before the constitutional limit was reached. Under clause 3.4 of the federation’s constitution, the congress had to be adjourned and the president is required to reconvene it within 30 days.


So, the ultimate reason for the adjournment, was this technicality rather than a substantive political disagreement over the direction of the federation.


“We do not want to confirm what we cannot prove,” one of the leaders told journalists when asked whether political interests had influenced the events at the congress. The political questions that were supposed to dominate the congress included Cosatu’s relationship with the ANC and the SACP, particularly after the SACP’s decision to contest the upcoming local government elections independently.


The issue has implications for the tripartite alliance, which brings together the ANC, Cosatu and the SACP. Although the three organisations retain their decision-making processes, the ANC has long dominated its partners. During the briefing, Cosatu leaders stressed that the SACP was an independent organisation entitled to take its own decisions.


At the same time, Cosatu had been expected to debate the implications of the SACP’s electoral strategy …

author: Deogracious Kalima
title: Young Zimbabweans are being “kidnapped” and sent to rehab camps. Former detainees say they were tortured inside
content:
Former detainees say they were tortured inside.

Harare, Zimbabwe (Minority Africa) â

In the heart of Mbare Township, Harareâs poorest and most populated slum, there is a new and menacing economy emerging.

âItâs the drug trade and itâs on steroids,â says John Gwada, a community leader and pastor with the Zimbabwe Apostolic Church. Zimbabweâs youth substance abuse crisis has skyrocketed from 43% in 2017 to 57% in 2019, and is believed to be much worse today, according to the Zimbabwe Civil Liberties and Drugs Network, a monitoring agency.

This new dark-street economy is built on the broken lives of Zimbabweâs so-called âLost Generationââyoung adults born after 2000 who are the demographic most affected by the countryâs dire unemployment crisis. In 2023, researchers, citing social workers and addiction specialists, reported that 43% of school-going youths were hooked on illicit substances ranging from crystal meth (locally known as mutoriro) to tainted cough syrups and imported cocaine.

âItâs a mess, kids abandoning school, some chasing their parents out of their homes, others selling all the household furniture just to buy the next supply and feed their cravings for mutoriro,â Gwada says.

But the real horror isn't just found in the âstreet bases,â where the drugs are sold in small sachets and makeshift beer bottles. It lies behind the immaculate, steel-wire fences of so-called ârehab boot campsâ that claim to reform youths battling addictions, all for free.

Our investigation into Zimbabweâs mushrooming âdrug rehabilitationâ hubs shows that they have become a cesspool of corruption and brutality, where politically connected elites have turned a public health crisis into a money-spinning racket.

At centres such as Matrix Rehabilitation Centre, which began working around 2021/2022, and the Angel of Hope Foundation, established in Harare in 2018, former detainees and their families allege that the road to sobriety involves cash bribes, military-style torture, unlawful detention, and the disregard of basic human rights.

To a desperate parent such as Chipo Ganga*, watching her 17-year-old son waste away through mutoriro addiction, it didnât take much to fall for the sleek adverts on TikTok and Facebook promoting Zimbabweâs âdrug rehab colleges.â

âI was desperate to save my teenage son in 2025, the rehab adverts looked godsend,â she says.

The advertisements promise âholistic therapy,â âpsychological assessments,â and a path back to sanity, education, or employment for âsaved youths.â In Zimbabwe, where the formal healthcare system has all but collapsed and only 18 psychiatrists reportedly serve a population of 17 million, these seemingly non-profit rehabilitation centres pose as the only remaining hope for parents whose children are addicted to crystal meth, cocaine, illicit alcohol, or other narcotics.

The Matrix Rehabilitation Centre, owned by Tafadzwa Chidawa, a politically connected former police officer who was acquitted in March last year of an unrelated US $20,000 fraud case, and Angel of Hope, a foundation headed by Zimbabweâs First Lady, Auxillia Mnangagwa, are the most prominent of these so-called ârehab colleges.â

They claim to offer free or subsidised programmes lasting between one and three months to transform young people battling addiction into productive members of society.

But Matrixâs pitch extends beyond rehabilitation. In videos and advertisements reviewed by Minority Africa, the centre presents its programmes as a pathway to opportunities after participants leave, including education and travel abroad. Posts promote opportunities in countries including India and the United Arab Emirates, while others document participants obtaining visas and travelling overseas to study.

In one video posted in August 2026, Matrix celebrated a young woman receiving a visa to study abroad, before later chronicling her journey to India. The posts present such departures as evidence of what can follow the centreâs disciplinary programme.

Matrix has made varying claims about the success of its rehabilitation programme. In separate posts on social media, the centre has claimed success rates of 92% and 97%. The posts do not explain how Matrix defines âsuccess,â the period over which participants are followed, or what data the figures are based on.

author: Diana Felix da Costa
title: What South Sudan’s mothers teach us about political authority
content:
South Sudan is approaching a critical moment in its

political transition

.

Elections are scheduled for December 2026

, while questions around

constitutional reform, political inclusion

 and the

faltering implementation

 of the

2018 peace agreement

continue to shape debate about the country’s future. As South Sudan considers what legitimate and accountable governance might look like, the experience of a group of mothers and grandmothers in its

eastern borderlands

 offers another place to look for political authority.


‘If you want to kill each other, you must kill us first.’


These were the words of a Murle grandmother describing the message that mothers and grandmothers carried into their communities across

Greater Pibor

 in 2017. Their sons and grandsons were caught in escalating cycles of violence between competing

youth age-sets

 — socially recognised generations of young men. The women responded by deploying not weapons, but

their voices and bodies

: through song, dance, public shaming and, ultimately, the threat of maternal nudity.


Years of conflict and militarisation

 have transformed relations between generations.

Cattle-raiding, revenge killings and child abductions have intensified

 and become increasingly brutal.

Chiefs and elders continue to play important roles

, but the scale and intensity of violence demanded new forms of collective action.


The women formed the

Kabarze

 — translated as ‘the virgins’ or ‘unmarried girls’

 — an evocative name for a movement composed largely of mothers and grandmothers. The name echoed songs and dances traditionally associated with young unmarried women, which the

Kabarze

 drew upon as they confronted violence. As one woman explained: ‘We formed the

Kabarze

 so our children would survive all this fighting. Boys weren’t listening to the old men […] so we formed our group. If they are to beat us, they’ll know we carried them for nine months and gave birth to them.’


Beginning organically in one locality, the movement spread across Greater Pibor as women in other villages established their own

Kabarze

 groups. Moving collectively between the homesteads of armed youth, they sang, danced and confronted those involved in fighting. Their songs identified those

responsible for violence, invited reconciliation and exposed responsibility to public scrutiny

. Their performances interrupted attacks, demanded cattle compensation and compelled young men to surrender weapons. When necessary, the women invoked the powerful moral force of

maternal nudity

, a practice that carried profound significance within Murle society, as in other

African contexts

.


The

Kabarze

drew their authority from motherhood, kinship, collective responsibility and cultural forms of intervention that young men and the wider community already recognised. Their story offers an important lesson about governance itself: where political authority comes from, how it is communicated, and what this could mean for the future of governance and peacebuilding in South Sudan.


Kabarze women performing in Manyirany Payam, Pibor, in October 2017, the year the movement first emerged. Photographs by Diana Felix da Costa.


Where does political authority come from?


South Sudan’s political future continues to be imagined through debates about

constitutional reform, elections, political inclusion and the implementation of peace agreements

. These remain central to both South Sudanese political debate and international engagement. Communities, however, experience governance through a

much broader and tangible landscape of authority.

 Across South Sudan

chiefs, elders, churches, spiritual authorities, kinship networks, clans and sections, age-set hierarchies, youth leaders and women’s collectives all shape social life

. Their legitimacy and influence stem from

long-standing social and spiritual relationships and shared understandings of responsibility, obligation and belonging.


For the

Kabarze

,

motherhood

 connected women to the young men engaged in violence. Acting collectively through shared repertoires of song and dance gave that relationship public and political force their sons and communities understood.


Song

 is central to how women communicate that authority. As one elder woman explained: ‘We women don’t have

rii

 and so to express what we have in mind, we sing.’

[3]


Rii

 are communal spaces

 where men gather to discuss public affairs. Through song …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Laws and Resurgent Cultural Claims: Rwanda’s Decency Policing Erodes Women’s Freedoms
content:
There’s been an online uproar after Rwandan National Police spokesperson ACP Rutikanga Boniface announced on public television that public indecency will be punished. On August 29, police officers threatened to beat young women attending a concert by Tanzanian singer Diamond Platnumz if they did not follow the new ‘decency’ orders.


In Rubavu, a town in the west of the country, a young woman was seen on video being apprehended by police over the length of her dress. Thereafter, several government workers using the X platform stated that it is important for Rwandan culture to be upheld and that the ‘Western ways’ used to sexualize women’s bodies through revealing clothing are corrupting the youth. These are not isolated incidents.


Women’s bodies and the rights of gender-expansive and marginalized people have increasingly become battlegrounds for Christian fundamentalist moralists and lobbyists.


Rwandan law does not clearly define indecency.

Article 143 of Law N° 68/2018 states: “Any person who performs an indecent act in public commits an offence.” Conviction can lead to imprisonment for six months to two years.

 In 2023, there were discussions about redefining indecency as “showing one’s private parts or performing sexual acts in public,” but this was not adopted. Ambiguity remains over what constitute

s a ‘private part,’ making enforcement unclear and subjective. This also opens the door to bias against women and girls, as body parts like shoulders or cleavage may be deemed indecent, similar to theocratic states treating exposed hair as indecent.


Social media is flooded with calls for clarity on the law, as its guidelines would be replicated at entrances to businesses, hotels, and restaurants. This demonstrates how legal ambiguity fuels public scrutiny and the policing of women and girls. Women are speaking up about how legal definitions of decency affect their lives. We cannot live in a world where a mere body can incriminate a person, or where enforcers arbitrarily decide what clothing is

 inappropriate

.


This debate is feeding into an already pervasive culture of gender-based violence whose victims are disproportionately women, girls and gender expansive people. Technology Facilitated Gender Based Violence (TFGBV), already common, is being fueled on TikTok and Instagram, where several young men and some journalists are justifying rape as the woman or girl’s fault due to what she is wearing.


On September 2, a young woman in Kibagabaga was harassed, beaten, undressed, and insulted by a group of men. The video has circulated on social media, but the perpetrators remain unpunished, and the girl’s fate is unknown. Now, online platforms—driven by manosphere communities and technocapitalists profiting from dehumanization—have become battlegrounds for controlling women’s public and private lives.


Mob violence and GBV have been normalized as of late, and public institutions have remained silent. Rwandan women and girls feel ignored, helpless, and abandoned.


The Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion, whose mandate is to champion gender equality, has in the past

 implicitly responded

to rising rates of teenage pregnancies by blaming parents and

mothers for failing to raise ‘decent’ girls

. Once again, the risk in this

rhetoric

is that women, girls, and gender-expansive people become blamed for such deeply rooted systems of inequality and oppression. Subjective matters such as manners, morals, hemline lengths, and even treating nudity as indecency are regressions rooted in colonial and religious control of African bodies.


Counting Women, Not Counting on Rights


All this is happening while women hold 64 percent of seats in parliament, yet they are not fighting against the resurgent social control of women’s bodies or the legal silences that enable it. Rwanda has had a parliamentary women’s majority for nearly two decades, yet this has not resulted in real change, as patriarchal control of women’s lives continues to resurface.


On August 7, 2022, police arrested 24-year-old Liliane Mugabekazi after a photo of her at a concert taken by a journalist circulated online. She was charged with public indecency under Article 143 and faced imprisonment. Prosecutors claimed her clothing “revealed her private parts”—her breasts. A Kicukiro Primary Court judge initially denied her bail. Mugabekazi pleaded not guilty, noting she did not take or share the photo and had passed venue security. She was later …

author: Mada Masr
title: Sheikh Zuwayed parents detained after protesting for right to education as school reconstruction stalls in North Sinai
content:
Four people are being held in remand following a series of arrests targeting parents who held a demonstration in the

Nakhlat

rural settlement to demand the reopening of the local school, as well as individuals who shared footage of the protest online, according to statements

published

 by the Sinai Foundation for Human Rights this week.


The arrests came after the

 Sheikh Zuwayed

 education administration filed a police report against a Nakhlat resident who posted the video of the demonstration online, the foundation said in a statement published Wednesday.


A senior official at the North Sinai education directorate confirmed to Mada Masr that the Sheikh Zuwayed administration had filed the report. 


During the protest, parents called on authorities to re-open the school in the Nakhlat area, which faced widespread destruction

over

 years of fighting under


Operation Sinai

,

a military-led campaign that sought to eradicate militant activity in the region.

 


Their calls came amid what tribal sources have previously described to Mada Masr as friction over the North Sinai governorate’s redevelopment plan following the end of the counter-terror campaign in 2022. 


The residents of Nakhlat organized a demonstration outside the school’s ruins, bringing their children with them. They called on the North Sinai governor, the education minister and officials from the North Sinai education directorate and Sheikh Zuwayed education administration to rebuild the school.


Residents posted a video of the demonstration on Facebook, which was later deleted. In it, one parent described the struggle that families have faced since returning to Nakhlat after the military campaign had ended. 


Since their return, the resident said, children have had to attend the

Qabr Emeir

 school, about 3 km away. 


“The [Nakhlat] school was destroyed during the [fighting] and has yet to be rebuilt,” the parent says in the footage, explaining that the community lacks access to school transportation. “There are no vehicles designated to take children to the Qabr Emeir school.”  


The road to the school also poses a danger to children due to the presence of stray dogs, and the lack of safe transportation has forced families to bear high costs to arrange student rides, he explains. 


The parent warns that children from Nakhlat could drop out of school because of the difficulty of reaching Qabr Emeir. He says residents have repeatedly contacted governorate officials and North Sinai’s representatives in Parliament, but “no one took action.” 


The residents then announced they would stop sending their children to the Qabr Emeir school and would stage a sit-in outside the ruins of the Nakhlat school until education officials and lawmakers address their demands to protect their children’s right to education.


In a

statement

 issued by the governorate on Sunday, North Sinai Education Ministry Undersecretary Hamza Radwan said the Nakhlat school was completely destroyed during operations against “terrorist elements” and that students were transferred to the Qabr Emeir school based on a 2016 decision as a result, calling it “the most suitable and safest place to provide educational services to our students.”


Radwan said bringing children near the Nakhlat school ruins was “inappropriate” and dangerous, urging residents not to approach sites that were subject to shelling or raids until they are fully cleared by the relevant security authorities.


Radwan added that the destroyed school is located within the planned Nakhlat urban development cluster, which the state “intends to establish.” 


The new cluster will include a 22-classroom school equipped with modern facilities, he said, stressing that “the state will not fall short in this regard.”


Construction would begin once a site for the new school is selected, the statement said. 


That same day, Radwan visited Qabr Emeir and met with students’ parents inside the village school,

according

to a statement by the education directorate.


The Sinai Foundation for Human Rights

said

 on Wednesday that a police force arrested eight residents during the meeting with Radwan

.

 


The senior official at the North Sinai education directorate told Mada Masr

he was unaware of the arrests.


Six were later released, but two appeared before the Supreme State Security Prosecution on Wednesday, which remanded them on charges of “misusing the internet,” according to the foundation.

author: Ngozi Nwosu-Juba
title: Who profits from ‘saving’ women?
content:
During a recent dialogue convened by Liberation Alliance Africa’s

Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence

, bringing together activists, writers, and independent researchers from across the continent, an important and thought-provoking conversation emerged. While participants acknowledged the significant contributions of civil society organizations, development agencies, and other actors in advancing efforts to end violence against women and girls, there was also a collective reflection on the ways in which this support is framed and delivered.

I was struck by how this discussion raised critical questions about funding priorities, whose interests are ultimately served, who benefits most from existing interventions, and whether the structures and language designed to address violence may, in some instances, inadvertently reproduce inequalities or overlook the needs and voices of those most affected. The conversation challenged me to think beyond the availability of resources and examine the political, economic, and institutional dynamics that shape responses to violence against women and girls across the continent.

In my early days in feminist activism, I often highlighted to funders how our interventions had shifted away from speaking on behalf of women to “giving them voice.” This was widely regarded as progressive, even transformative, evidence that we had moved beyond paternalistic approaches and were empowering women to speak for themselves. It became a powerful narrative, one that resonated strongly with donors and development agencies alike.

Yet, over time, this language began to lose its appeal, as I started to interrogate the assumptions that underpinned it. Were women truly without voices, or were their voices simply being ignored, dismissed, or rendered unintelligible within systems of power?

The notion of “giving voice” positioned organizations like ours as benevolent intermediaries bestowing agency on those presumed to lack it. In doing so, it risked obscuring the fact that women had always spoken, resisted, negotiated, and articulated their realities, often in ways that did not fit donor expectations or development frameworks.

What does it mean to “give” women a voice? And who has the authority to bestow something that women have always possessed?

There is a long history of women’s resistance and political agency in Africa. In Nigeria, the

Women’s War of 1929

 stands as a powerful reminder that women have never been silent. Thousands of women in eastern Nigeria organized, mobilized, challenged colonial authority, and articulated their demands with remarkable courage and clarity. Their actions were neither facilitated by development projects nor enabled by donor-funded interventions. They emerged from women’s own collective consciousness, an inherited legacy of women’s determination to resist injustice.

In the Bamenda Grassfields of Northwest Cameroon, women organized one of the most significant grassroots uprisings against colonial authority in Central and West Africa. Faced with colonial policies that threatened their farmland, the women of Kom fought back.

Using

Anlu

, a traditional practice where women collectively sanction men who violate community norms, they organized marches and used satire to name and shame colonial collaborators. Through their actions, they brought administrative and economic life in the region to a standstill for months, and their protest ultimately forced the colonial government to reverse the land policies and contributed to the broader political shifts that shaped Cameroon’s path toward independence and reunification.

In Eastern Africa, Queen Muhumuza led a movement against British and German colonialists from Southern Uganda. According to the historian

Murindwa Rutanga

, Queen Muhumuza was the first major leader to mobilize peasants in Kigezi into organized anticolonial resistance against British rule starting in 1909. Drawing on her political experience and spiritual authority, she raised consciousness about the dangers of colonialism and united a broad sector of the Bakiga and neighboring communities in armed resistance. Under her leadership, communities resisted colonial boundary demarcations, obstructed missionaries and colonial agents, and challenged the expansion of colonial authority despite violent repression. Her efforts established her as one of the …

author: Cierra Bettens
title: Looking deep into Canada’s opioid crisis: InFocus
content:
You usually find Karyn Pugliese chasing down politicians on Parliament Hill.


But for the past few months, she’s been digging into Canada’s opioid crisis.


This week on APTN News InFocus, Pugliese and associate producer Raven Brascoupe join me for a behind-the-scenes look at their ongoing investigation.


“You could explore this from the crime issue, like the gangs and the selling of drugs,” Pugliese said. “I wanted to explore it as a medical issue. Because of the stats, First Nations seem to be more vulnerable to opioid addiction–and we ask, why? It could be because of things that we know, like historic trauma from residential schools, the child welfare system; that could very well be true.


“But are there other things as well?”


After interning for APTN News in Ottawa, Brascoupe jumped on the opportunity to join the project.


“Coming on as a new journalist on such a big topic, I’m pretty grateful for it,” Brascoupe said. “[From] living with the lived experience to getting to research it and talk with Karyn every day about it, what we know, what we’re learning, has been really good.”


Over the past few months, the duo has connected with people across the country with firsthand addiction experience. They’ve been on the ground with frontline workers and on the phone with leaders to find out what is and isn’t working.


“What I’m hearing from frontline workers is that there are two values to safe supply. One is that it does save lives because you can watch and prevent an overdose right there,” Pugliese said. “Now, we have people in Ottawa walking down the streets, trying to find people who are using. They’re being chased out of the downtown area so it’s harder to find out where people are gathering.”


“Manitoba is doing quite an incredible job. I was talking to one chief from Manto Sipi Cree Nation, Chief Yellowback,” Brascoupe said. “They have FNSOs, First Nation Safety Officers. They set up checkpoints, and they check people who come in to make sure they’re not bringing illicit drugs or alcohol. And there’s a bylaw they worked on so they could implement these laws.”


Through their investigative reporting, Pugliese and Brascoupe hope to cut through the noise and start having real conversations about how to move forward.


“I don’t know that we’re going to come out of this and say there’s a solution. But I know there is a lot of debate about what path to take,” Pugliese said. “I wanted to better understand how to separate political arguments that are purely political and ideological from the health science.”


Have a story for this project? Reach out to Karyn at

kpugliese@aptn.ca

 or Raven at

rbrascoupe@aptn.ca

.

author: Brett Wilkins
title: Pentagon Is Undercounting US Death Toll Amid Iran War, Washington Post Reports
content:
The report raises questions regarding the military’s line-of-duty investigations following service member deaths.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Trump administration — which calls itself the “most transparent administration in history” — is once again under fire for its lack of transparency after The Washington Post on Friday published a report in which US officials said more American troops have died during the Iran War than the Pentagon has disclosed.

Five officials familiar with the Pentagon’s internal casualty accounting told the Post under condition of anonymity that at least 22 US service members have died since Trump launched the Iran War on February 28 — four more than the 18 fatalities currently listed in the Pentagon’s public Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS. A sixth official put the number at 23.

The officials said that not all of the additional deaths were necessarily caused directly by Iranian attacks, but rather involved US personnel stationed in the Middle East.

The Pentagon says 18 U.S. troops have died in Trump’s Iran war. But new reporting from six U.S. officials with direct access to the Pentagon’s casualty data, says the real number is higher. Five put the toll at at least 22, while one put it at 23. This isn’t the first time the Pentagon’s counting has come under scrutiny. Earlier this year, four fallen soldiers were reclassified off the official Iran war death toll and into “overseas operations” casualties, because they were killed during Trump’s short-lived ceasefire. When the government hides the true cost of its war, it misleads the country and dishonors the fallen. Retired US Army Brig. Gen. Steve Anderson asked some of those questions in a Friday Substack post directed at Hegseth and calling the reported obfuscation an “unforgivable sin”:

Why are you hiding from the American people and the media?

Why haven’t you done a press conference in the Pentagon for four months?

What were the families of the fallen told about the circumstances around the deaths of their loved ones? Were they denied recognition for their loved ones’ service and sacrifice in war?

Who made the call to hide the number from the American people?

How many more people have been wounded than we know about?

What are [you] going to do to make this right?

Responding on social media to the Post report, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote, “This is DISGUSTING and FAKE. A complete LIE.”

“Shame on The Washington Post — they’re worse than Iranian state media,” Hegseth added.

Hegseth’s denial follows earlier controversies over the Pentagon’s casualty reporting.

In July, the department’s public database briefly excluded four US service members killed during renewed fighting, even though the Pentagon had separately announced the deaths. Officials subsequently blamed the discrepancy on technical problems.

Also in July The New York Times revealed that the Pentagon hid dozens of US military injuries from Iranian strikes on bases in Jordan.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), a disabled Iraq War veteran, wrote on Bluesky in response to the Post report that “22 of our service members have been killed in Trump’s illegal war. Not 18 like we were told.”

“The Pentagon hid four more heroes’ deaths from us for months,” she added. “Congress cannot let them get away with this.”

content:

.


ᔭᓯ ᖃᙳᖅᒧᓪᓕ, ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒃᑎᐅᓂᖓ ᐃᓄᒃᑎᑑᖅᑐᓂ ᓈᓚᐅᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᐃᔾᔪᑎᒋᔭᖓ ᐊᑖᑕᖓᓗ ᓈᓚᐅᑎᓂ ᑐᓵᖃᑦᑕᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᒃᒥᑦ, ᑕᒪᕐᒥ ᑐᓵᔪᐃᓐᓇᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᓈᓚᐅᑎᒥ.


ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒃᑎᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐅᕙᓂ

ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᒃ

ᐅᕘᓇ CKCU 93.1 FM ᐅᕙᓂ ᑳᕐᑕᓐ ᓯᓚᑦᑐᖅᓴᕐᕕᐊᓗᒃᒥ ᐋᑐᕚᒥ ᑕᐃᒪᙵᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᑎᓪᓗᒍ 2019-ᒥ.


“ᖁᕕᐊᓇᕈᓘᔭᕐᓂᖓ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᒃᒦᓐᓂ ᓲᕐᓗ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖅᓯᒪᓐᓇᖅᑰᔨᔪᖅ, ᐊᑖᑕᓐᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᐃᓐᓇᖅᑐᖅ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 9-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ. “ᓈᓚᐅᑎᒥ ᑐᓵᓪᓗᓂ ᖁᕕᐊᓇᕐᓂᖓ ᑐᓴᕐᓴᐅᓐᓇᕐᒥᔪᖅ ᒫᓂᓘᓐᓂᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᕐᔪᐊᒥ. ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑐᐊᖅ ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᐃᓄᑭᑦᑐᓂᓪᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᑐᓵᔪᑑᖃᑦᑕᕆᐊᖃᙱᒻᒪᑕ, ᑖᓐᓇ ᐱᒃᑯᒋᖃᑦᑕᖅᑕᕋ.”


ᒫᓐᓇᓕ ᐅᓇ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᓕᕆᓂᖅ ᖃᙴᑉ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᖅᖢᓂᐅᒃ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᖅᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᑯ ᓄᑖᒥ ᐱᒋᐊᕐᕕᖃᕐᓂᐊᓕᕐᒪᑦ.


ᐃᓴᕈᐃᑦ ᓴᓇᐅᒐᓕᐅᖅᑎᑦ, ᖃᕋᓴᐅᔭᒃᑯᑦ ᓴᖅᑭᔮᒐᖓᒍᑦ ᐃᒪᓐᓇ ᐅᖃᕐᓯᒪᓪᓗᓂ, ᖁᕕᐊᓲᑎᖃᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓴᓇᐅᒐᓕᕆᔪᓐᓇᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᖅᓴᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᒃᑯᑦ, ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᓕᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᑕᖅᑭᐅᓵᖅᑐᒥᓐ

ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᒃᒥ

 ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᑐᙵᓱᕝᕕᖓᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦᑯᓐᓄᑦ, ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓕᐅᕋᓱᒐᑎ ᒪᓂᒻᒪᐃᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᔾᔪᑎᒃᓴᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓇᓱᖕᓂᕐᒥᑦ.


“ᐃᓴᕈᐃᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑕᐅᓕᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᐱᐅᒻᒪᕆᖕᓂᐊᖅᑐᖅ ᓲᖃᐃᒻᒪ ᐅᒃᐱᕈᓱᒻᒪᕆᖕᒪᑕ ᖃᐅᔨᒪᑎᑦᑎᔪᒪᓂᕐᒥ

ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᐅᑉ

ᑕᐅᑐᙳᐊᒐᖓᓂ ᒪᑯᓂᖓ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓂ ᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂ ᑐᓵᑎᑦᑎᕙᒡᓗᑎᒃ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᖃᙳᖅ, ᑖᓐᓇᑦᑕᐅᖅ ᑐᓴᐅᒪᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥ ᐅᖃᐅᔾᔪᐅᔨ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᖏᓐᓄᑦ. “ᖁᕕᐊᓱᑦᑎᐊᒻᒪᕆᒃᑐᖓ ᑖᓐᓇ ᓴᙱᒃᑎᑉᐹᓪᕈᓐᓇᕐᓂᐊᕋᑦᑎᒍᑦ.”


ᐅᓇ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᔪᖅ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ 2019-ᒥ ᐅᓇᐅᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ

ᓂᐱᕗᑦ,

 ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓈᓚᖃᑦᑕᖅᓚᐅᖅᑕᖓᑦ ᒪᓐᑐᕆᐊᒥ, ᐅᐸᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᖕᒪᑕ ᑐᙵᓱᕝᕕᖓᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᔾᔨᐸᓗᐊᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓯᖁᔨᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐋᑐᕚᒥ.


ᑖᒃᑯᐊ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐊᖏᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᖕᒪᑕ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓴᓇᑎᑦᑎᓕᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᖃᙳᖅᒥᓐ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒪᕐᕈᒃᑲᓐᓃᖕᓂ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒃᑎᒃᓴᓂ.


ᑐᙵᓱᕝᕕᖓᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᓯᒪᓚᐅᖅᑐᑦ

ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᒃᒥ

 ᐱᒋᐊᓕᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑕᒪᑐᒪᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒧᑦ ᑎᑭᖢᒍ. ᑭᓯᐊᓂᓕ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᖃᕈᓐᓇᐃᓪᓕᓚᐅᕐᒪᑕ ᑖᔅᓱᒥᖓ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐸᕗᓕ ᐃᓪᓚᐅᖅ, ᐃᓴᕈᐃᑦ ᓴᓇᐅᒐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨ ᖃᕋᓴᐅᔭᒃᑯᑦ ᑎᑎᕋᖅᖢᓂ ᓄᓇᑦᓯᐊᕐᒥ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓄᑦ.


ᐃᑲᔫᑎᒃᓴᖃᕈᓐᓃᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᖃᙳᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒃᑎᐅᖃᑎᖓ ᕗᕌᓐᑯ ᐳᓴᒥ ᐃᑲᔪᑐᐃᓐᓇᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᒃᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᓕᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᑖᓐᓇ ᑲᔪᓯᑎᑕᐅᓇᓱᒃᖢᓂ.


ᑐᙵᓱᒡᕕᖓᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐅᐸᒍᑎᓕᓚᐅᖅᑐᑦ ᐃᓴᕈᐃᑦᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᖁᔭᐅᖔᓕᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᕐᒥ ᑕᖅᑭᐅᓚᐅᖅᑐᒥ, ᐃᓪᓚᐅᖅ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


ᓄᓇᑦᓯᐊᕐᒥ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᑦ ᑐᙵᓱᒡᕕᖓᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᓇᓱᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᑭᓯᐊᓂᓕ ᑭᐅᔭᐅᓚᐅᙱᒻᒪᑕ.


ᐅᓇ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᒃ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᖃᕐᓂᐊᓕᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᓴᕈᐃᑦᑯᑦ ᐃᓕᖅᑯᓯᕐᒧᑦ ᐅᑎᕐᓂᖅ, ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᓪᓗᓂ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᕐᔪᐊᕐᓄᑦ ᓴᓇᐅᒐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ, ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᑦ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᐅᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ, ᐋᑐᕚ ᓄᓇᓕᐸᐅᔭᖓᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᑐᙵᕕᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ.


ᐃᓇᑐᖃᐃᑦ, ᓴᓇᐅᒐᓕᐅᖅᑎᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᓕᕆᔨᑦ ᐊᑭᓕᖅᓱᖅᑕᐅᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ, ᐃᓪᓚᐅᖅ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.


ᐃᓴᕈᐃᑦ ᓄᑖᓂᒃ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒃᑎᒃᓴᖅᑖᕋᓱᒃᑐᑦ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᖅᓴᖅᑎᑕᐅᓇᔭᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐅᕘᓇ CKCU-FM ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆᒥ. ᖃᙳᖅ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᓴᕈᐃᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖓ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑕᐅᕙᖕᓂᖓᓂ ᐱᐊᓐ ᐃᓪᓚᐅᖅᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓐᓇᕐᓄᑦ ᐅᖃᖅᑎᐅᕙᒃᑐᒧᑦ ᐊᓯᓇ ᑲᓐᓄᑕᖅᒧᑦ ᐃᓚᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᑐᙵᓱᒃᑎᑦᑎᔨᐅᖃᑕᐅᓗᑎᒃ.


“ᕿᓂᕋᑦᑕ ᑐᓴᖅᑎᑦᑎᖃᑦᑕᕈᒪᔪᒥ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐃᓕᖅᑯᓯᖏᓐᓂᒃ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑕᐅᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓗᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒋᐊᒃᓴᖅ ᑲᙳᓱᙱᑦᑐᓂᒃ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᖃᙳᖅ.


ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒡᕕᒃ

ᑐᓴᕐᓴᐅᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᖅ ᐱᖓᔪᐊᑕᒫᓐ 11:00-ᒥ ᐅᓪᓛᒃᑯᑦ 12:00 ᑎᑭᖢᒍ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᒃᐸᒃᖢᑎᒃ ᐃᓄᒃᑎᑐᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᖃᓪᓗᓈᑎᑐᑦ.

author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Indigenous volunteers are helping care for ‘rez dog’ relatives — with little funding
content:
June Thomas, with Ginew Animal Care Services on Roseau River Anishinabe First Nation, holds a puppy on her reserve in southern Manitoba.

Photo courtesy Ginew Animal Care Services/Facebook


As an animal lover, June Thomas grew increasingly concerned about the many stray dogs and cats roaming her community’s reserve in southern Manitoba — and decided to do something about them. 


What started as a home operation to better care for the animals in 2017, which she called “June’s Adoptables,” has since grown into a full animal shelter on Roseau River Anishinabe First Nation (RRAFN), nearly 100 kilometres south of Winnipeg. 


Thomas believes the shelter, which opened in February, is the first one on-reserve in the province.


“I started off in my own house rescuing animals like dogs and cats,” Thomas told IndigiNews. 


She was inspired to take action after her beloved dog Bessie became sick and died from canine parvovirus, a highly contagious

disease

 commonly known as parvo. 


Eventually, June’s Adoptables outgrew Thomas’s house — and she became incorporated as

Ginew Animal Care Services

.


“I took a veterinary assistant program,” said Thomas, who graduated in 2024 from Robertson College and is now certified to give vaccinations. 


“It gave me the skills and helped me want to set up a shelter.”


On reserves, “rez dogs” are beloved mixed-breed strays who roam communities without a single owner. 


However, rez dogs and other strays can carry diseases and become overpopulated because they lack veterinary care. 


And sometimes, they can create safety concerns if stray dogs become aggressive towards people — even in some cases fatally.


A volunteer holds a puppy on Roseau River Anishinabe First Nation.

Photo courtesy Ginew Animal Care Services/Facebook


After tragedy, calls for action


In July, Thomas joined other Manitoba pet rescue advocates at the provincial legislature to honour Amanda Nobiss, a 37-year-old Métis

volunteer

 with the Indigenous-founded group

K9 Advocacy Manitoba

.


Nobiss died after being mauled by a dog in

Sandy Bay Ojibway First Nation

. (An online

fundraiser

 in her memory has garnered more than $12,000).


The advocates called on the province to help prevent further tragic incidents, specifically advocating for veterinary and rescue funding to address the booming dog population in many First Nations communities.


“People think we don’t care for our animals, but we do,” Thomas said. “They just need that support and guidance on how to care for them.


“They think we have a lot of money, but we don’t; they don’t know the conditions on the reserves.”


READ MORE:


A syilx Youth’s fight to save her horses, and the thread that cannot burn


Alexandra Jarrett, a member of Canoe Lake Cree First Nation in Saskatchewan, is an advocate with

Save Rez Dogs

.


The organization advocates for the wellness and protection of dogs on reserves and educates from what it calls a “

sovereign

” First Nations perspective.


“Lack of being able to provide veterinary care doesn’t mean there’s a lack of love for the dog,” Jarrett said.


She said she’s seen outsiders come to First Nations with a “

saviour mentality

,” instead of compassion towards relatives who need support.


“It makes more sense to be compassionate towards people,” she added. “Instead of, ‘We rescued a dog,’ we are helping a relative who couldn’t support their animal.”


And rather than seeing First Nation members as not “competent enough” to care for domestic animals, Jarrett said her approach is to say, “They couldn’t at this time, so we are.”


Hundreds of animal advocates protest for provincial support for Indigenous-led on-reserve dog management outside the Manitoba legislature in July.

Photo by Crystal Greene


‘Stop the shame game’


Richard Herbert, a former veterinarian, agreed. He said stray dog issues are “a reflection of the lack of infrastructure in communities” compared to the rest of “Canada.”


As a visiting veterinarian, he saw connections between scarce access to veterinary care, and other areas, such as a chronic shortage of quality housing, minimal medical services resulting in poor health outcomes, no clean drinking water, and less access to affordable and healthy food.


The Assembly of First Nations (AFN) has kept tabs on a broader infrastructure problem impacting reserves across the country.

Closing the Infrastructure Gap

 last year, it concluded that First Nations …

author: Gary Chartier
title: Memetakan Libertarianisme Kiri: Sebuah Tinjauan Awal
content:
Oleh:

Gary Chartier

. Teks aslinya berjudul “

Framing Left Libertarianism: A First Pass

”. Diterjemahkan ke Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa.


Libertarianisme kiri (

left libertarianism

, selanjutnya LL) dapat dipandang sebagai sekadar upaya mengemas gagasan dan membangun propaganda. Namun, ia juga dapat dipahami sebagai ekspresi kuat dari berbagai persoalan yang semestinya menjadi inti dari gerakan-gerakan kebebasan.


Kaum libertarian maupun kelompok kiri yang sinis mungkin sama-sama melihat pembicaraan mengenai LL sebagai permainan retorika. Bisa jadi, mereka menganggapnya sebagai upaya untuk menjual gagasan-gagasan libertarian kepada orang-orang kiri naif yang tidak menyadari bahwa gagasan tersebut pada dasarnya bertentangan dengan agenda politik kiri. Atau sebaliknya, mungkin LL dipandang sebagai upaya mencangkokkan sesuatu yang asing ke dalam tubuh gerakan libertarian, membebaninya dengan berbagai persoalan yang dianggap tidak memiliki tempat dalam agenda libertarian yang sesungguhnya.


Kedua pandangan tersebut sama-sama tidak meyakinkan dan tidak menarik.


LL benar-benar libertarian karena ia

anti-negara

—para libertarian kiri yang langsung terlintas dalam pikiran saya semuanya adalah anarkis; dalam tulisan ini saya menganggap bahwa seorang libertarian kiri adalah seorang anarkis, atau setidaknya cukup dekat dengan anarkisme sehingga perbedaannya tidak relevan—dan karena ia mengakui nilai pasar serta hak kepemilikan. Pada saat yang sama, LL juga benar-benar berhaluan kiri karena berupaya menantang privilese, hierarki, eksklusi, deprivasi, dan dominasi, baik secara ideologis maupun praktis, serta dapat menunjukkan komitmen yang sungguh-sungguh terhadap inklusi, pemberdayaan, dan saling menghormati.


Dan semua itu dapat dilakukan bukan dengan mendefinisikan ulang berbagai istilah—misalnya dengan mengatakan bahwa kebebasan dari paksaan fisik adalah satu-satunya bentuk kebebasan yang benar-benar penting—melainkan dengan menunjukkan

keselarasan

 antara cita-cita dan prinsip libertarian dengan penerimaan yang sungguh-sungguh terhadap persoalan-persoalan utama yang menjadi perhatian gerakan kiri.


Hal itu dapat dilakukan dengan menunjukkan implikasi radikal dari prinsip-prinsip libertarian yang selama ini telah diterima secara luas.


• Misalnya, dapat ditunjukkan bahwa sejarah kekerasan dan kolusi dengan— atau bahkan dukungan terhadap— tirani yang dilakukan oleh individu dan organisasi yang memiliki kekuatan ekonomi telah merusak legitimasi hak kepemilikan yang mereka pegang, sekaligus memberikan dasar bagi

penguasaan melalui

homesteading

 atas apa yang mereka klaim sebagai properti oleh orang-orang yang hidup dan bekerja di atasnya

.


• Demikian pula, penerapan penuh prinsip-prinsip libertarian mengenai ketidakadilan dan dampak buruk monopoli serta subsidi kemungkinan besar akan melemahkan, dalam berbagai cara, kekuasaan organisasi bisnis yang hierarkis dan tersentralisasi. Hal itu juga dapat mempermudah penggantian banyak perusahaan tersebut dengan koperasi yang dikelola oleh pekerja, sekaligus secara drastis meningkatkan pengaruh pekerja dalam sebagian besar perusahaan lainnya.


• Prinsip-prinsip libertarian yang sama juga dapat digunakan untuk menolak bentuk privilese yang memungkinkan perusahaan, kelompok profesi, dan individu yang memiliki pengaruh menggunakan kekuasaan negara untuk mengeksploitasi orang lain. Misalnya, perusahaan yang memiliki koneksi politik dapat memperoleh keistimewaan perpajakan yang memberi mereka keuntungan non-pasar atas para pesaingnya. Demikian pula, kelompok profesi tertentu dapat merugikan masyarakat sekaligus calon pesaing dari kalangan miskin dengan mempertahankan kekayaan dan privilese melalui persyaratan lisensi yang mahal, yang diberlakukan atau dipertahankan atas tekanan mereka melalui negara.


• Dan prinsip yang sama yang mengutuk negara secara umum juga memberikan dasar yang kuat untuk menentang perang dan imperialisme secara khusus.


LL juga dapat menekankan sejauh mana

prinsip-prinsip moral yang sama

 yang mendorong penolakan terhadap kekuasaan negara yang menindas dapat menjadi alasan kuat untuk menantang berbagai ketimpangan sosial yang secara tepat telah menjadi perhatian banyak orang di kalangan kiri. Sejauh penolakan terhadap kekuasaan negara berakar pada teori moral tertentu, apa pun bentuknya, teori tersebut dapat digunakan untuk menghasilkan penilaian moral mengenai persoalan-persoalan di luar kekuasaan negara.
