author: rti_admin
title: AI for Humanity: A Buddhist Ethical Framework for the Age of Artificial Intelligence
content:
Artificial Intelligence is rapidly becoming one of the most transformative technologies in human history. In a remarkably short period, AI has moved from a specialised computational technology to a general-purpose tool capable of writing, designing, analysing, reasoning, generating images and video, assisting scientific research, and increasingly performing tasks once considered uniquely human.

This extraordinary development has produced two contrasting visions of the future. One imagines AI ushering in an age of unprecedented abundance, where machines perform much of the world’s intellectual and physical labour and humanity is liberated from scarcity. The other warns that increasingly autonomous and powerful AI systems could become difficult to control and, in an extreme scenario, pose an existential threat to humanity.

Both possibilities deserve serious consideration.

The crucial question, therefore, is not simply how intelligent AI can become, but what values will guide that intelligence.

Intelligence without wisdom can become dangerous. Power without character can become destructive. Knowledge without compassion can become indifferent to human suffering. And technological progress without concern for society’s welfare can increase inequality rather than reduce it.

This is where an ancient ethical tradition offers a remarkably relevant perspective.

The Buddhist concepts of Prajñā (wisdom), Śīla (ethical conduct or character), Karuṇā (compassion), and Bahujan Hitāya–Bahujan Sukhāya (for the welfare and happiness of the many) can provide a useful philosophical framework for thinking about the future of Artificial Intelligence.

Intelligence Is Not the Same as Wisdom

Modern AI is fundamentally an achievement of intelligence: the ability to process enormous quantities of information, recognise patterns, generate responses, optimise objectives and increasingly perform complex reasoning.

But intelligence and wisdom are not synonymous.

A system can be extraordinarily capable at achieving an objective while having no intrinsic understanding of whether that objective is morally desirable. An AI system may be able to determine the most efficient way of achieving a goal, but efficiency does not answer the question: Should that goal be pursued in the first place?

This distinction is central to the future of AI.

Human civilisation has repeatedly demonstrated that technological capability does not automatically produce moral progress. The same scientific knowledge that gives us medicine can also produce devastating weapons. The same communication technologies that connect billions of people can also facilitate manipulation and hatred.

Therefore, as AI becomes more powerful, humanity needs something beyond greater computational intelligence.

In the Buddhist intellectual tradition, Prajñā is associated with deeper understanding and discernment: the capacity to see reality clearly rather than merely accumulate information. Applied to AI governance, this suggests that every major AI decision should involve a fundamental question:

Is this action merely possible, or is it wise?

An AI system may be capable of doing something. A corporation may find it profitable. A government may find it strategically advantageous. But none of these facts establishes that it should be done.

Prajñā introduces the missing dimension of judgement.

Śīla: Intelligence Must Operate Within Ethical Boundaries

The second principle is Śīla, broadly understood as ethical conduct, discipline, and moral character.

One of the central challenges of advanced AI is that systems are increasingly capable of operating autonomously. They can make recommendations, execute tasks, interact with other systems, and potentially influence decisions affecting millions of people.

The greater the autonomy, the greater the importance of ethical constraints.

An AI system should not be designed merely to maximise whatever metric its creator specifies. A recommendation algorithm designed exclusively to maximise engagement, for example, may discover that outrage, addiction or sensationalism produces better engagement than balanced information.

The algorithm may be performing exactly as designed.

The problem is the design objective.

Śīla therefore suggests a deeper principle:

The means by which AI achieves its objectives must be subject to ethical constraints, not merely judged by the outcome.

AI systems should be designed around principles such as honesty …

author: ALR Editors
title: Announcing Asian Labour School Oct-Nov 2026 Semester
content:
Dear friends,


We are back with an amazing list of new and returning courses for the Asian Labour School. If you are interested in

acquiring democratic facilitation skills, navigating conflicts and taking collective care, working cooperatively, strengthening a union core or leading your own radical walking tours

, please check out the course information below and study with Asian Labour School.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Chie Matsumoto


We all have attended meetings where decisions were made by only a few members, most outspoken ones or someone at the top. We may have once thought, “Why am I even here?” and left without saying a word. Democracy starts in the smallest conversations, dialogues and meetings by raking in most diverse opinions and ideas, piecing them together to create something new and meaningful to all participants.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Facilitators: Emi Do and Matt Noyes


Worker cooperatives are enterprises that are owned and governed by workers. When all of our working experiences have been in profit-maximizing enterprises, or in workplaces that are structured hierarchically, it is no wonder that we can encounter challenges when attempting to work together cooperatively. In this course we will explore the challenges and tensions when there are no bosses to hate!


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Facilitator: Nash Tysmans


Movements are built through relationships. Yet the pressures of organizing (urgency, conflict, exhaustion, political disagreement, and unequal power) can strain those relationships and undermine our collective capacity. How can we build movements that are both effective in challenging injustice and caring in how we work together?


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Sithar Chhim


In order to win any campaign at workplace, unions need to be strong enough to pressure the company. Building a strong and representative committee is the only way to win over the bosses who have well organized structure at workplace compare to workers.


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)


Facilitator: Kevin Lin


Have you ever thought about leading your own radical walking tour to share with friends the significance of places and histories in your city? Leading and participating in a radical walking tour is not only educational but fun and always memorable. A walking tour provides a concrete sense of places, people, and histories. This course will walk you through the conceptualisation, research and logistics of a radical walking tour, and hear ideas and experiences from other participants across Asia.


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)

author: John David Parol
title: US bases noon, Pax Silica ngayon; kabataan, nagprotesta kontra panghihimasok ng US
content:
Nagsagawa ng kilos-protesta ang iba’t ibang grupo ng mga kabataang estudyante mula sa UP Manila patungong US Embassy upang gunitain ang makasaysayang desisyon ng Senado ng Pilipinas na tanggihan ang renewal ng US Military Bases Agreement (MBA) at ratipikasyon ng RP-U.S. Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation, and Security noong 1991.

Bitbit nila ang samu’t saring panawagan kabilang ang pagbasura sa Pax Silica, pagbuwag sa Luzon Economic Corridor, at pagpapalayas sa mga tropang Amerikano at kanilang mga base-militar sa bansa sa ilalim ng Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA).

Bagamat hindi nakalapit sa mismong tarangkahan ng embahada ang mga nagpoprotesta, ipinagpatuloy ng grupo ang kanilang maikling programa sa Kalaw Avenue sa Maynila.

Ayon sa mga nagprotesta, hindi hiwalay sa pang-araw-araw na kalagayan ng mamamayan at kabataan sa Metro Manila ang krisis dulot ng patuloy na pagyuko at pagsuko ng administrasyong Marcos Jr. ng soberanya sa malalaking dayuhan tulad ng US. Anila, sa halip na tunay na pambansang industriyalisasyon, nagpapatuloy ang banta sa likas-yaman at batayang serbisyo gaya ng kuryente at tubig na lalong magpapabigat sa gastusin ng ordinaryong pamilya.

“Ngayon pa lang, sobrang taas na ng singil sa kuryente. What more kung magkakaroon ng Pax Silica? Tayo ang magbabayad ng kuryente na ginagamit ng US,” diin ni Carla Espera mula sa Liga ng mga Kabataang Propagandista (LKP).

Kinakailangang mag-supply ng 3 Gigawatt (GW) na kuryente para gumana ang itatayong industrial at manufacturing hub sa ilalim ng Pax Silica Initiative. Katumbas ito ng 16% kabuuang current grid capacity ng Luzon. Ani Espera, hindi na nga natutugunan ng gobyerno ang pangangailangan at mas murang kuryente para sa mamamayan, may pangamba pang balikatin ng mamamayan ang posibleng kasalatan sa kuryente o mataas na singil sa kuryente kaugnay sa pagpapatayo at pagpapagana sa Pax Silica.

Bahagi rin sa isinusulong ng administrasyong Marcos Jr. ang nuclear energy at liquefied natural gas (LNG) upang tugunan ang lumalaking pangangailangan sa kuryente. Gayunman, ang pagpapalawak ng mga energy at industrial infrastructure ay may usapin din sa paggamit ng lupa. Sa ilalim ng Special Economic Zone Act o Republic Act No. 7916, maaaring ma-convert ang agricultural lands para sa ilang industrial at economic-zone developments, habang may mga probisyon para sa compensation sa mga residenteng maaaring ma-displace.

Pinalawig naman ni Zamann Milagrosa ng Kabataan Partylist (KPL) ang epekto ng Pax Silica sa New Clark City sa Tarlac, na siyang sentro ng proyektong digital sa ilalim ng Luzon Economic Corridor na nagdurugtong mula Subic, Clark, Maynila, hanggang Batangas.

“Hindi dahil malayo ang (Metro Manila) sa Tarlac, ay hindi na tayo maaapektuhan, kasi connected siya sa Luzon Economic Corridor. Papunta siya sa Pax Silica, marami tayong proyekto na patungo sa Pax Silica, may ginagawang highway na maapektuhan yung pagputol ng puno at malakihang pagputol ng puno, at yung mga tubigan natin na mawawalan tayo ng malinis na tubigan,” ani Milagrosa.

Noong 2024, naglatag ang National Economic and Development Authority ng 21 proyektong isinasaalang-alang sa pagtataguyod ng LEC. Aabot sa trilyong piso ang halaga ng mga proyektong ito. Lima sa mga ito ang may direktang koneksyon sa Metro Manila. Kabilang dito ang North-South Commuter Railway, Laguna Lakeshore Road Network, North Luzon East Expressway, Manila Bay–Pasig River–Laguna Lake Ferry System, at ang Subic-Clark-Manila-Batangas Railway.

“’Yong mga magsasaka natin mawawalan ng tirahan at papalayasin sila sa lupang ninuno nila. Imbes na ‘yung tubig na napupunta sa irigasyon—dahil magkakaroon pa tayo ng super El Niño, mawawalan sila ng malinis na tubig. ‘Yong kuryente na dapat napupunta sa mga taong bayan sa Gitnang Luzon, sobrang laki ang mapupunta sa Pax Silica. Tatlong gigawatts ang kukunin nila,” dagdag pa ni Milagrosa.

Bukod sa banta sa kabuhayan ng mga katutubo at magsasaka, iginiit ng mga nagpoprotesta na ang panghihimasok ng US sa bansa sa pamamagitan LEC, Pax Silica at iba pang mga hindi pantay na kasunduan ay tahasang naglalagay sa Pilipinas sa umiigting na girian ng mga makapangyarihang bansa, partikular ang US at Tsina sa rehiyon.

“Gagamitin ang Pax Silica bilang pagawaan ng materyales pandigmaan. Ibig sabihin, gagamitin tayo bilang base ng US para madali na silang makapag-atake ng karatig-bansa na umaatake sa kanila. Kumbaga, gagawin tayong base for war dahil nandito sa atin ang siyam na …

title: Sleeper-Cell Report July 2026 – Global Coalition reports 0 confirmed ISIS attacks
content:
An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in al-Zubari, eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside


 


Key Points


– Six sleeper-cell attacks recorded by RIC, but the Global Coalition claims 0 attacks were officially claimed by ISIS


– One military personnel was killed, and a further five injured


– A minimum of seven alleged ISIS members were arrested


– A total of 36 civilians were injured, two killed


– An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in Deir ez-Zor


–

Two Tunisian families linked to ISIS mercenaries repatriated from Roj camp


 


In-Depth


In July of 2026, RIC

recorded six sleeper-cell attacks which some publications have attributed to ISIS, according to


North Press Agency

 one of these attacks was claimed by ISIS whereas the


Global Coalition


reported that July was the first month since the territorial defeat of ISIS in 2019, where they claimed 0 attacks. Also this month at least 7 members of ISIS cells were arrested.


On July 7, Bombings struck central Damascus near the Ministry of Tourism and the Four Seasons Hotel, during the visit of Macron the president of France to Syria. Ministry of Interior has attributed the attack to ISIS, the bombing resulted in the killing of one civilian and injury of 36.


On July 8, three attacks happened during the same day and the are believed to have been carried out by ISIS members.

Unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle used machine guns to target an oil truck in Abrahyah town in eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside, killing the driver.


Similarly, unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle, attacked a checkpoint of the Internal Security Forces near al-Baserah city bridge.


According to North Press Agency, also on July 8 ISIS

claimed responsibility for the killing of Rashad Khalaf al-Ghurair in the northern countryside of Deir ez-Zor.


On July 15,

unknown gunmen on a motorcycle opened fire on a member of the 72nd Division on the road linking al-Arimah and Manbij in eastern Aleppo countryside, injuring the him.


On July 18,

two unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle opened fire directly on member of the Defence Ministry


near al-Awsajli junction in eastern Manbij city.


On July 9,

Syria’s Interior Ministry announced its security forces had dismantled several ISIS cells in southern Syria, arresting a senior leader and several members accused of involvement in assassinations and financing terror.


On July 28,

Syrian Internal Security Forces and the General Intelligence Service in Aleppo announced the arrest of individuals allegedly affiliated with the ISIS, during a security operation in Aleppo and its surrounding countryside.


An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in al-Zubari, eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside, in an incident that sparked widespread concern among residents.


During July, Two Tunisian families linked to ISIS were repatriated from


Roj Camp, which houses families of ISIS members, and returned to Tunisia. Additionally, Tunisian citizen Bilal Chawachi was sentenced to 55 years in prison after being convicted on terrorism-related charges, specifically traveling to Syria and fighting alongside the extremist organization.


Germany sentenced an Iraqi man to life imprisonment and his former wife to nine years and six months in prison after convicting them of enslaving and torturing two Yazidi girls while they were members of ISIS in Syria and Iraq between 2015 and 2017.


Three U.S. citizens pleaded guilty to terror charges, prosecutors said the defendants communicated through encrypted messaging applications between July and November 2025 and planned to travel to Turkey before crossing into Syria to join ISIS. 


* Due to the low rate of confirmed ISIS attacks RIC has decided to stop publishing monthly sleeper-cell reports and instead share a bi-annual summary of ISIS activity throughout Syria.

author: Jeremy Ray Jewell
title: A Singapore Contract, Beijing’s Red Lines
content:
APPLY TO TEACH for Polly English and, before entering a classroom, the platform presents a screen titled “Sensitive Content Compliance Agreement.” Under “DO NOT Talk about,” it prohibits discussion of “Political issues, including Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macao, Xizang (Tibet), and Xinjiang.”

The next section is harder to dismiss as ordinary classroom etiquette. Under “Consequences of Violation,” the screen lists “Immediate termination of my Service Agreement,” “Potential legal action,” and “Responsibility for any resulting damages.” It does not say what kind of legal action, which damages might qualify, or how far those consequences reach. A teacher working outside the PRC is asked to accept an open-ended legal and financial warning for discussing some of Beijing’s most sensitive political questions.

Nothing on that screen is presented as PRC law. Polly English describes itself as an online English teaching company based in Singapore, and its teacher terms name Little Moon Pte. Ltd. as the contracting party and place the agreement under Singapore law and Singapore courts. That makes the arrangement more revealing, not less: recognizable PRC political red lines appear inside a private contract governed somewhere else.

The ambiguity lands in a context in which Beijing has increasingly asserted that politically defined conduct can be punished even when the accused is outside territory under its effective control. In June 2024, five PRC authorities issued guidelines allowing trials in absentia for alleged separatist offenses related to Taiwan independence. In 2026, Article 63 of the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress turned to organizations and individuals outside the PRC. They may be held legally liable for acts against the PRC that are deemed to undermine ethnic unity and progress or to create ethnic division. Amnesty International calls its core prohibitions broad and undefined; the European Parliament reads its extraterritorial reach as allowing prosecution abroad.

There is no publicly available evidence that Polly is enforcing those laws, or that any Chinese authority instructed the company to write this agreement. The mechanism is what matters. A platform can absorb political pressure originating in one market, convert it into a private contractual rule, and place the risk on workers in another jurisdiction. This is not only a story about Beijing’s reach, but about how platform work is built: nominal independence for the worker, centralized rule-making for the company. Political restrictions are the conspicuous cargo. The machinery that carries them already governs labor, and it does not stop at borders. That makes what Nick Srnicek and others have called “platform capitalism” more than a labor question. It is a question of political sovereignty.

Polly recruits English-speaking teachers, largely from North America and the Philippines, for one-to-one classes. Its recruitment portal runs on a Chinese country-code domain, and the apps are distributed through app stores in the PRC. The consumer site is in Simplified Chinese, selling lessons with American and Canadian schoolteachers to parents who sign a course subscription agreement on the same domain.

Plenty of employers tell staff to keep politics out of the classroom, and in a service for children that would be unremarkable. But Polly’s list names five specific places, and those five are the territorial, sovereignty and ethnic-political questions Beijing treats as core red lines. Four turned up in the 2018 Marriott episode, when a customer survey listing Tibet, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan as countries prompted Shanghai’s cyberspace regulator to order Marriott’s Chinese website and app shut for a week, the same year the civil aviation regulator instructed 44 foreign airlines to relabel Taiwan.

One of those names is written “Xizang (Tibet).” Since a State Council white paper in November 2023, PRC state media have systematically substituted “Xizang” for “Tibet” in English, a shift Tibetan groups read as displacing an internationally established name. Terminology alone proves nothing about who drafted the clause, but the ordering is worth noticing: the PRC’s preferred term leads, the internationally recognized one trails in brackets. A company that presents itself to recruits as Singapore-based has adopted Beijing’s sequence.

Corporate self-censorship to preserve Chinese market access is old news: a boycott, an apology, a firing. Roy Jones, the Marriott …

author: Unknown
title: "From Jina to Today: Jin Jiyan Azadî" event held in London
content:
Organized by the Jiyan Women’s Assembly under the slogan "From Jina to Today: Jin Jiyan Azadî," a memorial took place at the London Kurdish Community Centre. The gathering paid tribute to Jina Amini and all women who lost their lives, and discussed the historical legacy of the Jin, Jiyan, Azadî struggle as well as the current state of the women’s freedom struggle.


YPJ spokesperson Rûksen Mihemed participated in the event online, while KJAR activist Zeyneb Bayazîdî and Civil and Women’s Rights Activist Sadiye Wekîlî spoke at the venue.


Many years of women's struggle have gone by


Rûksen Mihemed emphasized that the women’s freedom struggle cannot be viewed as a four-year process that began after Jina Amini. “This is not a struggle that has lasted only four years; women’s struggle goes back many years,” Rûksen Mihemed said, noting that through years of organizing and struggle, women have increasingly asserted their own identities and agency.


Mihemed stressed the importance of women existing through their own words, will and identities, and added: “Our language, our thoughts, our spirit, our bodies and our emotions belong to us.” She stated that the gains achieved must be protected and called for stronger solidarity and collective struggle among women.


Executions cannot eliminate the demand for freedom 


Sadiye Wekîlî drew attention to executions, prisons and the situation of political prisoners in Iran. Recalling that the Iranian government is attempting to suppress social dissent through executions and policies of repression, Sadiye Wekîlî said that it cannot silence the people’s struggle through executions, imprisonment and torture.


Referring to Shirin Alam Hooli and Zeinab Jalalian, as well as Pakshan Azizi and Warisha Muradi, Sadiye Wekîlî said, “Executions, prisons, torture and repression cannot eliminate the people’s demand for freedom.”


Zeyneb Bayazîdî also emphasized that the slogan Jin, Jiyan, Azadî did not emerge with Jina Amini. “The slogan Jin, Jiyan, Azadî already existed in Kurdistan,” she said, adding that following Jina Amini’s killing, tens of thousands of people chanted the slogan together at her funeral and that it subsequently became a shared expression of a broader social movement.


Zeyneb Bayazîdî said Amini’s death should not be viewed solely through the issue of compulsory veiling, and added: “The main issue is the control of women. It is also about controlling society through the control of women.”


Final declaration 


At the end of the event, the women in attendance came together on stage and joined in reading the Jiyan Women’s Assembly Declaration. The declaration emphasized that women are the founding subjects of a free life, peace and a democratic society. It called for an end to state and male violence against women, an end to torture and political repression, guarantees for women’s rights to organize and express themselves, the freedom of women political prisoners, and an end to executions.


The Jiyan Women’s Assembly announced that the demands set out in the declaration would be conveyed to international women’s and human rights organizations, particularly Amnesty International.


The gathering concluded with the women collectively chanting “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî,” accompanied by ululations and erbane drums.

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Lance Selfa
title: Away from the cameras, Trump’s mass deportation campaign grinds on
content:
In the opening days of 2026, the Trump administration’s mass deportation operation faced a crisis, thanks to the brave resistance of ordinary people in Minnesota’s Twin Cities area. After Trump’s armed thugs murdered Renée Goode and Alex Pretti in broad daylight, when hundreds of cell phone videos refuted the Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s bald-faced slanders of the dead, the administration reset.

Trump fired Noem and cashiered Greg Bovino, a white supremacist Customs and Border Protection commander. Both Noem and Bovino had revelled in displays of immigration cops’ brutality and degradation of immigrants caught in their dragnets. They brought camera crews with them to create “content” of the terror campaign against immigrants for MAGA-aligned media.

Trump put “border czar” Tom Homan in charge of operations in Minnesota and then appointed Senator Markwayne Mullin to take over for Noem. These two dullards are no less committed to Trump’s anti-immigration agenda than were Noem and Bovino. But they have the good sense to keep themselves out of the limelight.

Trump suffered a political defeat in Minnesota. But in the months since, the mass deportation campaign has ground on. In fact, it may be achieving its aims more successfully while minimising social media images of armed goons terrorising neighbourhoods.

Let’s take note of the sheer breadth of the deportation machine. According to the latest figures the 

Vera Institute of Justice

 compiled (current as of August 2026), Immigration and Customs Enforcement detains around 70,000 people per day in more than 1,400 facilities across the US and its territories. Detentions peaked in January (73,000 per day), fell sharply to about 55,000 in mid-May, and climbed again to 68,000 per day by early August.

These patterns suggest the Department of Homeland Security pulled back from the high-profile mass raids that hit a wall of opposition in Minnesota. But that step back looks like a temporary regrouping of forces before ramping up arrests again. DHS is on pace to “remove” (aka deport) about 460,000 people this year, according to 

Open Immigration

, a database of US immigration court records.

These numbers also reflect Congress opening the floodgates of money earmarked for immigration roundups and creating a gulag archipelago of “detention centres” (perhaps more accurately described as concentration camps). The enormous budget passed in 2025, authorising $170 billion for immigration enforcement over most of Trump’s term, represents a five-fold increase in ICE’s and CBP’s pre-Trump budgets.

In June, Republicans used “budget reconciliation”, a legislative tactic that lets Congress pass budget-related bills by simple majority (end-running the Senate filibuster), to add another $70 billion to ICE and CBP through the end of Trump’s term.

One of the most effective uses of these vast sums is to recruit local law enforcement agencies as deputies in the mass deportation machine. Homeland Security’s “287(g)” program, created by Democratic President Bill Clinton’s administration in 1996, helps law enforcement agencies that sign up to collaborate with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and CBP.

To DHS, agreements with locals are a “force multiplier” because immigrants who might have an encounter with a cop over a trivial traffic violation might quickly find themselves being turned over to ICE. The symbiotic relationship between the Feds and the locals is clear. Police agencies receive millions in federal assistance, and the Feds receive bodies to feed into the deportation maw—without facing the political blowback that armed goons snatching people off the streets generates.

In January 2025, at the beginning of the Trump administration, 139 local agencies, representing areas covering about 15 million people, had 287(g) agreements with the Feds. In September 2026, that number has ballooned to 2,054 agencies covering 56 million people (or one-sixth of the US population), according 

to 287(g) Watch.

DHS agreements with local law enforcement extend to contracts turning city and county jails into immigration jails.

“As of August 5, ICE has detained 104,800 people across 303 jails in 2026. Compared to the same period in 2024 under the Biden administration, this reflects an 84 percent increase in the number of local jails used for ICE detention and triple the number of people held by ICE in local jails”, the 

Vera Institute reported

author: AWSM
title: Errico Malatesta – Vote? What For?
content:
George: This beer’s not too bad, is it?

Jack: Yes, it’s alright, but what a price!

George: Shocking – especially when you remember what things used to cost. Still, you can’t wonder with all these taxes. It costs you twice as much to live as it used to. They put up the price of some things, and say you can do without them. But you can’t do without bread, and food, and clothes – you have to pay the rent all the same, and then there are the taxes on this and the rates – on our wages too! What a life! And it’s our own fault! If we wanted to we could alter things. The working class has the remedy in its own hands.

George: Easy enough! You’ve got a vote?

Jack: What’s that got to do with it?

George: Have you, or haven’t you?

Jack: Well, I’m entitled to a vote – but I never make use of it.

George: There you are! You’ve got a vote, but you just won’t take the trouble to use it, and then you wonder why things are so bad. You deserve all you get, honestly! People like you are responsible for all the trouble in the world!

Jack: Alright, alright, keep your hair on! Just tell me what’s the good of voting?

George: It’s obvious. Who makes the laws? The M.P.’s. Elect good M.P.’s and you get good laws.

Jack: Good councillors and good M.P.’s? We’ve heard that for a long time. But you’d have to be deaf, dumb, and blind not to notice it’s the same stooges that always get in. Oh, it’s wonderful to hear them when they’re after votes at election time. They pat you on the back, ask after the wife and kids, kiss the baby, promise you railways, bridges, work, cheap bread, less taxes, higher wages, protection – absolutely everything! And once they get in, they’re no better than anyone else. Goodbye promises! The wife and kids may starve, there’s no more or less work than before, the whole town can be falling to pieces for all they care. They’ve other things to think about than your troubles! Then a few years later they start the ballyhoo again. It doesn’t matter what colour the party is: they’re all the same. As soon as they’re elected, they forget all about you. They’re in their clubs and at their select dinners, and they don’t even trouble to come and have a look at you until the next election.

George: That’s correct! But why elect the rich? Don’t you know that the rich only live on the work of the masses? So how do you expect them to worry about the masses? All they think of is getting as much out of the ordinary man as they can.

Jack: Now you’re talking! But it’s not only the rich. There’s the other type, who want to get elected so they can become rich.

George: That’s true. So don’t let’s vote for them. Let’s elect workers, experienced friends of ours, as you might say, and then we won’t be fooled.

Jack: Oh, we’ve got some of your “experienced friends” in now, and they’re no different from our acknowledged enemies! Anyhow, what do you mean, “let’s elect – let’s elect.” As if we – you and me – could do as we like!

George: But it’s not only us two. If each one of us tried to convert other people and they would do the same, labour would have a majority, and we could elect whoever we liked. And that’s when we could form a government of the workers, and then . . .

Jack: And then it would be a paradise – I mean for those who were in Parliament! You’re arranging things a bit too quickly! Those in command always have the majority. The rich are always in power. Just imagine a poor worker, perhaps with an ill wife and four hungry kids, and you tell him to risk his job and get thrown out of his house to starve; just to give his vote to a candidate his master doesn’t like. Just try and convince those poor devils who can be thrown out of work by their boss whenever he likes. They’re never free; if they want to be free, they don’t want to waste their time voting – just take what they need.

George: But if we didn’t do that, no-one would vote. We couldn’t go to the workers and ask them to vote for our party, and say at the same time that votes were useless.

Jack: That’s just it! And on top of that you have to make election promises you know you can’t keep. And then you have to stand in with the Government, and mix with the well-to-do, and all the rest of it. As soon as any of your men are elected they have to kow-tow to the people you admit are the opponents of the workers. So why the hell talk about propaganda when the first thing you do is to counteract propaganda?

George: But you must admit, it’s an advantage to have our own men with …

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Ed Sheeran is a spineless twat
content:
“I just have a little message for you: there are two kinds of people in this world, Ed. There’re people who do the right thing—the rapper Macklemore would be one of those people. And there’re people—many of them, sadly little f ... excuse me, I nearly used the F-word then ... pricks—like you who do the wrong thing!”

So said Roger Waters, former Pink Floyd frontman and long-term supporter of the Palestinian people, via social media to singer Ed Sheeran, who has just committed a generational flop.

Bowing to the pressure of billionaires in a bid to stay “neutral”, Sheeran recently dropped rapper Macklemore from his

Loop

 tour due to Macklemore’s pro-Palestine stance. In solidarity with Macklemore, all of the supporting artists, including Ed’s own band, dropped out of the tour.

The controversy began when billionaire New England Patriots stadium owner Robert Kraft phoned Sheeran with a clear demand: Macklemore would be removed from the show, or the show would not go on.

Macklemore drew the ire of Kraft after declaring his support for Palestine and performing his song “Hind’s Hall” at a concert at MetLife Stadium. “Hind’s Hall” was written when the campus encampments in solidarity with Gaza were at their height in the US. It is a tribute to 5-year-old Hind Rajab, who was killed along with five family members and two paramedics by the Israeli military in January 2024 while fleeing Gaza City. Hind survived an initial attack on the family’s car, after which she spent hours on the phone to the Red Crescent, begging for help. Her body, and the remains of the paramedics sent to rescue her, were found weeks later, along with the car the family had been travelling in, which had been shot at more than 300 times.

With the words “Free Palestine” emblazoned behind him, Macklemore told the MetLife audience:

“The truth is, a big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I can stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine. I want those words to be loud and clear so the people all the way in Gaza, to the occupied West Bank, know that we have not forgotten about them.”

After the performance, singer P!NK criticised Macklemore on social media, reposting a meme that attacked the rapper for his pro-Palestine stance. In response, a group of stadium owners banded together to cancel Macklemore. Their ownership of stadiums across the US gave them a power that most of us don’t have—to decide who gets to say what and where.

Macklemore has used his music to highlight questions of oppression for decades. His 2012 hit “Same Love” was a declaration of support for marriage equality when same-sex marriage was banned in most of the world, including the United States and Australia. During the marriage-equality plebiscite in Australia, Macklemore performed at the NRL grand final, in what was seen as an implicit endorsement of equality. Macklemore has also been openly proclaiming his support for Gaza and the Palestinian people throughout the last three years of Israeli genocide.

In the last few years, many artists have been attacked for their support for Palestine. Irish rap group Kneecap were dragged through the courts on trumped-up terrorism-related charges due to their support for Palestine. The rap duo Bob Vylan was attacked by the media and cancelled from tours, and had their US visas cancelled, for chanting “Death to the IDF” at the Glastonbury festival.

As with Kneecap and Bob Vylan, Macklemore’s stance has drawn support from other decent musicians and celebrities who also oppose genocide. Finneas, the brother of Billie Elish, was also an act on the

Loop

 tour and pulled out in solidarity. His post declaring “Artists must not be silenced when they speak for the oppressed ... I stand with Palestine and its people” has more than 2 million likes on Instagram. Sheeran, on the other hand, has been left without support acts, without a backing band, and with just one ageing billionaire stadium-owner willing to associate with him. And Boy George.

Sheeran has also been exposed as having no spine and limited brains. The singer’s pathetic post responding to the controversy emphasised his desire to be “apolitical” and his concern not to corrupt the youth: “There is a reason I don’t use my professional platform for politics—my audience includes young people”. Someone should tell Sheeran that young people are affected by politics, particularly Palestinian …

author: Susan Price
title: ‘Ecological crisis creates a challenge and an opportunity for the left’
content:
Ayesha Ahmad, a Pakistani socialist-feminist activist, researcher, educator, and labour rights practitioner with the Haqooq-e-Khalq Party, was one of the guest speakers at the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, September 11–13. She spoke to Green Left’s Peter Boyle about the impact of the mounting global ecological crisis on politics in Pakistan.

The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal as a result of global warming and the melting of the Himalayan glaciers were a warning to the world, but does it have a special significance for Pakistan, which also borders the Himalayas?

The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal are a profound warning for Pakistan. For years, Pakistan has been among the countries most exposed to the climate crisis in South Asia, and we have already witnessed what a warming Himalaya can do — from the catastrophic 2022 floods, to increasingly frequent glacial lake outburst floods in Gilgit-Baltistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The Nepal disaster tells us that we may be entering an even more dangerous phase of the Himalayan climate crisis.

But for me, there is a much deeper question here. South Asia shares a history. We share the history of colonial extraction, of loot and plunder, of resources being taken from our lands to build wealth elsewhere. Political decolonisation did not necessarily mean economic decolonisation. The geography of extraction has changed, the language has changed, but the underlying relationship can remain remarkably familiar.

Today, we are being told that the answer is development, investment, critical minerals, energy security and even the green transition. But we have to ask: whose development, whose energy security and whose transition?

Climate change cannot be reduced to mining alone. But it would be deeply irresponsible to pursue accelerated extraction in an already climate-vulnerable Himalayan region without asking what extraction does to fragile ecosystems, watersheds, communities and the cumulative resilience of the region.

And this is where the history of colonialism matters. We cannot keep repeating the old colonial bargain under a new vocabulary: our mountains provide the minerals, our communities bear the ecological and social costs and the value is extracted into global markets elsewhere.

If the Global North needs minerals for its energy transition, then the question must be: Who owns them? Who decides? Who benefits? Who bears the environmental costs? And what happens to the people and ecosystems from which these resources are extracted?

We cannot continue with an economic model that treats our mountains, minerals, rivers and land as commodities.

We cannot call it a green transition if the transition is built on another round of extraction from the Global South. We cannot decolonise our politics while continuing to colonise our resources. And we cannot keep asking the people of Pakistan to pay the climate price for a development model from which they receive so little of the wealth.

For Pakistan, the lesson from Nepal is therefore not simply to prepare better for floods.

If extraction continues without ecological limits, democratic control and justice — and if the old unequal relationship between the Global North and resource-rich countries of the Global South continues under the language of “green development” — then the next disaster will not be a surprise. It will be a consequence of choices we already made.

Many years ago, we took part in an international campaign for the release of Baba Jan from Gilgit-Baltistan, who was dubbed the “first climate justice political prisoner”. How does the mounting ecological crisis impact repression and human rights?

The struggle is not only about environmental protection, but about who has the right to speak, whose land is protected, whose losses are recognised, and whether climate-affected communities are allowed to demand justice.

For me, the story of Baba Jan is one of the clearest examples of what climate politics looks like in Pakistan when it becomes a question of justice, rather than simply a question of climate change. And this tells us something very important about the space available to the left in Pakistan.

We are allowed to talk about climate change. We are allowed to talk about floods, melting glaciers, carbon emissions and resilience. But when we start talking about climate justice — about land, ownership, displacement, workers’ rights, resource extraction, reparations and who is …

author: Connor Knight
title: Anti-Hanson students strike again
content:
The second high-school student strike against Pauline Hanson in as many months took place on 17 September, with thousands of students across the country downing pens and taking to the streets, defying principals and politicians alike.

More than 3,000 marched in Melbourne, while 1,000 took to the streets in each of Sydney, Adelaide and Perth. Hundreds rallied in Brisbane, Canberra and Hobart, and more walkouts occurred in regional areas than during the previous national day of action.

The chants this time were the same but carried more urgency, given Labor’s plans to restrict immigration. They included “Migrants are welcome, racists are not!” and “Unite, unite, unite to fight the right!” The mood was irreverent. Right-wing provocateurs were taunted, and in Brisbane, protesters climbed on urban art sculptures and rode skateboards with red flags in hand. In Melbourne, far-right troll Avi Yemeni was surrounded by chanting students, against whom his bodyguards weren’t much use.

The right-wing media response to the first walkout was as patronising as it was sensational. An

Adelaide Now

headline is typical: “Teen anti-Hanson rallies: are students really thinking for themselves?” Hanson herself was furious, accusing students of “hating this country”.

The wonderfully impertinent attitude of students in light of these insults and accusations was well captured by high-school socialist Odessa, who told the Melbourne rally: “When the planet is burning, when we’re watching our world turn to dust ... They don’t get to tell us a single goddamn thing”.

The

Australian

reported that, in Sydney, “An organiser gave the crowd a moment to say how they felt about Senator Hanson after the protesters circled back to Hyde Park. Some could be heard shouting a number of profanities before dispersing”.

A striking feature of the protests was how many of the participants connected the rise of the right with capitalism. Signs and speakers consistently linked Hanson’s racist agenda to the interests of the billionaires and corporations who dominate politics and the economy.

“She is a battler for the bosses and the rich”, Queensland University of Technology student Sharon Binu argued from the platform in Brisbane. In Perth, year 10 student Esu put it this way: “When we look at the world today, who but those who grow fat off the misery of the many could doubt we need a total transformation of society?”

That total transformation will not be easy. But the high schoolers are at least giving it a shot, and showing up all those who choose to capitulate to, rather than resist, One Nation’s rise.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Students walk out of class again to protest Hanson’s racism and bigotry
content:
Thousands of high school and university students again walked out of class a second time to protest Pauline Hanson’s racism and bigotry on September 17. Rallies were held in 18 cities and towns across the country.

Students highlighted Hanson’s racist comments towards First Nations people and immigrants, her anti-LGBTIQ stance, her claim that domestic violence is a “two-way street” and her denial of the climate crisis.

Many pointed out that Hanson’s claim to be representing “ordinary Australians” is shown to be a lie because she is backed by Gina Rinehart, Australia’s richest person, and has consistently voted against pay rises and improved workers’ rights.

Students at the rally in Gadigal Country/Sydney told Green Left they did not support the vision for the country that Hanson is putting forward. “We’re the next generation of voters and we don’t want to see people like Pauline Hanson and One Nation who spread bigotry and hate in power,” one student said.

A year-12 student told Green Left he attended the protest to oppose Hanson’s racist rhetoric, and its adoption by Labor and the Coalition. “I’m here to stand in solidarity with women, immigrants, Palestinians, Indigenous people and queer people.”

Another student said they want politicians who are “for the people and not for billionaires”. “My mum is a person of colour and we don’t want someone who’s going to be racist.”

Atlas, an 18-year-old, said he came to the rally “because I am queer and people who I care about are in danger”.

Another told GL: “It’s hard to think that we could grow up in a future where someone like that could be deciding what happens in Australia. I think Pauline Hanson stands for racism, and I hate racism!”

Layla, from Newtown High, said she joined the rally to “stand against a monocultural Australia”.

“Australia is so much more interesting and multicultural, and to strip us of that would be to strip away everything good about this country.”

Grace Street, president of the University of Sydney Student Representative Council, told GL “high school and university students reject Hanson’s far-right politics”. “This is also a student issue — she just announced her plan to reduce the number of international students who come to the country and how many would be able to stay after they finish their degree.”

Rachel Evans, Socialist Alliance candidate for Heffron in the NSW elections in March, said it was exciting to see so many students campaigning against Hanson’s politics. “She is anti-refugee, anti-migrant, anti-trans and anti-woman, and it’s excellent to see young people start to organise.”

Another group of students told GL that Hanson’s beliefs are “destructive”. “Australia thrives off its multiculturalism and we’ll become the next laughing stock, after the US, if this continues.”

About 100 students joined the rally in Muloobinba/Newcastle. One student told GL they “don’t support what Hanson says about LGBTIQ people and people from other countries … this is a country that should be for everyone.

“She has no idea what she is doing and no idea what is right for the country or what we wants — she is totally out of touch.”

Another said Hanson was following the script of US President Donald Trump and his “Make America Great Again” movement.

[Join the speak-out against racism and bigotry in Glebe on September 26.]

author: AWSM
title: The anarchist case for abstentionism in elections
content:
The right to vote is seen by most as a necessary prerequisite for freedom across the world. People have fought and died for the right to vote in elections. Women across the world fought bitter battles for the right to vote. So why should anarchists question this as a right worth having?

The entire electoral show is designed to encourage us to believe that not only does our vote matter, but that it is the most important decision we could possibly make. Indeed, voting is held so sacred by many that the mere mention of not voting is enough to cause outrage. Pointing out that our vote makes no difference anyway, will see you accused of being apathetic, privileged, immature, and even being part of the alt-right!

But as noted anarchist Vernon Richards wrote,

“So long as we have capitalism and government, the job of anarchists is to fight both, and at the same time encourage people to take what steps they can to run their own lives.” [“Anarchists and Voting,” pp. 176–87, The Raven, No. 14, p. 179].

Electoralism ensures that a statist perspective becomes dominant. Everything is seen in terms of state intervention and following the decisions of the leaders, which has always proved deadly to encouraging a spirit of revolt, self-management, and self-help – the very keys to creating change in a society. Rather than being something other people discuss on behalf of working-class people, anarchists argue that politics should not be a specialised activity in the hands of the so-called experts (i.e., politicians) but instead lie in the hands of those directly affected by it in the process of participation, direct action, and self-management. Those that channel any “political” conclusions into electoral politics distort discussions into only what is possible within the current system. Given this, is it surprising that anarchists argue that the people “must organise their powers apart from and against the State?” [Bakunin, The Political Philosophy of Bakunin, p. 376].

Abstentionists get told, “If you don’t vote, you have no right to complain about the outcome,” but we consider the opposite to be true. It is those who have voted, who have agreed to the rules, and agreed to be governed by the winners who cannot complain. It is those who do not participate who have the right to complain about the outcome more than anyone else.

We get told that the reality is that voting does change things, but we can, and do, deny that. Voting attempts to provide the population with the illusion of change while in reality it reinforces the current system. A policy here and there may change, the faces may change, but the system of a wealthy minority ruling a poorer majority remains. People will continually be telling us that abstaining from voting will help the right-wing win the election, that it is better if the lesser evil wins. This may possibly be the case (although the argument is far from convincing), but why should we base our society on a compromise with evil? In fact, the “progressive” left wing party you vote for will often be ready to take the same actions as a right-wing government when it comes to imposing anti-working-class action upon us, (as we shall show later in this essay the state has a corrupting effect on those who enter politics with high principles). There should be a better way, and we say the dismantling of government, in all its existing and potential forms is that way.

Most of the left wing in Aotearoa, and quite a few people who claim to identify as anarchists, will support reformist parties in the upcoming election. You will hear them saying things like “vote Labour (or Green) without illusions,” or “vote Labour/Green but build a socialist alternative.” The slogans that these others may shout only reflect the idea that change can and should be brought about by a small number of elite politicians. Abstentionists do not say things like this. There are many problems with our electoral system of democracy, which we shall run through, but we must state that first and foremost, as anarchists, we see voting as against running contrary to our anti-statist and anti-hierarchy principles, and we see electoralism as contrary to our goals and practice. It reinforces the idea that society is divided into order-givers and order-takers. Famed French anarchist, Elisee Reclus, put it well when he said,

“Everything that can be said about the suffrage may be summed up in a sentence. To vote is to give up your own power. To elect a …

author: CMI Argentina
title: Tierra del Fuego: gran triunfo en la huelga docente del SUTEF
content:
Tras 46 días de paro por tiempo indeterminado, el gremio docente comunicó, tras la realización de un congreso provincial de 170 delegadas y delegados, que llegó a un acuerdo que incluye aumento salarial y el reconocimiento por parte del Gobierno Provincial del pago del Salario Mínimo Vital y Móvil (SMVyM) según su definición constitucional y legal para la docencia, entre otros puntos.


Horacio Catena


El Sindicato Unificado de Trabajadoras y Trabajadores de la Educación Fueguina (SUTEF) informó que la docencia resolvió la aceptación por mayoría del acuerdo discutido con los funcionarios provinciales el pasado 14 de septiembre.


La aceptación se resolvió con dos días de consultas en las instituciones educativas y un congreso provincial de delegados realizado el 17 de septiembre, donde participaron más de 170 delegadas y delegados. Allí, sobre un total de 220 mandatos, el resultado fue del 69% por la aceptación, el 29,5% por el rechazo y el 1,5% de empate.

Informe del acuerdo publicado por el SUTEF


Al finalizar el congreso, y desde el acampe frente a la Casa de Gobierno, el Secretario General del SUTEF, Horacio Catena, realizó una transmisión en vivo para informar los resultados a toda la docencia y a la comunidad.


Catena valoró la masiva participación y el nivel de conciencia demostrado por la docencia en los 46 días de paro por tiempo indeterminado, con movilizaciones y acampes en las tres ciudades de la provincia. “Para nosotros es el inicio, no es el final”, aseveró, afirmando que “en un contexto nacional de recorte, en un contexto nacional de ajuste, en un contexto nacional y provincial de pérdida de empleo, la docencia de Tierra del Fuego no va a perder ni una hora ni un cargo y esa es la mejor base para la pelea del salario mínimo, vital y móvil”.


En ese sentido, remarcó que se logró el reconocimiento por parte del Gobierno Provincial al pago del Salario Mínimo, Vital y Móvil (SMVyM) para la docencia, por lo que se constituirá una comisión técnica para establecer su monto, mecanismos de actualización y seguimiento; al respecto, explicó que, si bien se venía utilizando el valor calculado científicamente por el Frente de Sindicatos Unidos (FreSU), “ahora vamos a construir el nuestro”.


Asimismo, destacó la importancia de la lucha que arrancó el compromiso del Ejecutivo de decretar la emergencia del salario docente, planteando la necesidad de que “rápidamente el Gobierno de la Provincia saque el decreto que se compromete en el acta”.


“Acá se ha declarado la emergencia hídrica, la emergencia agropecuaria, la emergencia comercial, la emergencia forestal, la emergencia industrial; jamás en la historia de la provincia -y no quiero exagerar, pero en la historia del movimiento obrero- se ha declarado la emergencia salarial. Lo que ha logrado la docencia fueguina en total soledad política y gremial, porque la solidaridad gremial vino de afuera”, manifestó.

author: Lee Abbott
title: Fourteen Hundred Solar Manufacturing Workers Join the Steelworkers
content:
Workers at a Corning solar manufacturing plant in Michigan voted September 1 to join the Steelworkers (USW).


The vote was a close 520 to 512, following an intense anti-union campaign by the company.


Nakisha West, a wirecutter, voted yes for “fairness and accountability.” She and her co-workers use scorching heat and precision-cutting tools to turn polysilicon crystals, or boules, into slim squares, known as wafers, for solar panels.


“It’s a very dirty job, but somebody’s gotta do it,” she said.


It’s been more than a decade since that “somebody” was a worker in the U.S.; nearly all the world’s wafers are produced in China. But in January 2025, Corning received $325 million from the federal government to build a solar plant across the street from its semiconductor plant in Hemlock, Michigan, which employs more than 1,000 more workers.


The Hemlock Semiconductor plant is one of only two plants in the U.S. that produce the solar-grade polysilicon. Because it produces this material domestically, Corning is insulated from the effects of the 15 percent tariffs that the Trump administration imposed in August on imported products made with polysilicon.


The 1,380 Corning workers represent the largest victorious union drive in a manufacturing plant since the United Auto Workers

unionized

 a Volkswagen assembly plant in Tennessee in 2024. The Steelworkers also notched a big organizing victory in 2023 with

1,400 school bus manufacturing workers at a Blue Bird factory in Georgia

.


Corning employs 12,000 production workers in the U.S., in the fields of glass and ceramics, life sciences (laboratory tools), fiber optics, and solar. Its products include Gorilla Glass, ceramics for catalytic converters, optical communications cables, automotive glass, and iPhone screens.


The Steelworkers have long represented workers in several other Corning plants. After this win, the union now represents 4,400 Corning workers at facilities in New York, New Jersey, North Carolina, Kentucky, Virginia, and now Michigan.


But the company has increasingly been moving its operations to non-union facilities. Its fiber optic business is rapidly expanding, fueled by demand from data centers.


HARD FLOPS


The work at Corning is grueling and dangerous. The solar factory runs on a heavy production schedule, operating 24 hours a day, with workers on 12-hour shifts. They alternate between working two weeks on day shift and two weeks on night shift.


Another practice of Corning management, known as “hard flops,” means workers can suddenly be forced to go from night to day shift with very little notice. This, on top of the already brutal working hours, leads to more accidents, injuries, and write-ups.


Workers have to fulfill a strict daily quota of processing bricks into wafers. Workers say the task is difficult to accomplish when wirecutting machines break down frequently—repairing the machine can take an entire shift. When they don’t meet the quota, they get reprimanded and written up for poor performance.


West said workers were often disciplined for things that weren’t their fault, creating a high-turnover environment. “You ought to know who you’re hiring, put them in the right place,” she said. “Don’t set them up for failure. The job is very hard. We needed stability there.”


Many workers cited health and safety as major factors in their decision to support the union drive.


The factory itself was being built around her, West said, during her entire 11 months at Corning. It felt dangerous that her department would be operating wiresaws while contractors were still on site constructing the building.


Several fires and chemical leaks have occurred in the pulling department, West and others said. Workers there operate massive ingot pullers—two-story-tall machines that grow crystalline silicon inside a vacuum-sealed furnace.


Pulling is the most dangerous and potentially explosive department. A major accident there in March injured nine workers, adding urgency to the union drive.


BROKEN PROMISES


Workers also said the company has a long record of broken promises. For example, workers earn profit-sharing, but management recently changed that benefit to “goal sharing,” based on quarterly rather than end-of-year profits. This drastically reduced the added benefit workers had been promised.


“Their word wasn’t bond,” said West. “If it was, we wouldn't go through this.”

author: Unknown
title: Murat Çakır: Germany is openly playing a dangerous game
content:
Should Germany’s state elections and the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) be seen merely as a temporary shift in voting patterns? Or are they a direct consequence of the political establishment, Germany’s militarist turn and the deepening crisis of capitalism? Murat Çakır, a researcher at the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, said mainstream parties are legitimising fascist rhetoric by resorting to anti-refugee demagoguery, while the reformist left has deepened this political vacuum by moving away from genuine class politics. Caught between economic decline, deindustrialisation and growing hostility towards Russia, Germany is putting increasing pressure on workers at home while pursuing a dangerous course of militarism abroad that could open the door to nuclear catastrophe.


Writer and researcher Murat Çakır said the only way to confront the growing threats of fascism and war in Germany in particular and Europe more broadly is for migrants and workers to strengthen a common social struggle along anti-capitalist and anti-militarist lines.


I would like to ask about the elections in Germany, the possible scenarios and their potential short-, medium- and long-term implications. First, there was an election in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD made a strong showing. This was followed by elections in Lower Saxony, where the mainstream parties lost votes while the AfD increased its share. Berlin will hold its state election next Sunday. Although the Left Party appears to be ahead, the AfD is also seeing an increase in support there.


How would you define the AfD: as radical right, populist right, or explicitly fascist? How should the growing support for the party and the forces around it be interpreted?


The state elections in Germany and the AfD’s growing share of the vote are not merely a temporary shift in electoral preferences; they are a direct consequence of the deepening crisis of the political establishment and the capitalist system. As for how the party should be defined, it would be wrong to soften its character by describing the AfD merely as “populist” or “far right”. This party is directly racist and fascist in character. The real question, however, is what is fuelling this fascist force. Mainstream parties, the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD), the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the Greens and others, appear on the one hand to complain about the rise of the AfD, while on the other pursuing policies that legitimise its rhetoric.


What these parties are doing collectively is promoting the lie, or rather the demagoguery, that migrants and refugees are the root cause of all these problems. The political establishment has been doing this for a long time. Whenever there is a crisis, migrants or refugees are immediately portrayed as being responsible for it.


The absence of a genuine left-wing alternative that engages in class struggle, gives voice to people’s concerns and develops realistic proposals is pushing people towards fascist parties that offer simplistic solutions while simultaneously creating enemies.


There is, on the one hand, xenophobia and racism deliberately fuelled by the political establishment. By adopting the rhetoric of fascist parties and putting similar policies into practice, the establishment is effectively strengthening them. Look, for example, at the plans to establish detention camps in the Maghreb region of North Africa. This is already one of the demands of fascist parties. Ultimately, the far right is exerting serious pressure on mainstream parties of both the right and left to pursue increasingly radical policies.


From this perspective, we can say that the rise of fascist parties in Germany and other European countries is a consequence of the crisis facing the political establishment, preparations for war, the militarist transformation and neoliberal policies. The other side of the problem is the failure of a genuine left-wing party rooted in class struggle to emerge as an alternative.


In this context, we can speak in particular of the profound failure of German reformism. Although they have recovered some support in Berlin, we will see whether they can fulfil the promises they have made if they come to power. Failing to move beyond narrow identity politics and lecturing people from ivory towers about how they should live is not left-wing politics. It does nothing but drive people towards fascist parties that, like the Pied Piper of Hamelin, offer …

title: Die Berliner AfD vor der Wahl
content:
Am 20. September soll in Berlin das Abgeordnetenhaus (AGH) und in den Bezirken die Bezirksverordnetenversammlungen (BVV) gewählt werden. Die AfD tritt mit insgesamt 222 Kandidierenden an – alle Namen und Portraits sind zu finden auf https://noafd.info. Das sind rund zehn Prozent ihrer Mitglieder in der Hauptstadt. Aktuelle Umfragen sehen für die AfD im Schnitt fast 18 Prozent der Stimmen voraus (1). Das wäre eine Verdoppelung im Vergleich zur Wiederholungswahl 2023. Damals haben sie 17 Personen ins AGH und insgesamt 64 in die zwölf Bezirksparlamente geschickt.


Die Stimmen wollen sie holen mit der Kampagnenklammer „Berlin. Stark. Machen“. Eine Mischung aus Migration, Ordnung/Sicherheit, nationale bzw. kulturelle Identität und ein Angriff auf „linke“ Politik. Sichtbar eigentlich nur auf rund 25.000 (2) Plakaten (viel dokumentiert: https://t.me/keinPlakatDerAfD): „Remigration ist nicht alles, aber ohne Remigration ist alles nichts.“ (Martin Kohler), „Berlin braucht Ordnung.“ (Marc Bernicke), „Für Sicherheit, Sauberkeit und Gerechtigkeit“ (David Eckert), „Gerne Deutsch.“ (Robert Eschricht), „m/w/d: männlich, weiß, deutsch.“ (Hendrik Pauli), „Lasst uns Berlin vor dem links-woken Wahnsinn verteidigen!“ (Marc Vallendar), „Gute Mobilität durch Verkehrsvielfalt statt Verkehrsideologie.“ (Rolf Wiedenhaupt), „Für Wissenschaftsfreiheit und gegen Cancel-Culture an unseren Unis.“ (Martin Trefzer) und auf Großplakaten „Migration braucht Grenzen“ oder „Berlin braucht Ordnung“.


Das Programm


Im Wahlprogramm finden sich diese plakativen Problembotschaften auch wieder. Wie schon in der ersten Veröffentlichung zur Berlin-Wahl auf Indy (3) und in der Analyse vom Apabiz (4) bemerkt, knüpft die AfD an bekannte Probleme an (z.B. Wohnen) und macht im Programm konkretere Vorschläge als in früheren Wahlprogrammen. Die Plakat-Kampagne ist dabei schmaler als das tatsächliche Programm – was nicht unüblich ist. Auch üblich ist, dass Parteien Versprechungen machen die sie wegen Finanzknappheit, Entscheidungskompetenzen (EU-Ebene, Bundesgesetze), Verfassungsrechtsproblemen und fehlendem Personal nicht umsetzen können. Die Kritik am AfD Programm sollte sich nicht auf die Umsetzbarkeit beziehen, sondern auf die politische Agenda. Es ist eine rassistische, nationalistische, sexistische und abelistische Politik, die die Machtverhältnisse weiter in Richtung besitzende Klasse verschieben soll und dafür vielen gesellschaftlichen Gruppen vergiftete Angebote macht.


Auf den zahlreichen Gegenveranstaltungen zu den Wahlkampfevents der AfD z.B. am Tierpark (5) oder in Charlottenburg (6) wurde das gut auseinandergenommen. Aber das reicht nicht, um die Stimmung in der Stadt zu kippen.


Die Kandidat*innen


Wer durch die Listen der Kandidierenden scrollt wird viele alte Gesichter erkennen. Der Großteil der Landesliste war schon vorher im AGH. In den BVVen haben sich viele ebenfalls länger etabliert und sind meist deckungsgleich mit den Bezirksvorständen der Partei. Ein paar neue Kuriositäten gibt es dennoch – der Tagesspiegel hat Andreas Quint (Platz 35 Landesliste und Anhänger der „Umvolkungs“-These) hervorgehoben (7). Andere sind z.B. eine Kathi Rödl aus Spandau, die als Bibliotheksleiterin der „Gedenkbibliothek zu Ehren der Opfer des Kommunismus“ auftritt und nun auf der BVV-Liste steht. Die Bilder der Kandiderenden hinterlassen den Geschmack von Consultants, Einzelunternehmer, KFZ-Mechaniker und vor allem ziemlich junge Rechte, die ebenso gut bei der Identitären Bewegung sein könnten (wo sie oft auch herkommen). Ein Teil des neuen AfD-Personals wurde bereits vor Jahren in der Jugendorganisation der Partei politisch sozialisiert und wandert nun geschlossen in die nächste Organisationsgeneration der Partei ein. Jan Streeck (JA Berlin, BVV und heutiger Platz 4 der Landesliste), David Eckert (JA-Landesvorsitz, Bezirksvorstand und ebenfalls Landesliste). Martin Kohler (erst JA/IB, aktuell Vorstand Generation Deutschland und jetzt Landesvorstand/Landesliste), Marc Bernicke (Polizist, JA, jetzt AfD-Parteiapparat und Landesliste) und Christopher Wiedenhaupt (Sohn des ehm. CDUlers und nun AfDlers Rolf Wiedenhaupt, auch JA, AfD/Bezirksstruktur und nun Landesliste). Es gibt leider bisher keine strukturierte Analyse der AfD Kandidiat*innen, mit der auch im Wahlkampf gearbeitet werden könnte. So hätte die bürgerliche Fassade den tatsächlichen innerparteilichen Netzwerken gegenübergestellt werden können. Diese analytische Schwäche ist ein Novum für Berlin aber …
