author: Unknown
title: İbtisam Azem: Filistinliler için hatırlamak, silinen tarihle bağı korumanın bir yolu
content:
Bir sabah bütün Filistinlilerin yok olduğu bir dünyaya uyansak ne olurdu? Filistinli yazar İbtisam Azem’in Türkçe çevirisi yakın zamanda yayımlanan romanı 

Kayboluş Kitabı

 bu soruyu ele alıyor ve kayboluşun ardından yaşananları Yafalı Alâ ile İsrailli komşusu Ariel üzerinden anlatıyor.


Tayyibe doğumlu olan ve bugün New York’ta Birleşmiş Milletler muhabirliği yapan Azem, romanını 2014 yılında anadili Arapça olarak yayımladı.

Kayboluş Kitabı

, daha sonra birçok dile çevrildi. O yıllarda yalnızca bir romanın kurgusu olan bu soru, Gazze’de üç yıla yaklaşan soykırımla birlikte bugün başka türlü okunuyor. Azem ise romandaki kayboluşu hiçbir zaman distopik bir fantezi olarak görmediğini söylüyor. Ona göre bu kayboluş, 1948’de yüz binlerce Filistinlinin sürülmesinin ve o günden beri kesintisiz süren “sessiz Nakba”nın bir yankısı.


Biz de kitaptan yola çıkarak Azem’le ‘48 Filistinlilerinin devletin okulda öğrettiği tarihle evde duyduğu tarih arasında büyümesini, hatırlamanın neden bir direniş biçimi olduğunu, 1967 işgalini eleştiren ama 1948’i sorgulamayan Ariel karakteri üzerinden İsrail’deki “makul” çoğunluğun suç ortaklığını ve Filistin edebiyatının ancak felaket anlarında ilgi görmesini konuştuk.


*İbtisam Azem, Kayboluş Kitabı (Arapçadan çeviren: Zafer Ceylan), Yapı Kredi Yayınları, 192 sayfa, 2026. 


“Nakba, hafızanın aktarımını kesintiye uğrattı”


Alâ defterine “Sanki son can simidim hafızaymış gibi…” yazıyor ama bir yandan da “Keşke daha çok sorsaydım ona” pişmanlığını dile getiriyor.

Kayboluş Kitabı

, hatırlamaya çoğu zaman geç kalmanın ve sorulamamış soruların da anlatısı. İsrail’in yok saymaya çalıştığı ‘48 Filistinlileri ve halkın kesintisiz süren varoluş mücadelesi düşünüldüğünde; “hatırlamak” Filistinliler için ne anlama geliyor ve bu “geç kalmışlık” duygusu sizde nasıl bir yer tutuyor?


Filistinliler için hatırlamak yalnızca geriye bakma edimi değil. Kim olduğumuzla, mekânlarımızla ve çoğu zaman bilinçli biçimde kenara itilmiş ya da silinmiş bir tarihle bağımızı korumanın bir yolu. Hâkim anlatı size tarihinizin ya hiç yaşanmadığını ya da yalnızca geçmişe ait olduğunu söylemeye çalıştığında, hafıza bir direniş biçimine dönüşebiliyor.


Bu, ‘48 Filistinlileri için özellikle önemli, çünkü çoğumuz resmî olarak öğretilen tarihle (devletin okulda anlattığı tarihle) evde duyduğumuz tarih arasındaki boşlukta büyüdük.


Romanda Alâ, anneannesine daha çok soru sormamış olmaktan pişmanlık duyuyor. Bu çok insani bir duygu bence. Anne babamıza ve büyüklerimize hayatlarını, çocukluklarını, evlerini, tanıdıkları insanları sormak için hep daha çok vaktimiz olacağını varsayarız. Sonra bir anda o vakit biter. Biri ölür ve asla dinleyemeyeceğiniz hikâyeler, asla soramayacağınız sorular olduğunu fark edersiniz.


Nakba insanları yalnızca fiziksel olarak yerinden etmedi, aynı zamanda hafızanın aktarımını kesintiye uğrattı ve o hafızanın içinde yaşadığı toplulukları yok etti.


Sözlü tarihin romanda bu kadar önemli olmasının sebebi bu. Yazı kaybedilen her şeyi geri getiremez, hafızadaki her boşluğu dolduramaz. Ama parçaları koruyabilir ve onları taşıyan kişinin ötesine geçmelerini sağlayabilir. Anneannenin hikâyeleri Alâ’nın hafızasının parçası oluyor, sonra Alâ’nın yazdıkları o hikâyelerin bir başkasına ulaşmasını sağlıyor.


Hatırlamak geçmişe hapsolmak anlamına gelmiyor. Tam tersine, farklı bir gelecek istediğimiz için hatırladığımızı düşünüyorum. Sömürgeleştirilenlere sık sık geçmişe saplandıkları ve artık ilerlemeleri gerektiği söylenir, oysa bugüne nasıl geldiğinizi anlamayı reddederseniz farklı bir gelecek kuramazsınız. Hatırlamak bir bakıma geçmişin yeniden gelecek olmasını engelleme çabası.


“Yafa benim bir parçam oldu”


Yafa romanda adeta canlı bir karakter gibi. Alâ, anneannesinin Yafa’sıyla her gün yürüdüğü Tel Aviv’i bir türlü üst üste oturtamıyor; “yaşadığımız bu şehrin üzerinde başka bir şehir olduğundan” emin. Anneannenin ısrarla “Kont Sokağı” demesi, Alâ’nın ise posta kutusuna İbranileştirilmiş adı (Sha’arei Nikanor) yazmak zorunda kalması bu silme politikasının somut bir göstergesi. İşgalin mekânı ve isimleri gasp ettiği bir şehri, “kayıp cennet” nostaljisine sığınmadan, hafızanın o eksik ve yaralı parçalarıyla yazmak sizin için nasıl bir anlam taşıyordu?


Benim için Yafa hakkında yazmak hiçbir zaman kayıp bir cenneti yeniden kurma meselesi olmadı. Filistin’in cennet olup olmadığı umurumda bile değil. Önemli olan, başımıza gelenleri hak etmemiş olmamız ve hiç kimsenin hayatlarımızı ve haklarımızı …

author: Susan Price
title: Singapore’s unfinished anti-colonial struggle
content:
The dominant history of modern Singapore was meticulously constructed under the banner of the “Singapore Story”. By presenting the material interests of the ruling elite as the universal interests of the nation, the state narrative reduces the mass anti-imperialist movement of the mid-20th century into a fable; one wherein a heroic bourgeois leadership single-handedly navigates a vulnerable island state through the perils of communism to construct a prosperous capitalist metropolis.

In his six-part oral history series with Pintjin (PJ) Thum, Dr Poh Soo Kai, former student activist, co-founder of the People’s Action Party (PAP) and the Barisan Sosialis (Socialist Front) — and former political prisoner detained for nearly 17 years without trial — delivers a vital historical materialist counter-narrative.

In 36 minutes of personal testimony, Poh unpacks the class dynamics, state coercion, and geopolitical shake-ups that dismantled working-class power and shaped Singapore's transition into a disciplined capitalist state.

Poh begins by recalling how post-World War II Malayan households were adorned with portraits of Indonesia’s Sukarno, India’s Nehru and Gandhi, and China’s Chiang Kai-Shek, who were seen as regional anti-colonial leaders. The struggle in Singapore was bound to broader anti-imperialist movements across Malaya, Indonesia, and Vietnam.

Poh’s account of the 1954 Fajar Trial undermines the state’s origin myth, which positions the trial of eight members of the editorial board of Fajar (Dawn) — the University of Malaya Socialist Club’s newspaper — as Lee Kuan Yew’s (LKY’s) personal legal breakthrough.

[Editor’s note: Harry Lee Kwan Yew co-founded the PAP, was a barrister and opposition figure and became Singapore’s first Prime Minister in 1959.]

As president of the University of Malaya Socialist Club, Poh helped publish Fajar, an anti-colonial paper opposing the anti-communist South East Asian Treaty Organisation (SEATO) and foreign military bases. When the editorial board was charged with sedition, Queen’s Counsel DN Pritt arrived to lead the defense. Poh recounts Pritt greeting him warmly at the Dolphin Hotel before turning to LKY, who was acting as local junior counsel, and saying, “Harry, now you can go.”

Pritt dismissed LKY specifically to formulate an anti-colonial strategy directly with the student activists, recognising that the trial was a political battlefield rather than a legal technicality.

This moment symbolises the clash between the radical student movement and LKY’s legalism, and how official history later repackaged a left-wing victory as an LKY solo masterstroke.

As the PAP rose to power, internal contradictions between its left-wing mass base and moderate leadership erupted.

Poh recounts how the left wing consistently pushed for true self-determination, confronting PAP Chair Toh Chin Chye to issue a public statement supporting then-Chief Minister David Marshall’s 1956 call for internal self-rule — a move that infuriated LKY upon his return from London.

[Editor’s note: Marshall was appointed Chief Minister after contesting the 1955 election as a candidate for the Labour Front. After failing to secure self-rule, he resigned as Chief Minister in June 1956.]

Chief Minister Lim Yew Hock’s violent crackdowns on trade unions and Chinese school students from 1956 onward served a dual purpose: suppressing working-class organisation while allowing LKY to position himself as the sensible alternative acceptable to British imperial interests and local capital.

When dissident MPs and activists walked out to form the Barisan Sosialis in 1961, every PAP branch including LKY’s own Tanjong Pagar constituency defected to the new party. The PAP was left as a hollow electoral vessel without organic mass support.

To preempt an electoral defeat, the state deployed Operation Coldstore in February 1963. Officially framed as a security operation against a communist plot tied to the 1962 Brunei Revolt, Coldstore was a draconian political purge that sought to decapitate the political opposition, dismantle union leadership and ensure PAP hegemony.

The state weaponised identity politics to divide the multi-ethnic working-class by branding Chinese-educated labour leaders and Barisan Sosialis members as “Chinese chauvinists”. It replaced class-based solidarity with state-directed multiracialism that contained labour organising within non-threatening boundaries.

author: Unknown
title: Türkiye-Yunanistan gerilimi: Sadece bir sınır sorunu değil emperyalist planda yer kapma meselesi
content:
Seyit Aldoğan [email protected]

Atina- Son dönemde Ortadoğu, Doğu Akdeniz, Ege ve İran ekseninde gelişen ABD-İsrail savaşının yaygınlaşma eğilimi, bir anlamda Türk-Yunan ilişkilerini de tetikledi. Bu durum Türkiye basınında “Atina’da deprem”, “Atina gerilim istiyor”, “Yunanistan ve İsrail ablukası” benzeri manşetlerin atılmasına neden oldu. Karşılıklı restleşmeler, uyarılar ve milliyetçi söylemlerle düşmanlığı körükleyen değerlendirmeler havada uçuşuyor.

Dünyada emperyalist rekabetin kızışmasına, pazar paylaşımı mücadelesine ve emperyalist savaşların yaygınlaşma eğilimi içine girmesine paralel olarak, üzerinde yaşadığımız coğrafyada da enerji nakil hatları, hidrokarbon rezervleri ve deniz taşımacılığı gibi etkenlere bağlı olarak Türkiye-Yunanistan ilişkilerinde yeni bir gerginliğe doğru gidildiği görülüyor.

ABD ve onun bölgedeki vurucu gücü olan İsrail yeni bir yapılanmayı hedeflerken, bölgedeki gerici yönetimler pastadan pay kapmak, emperyalist sistemin bir parçası olarak varlıklarını sürdürmeyi güvence altına almak ve bölgesel çıkar dengeleri içinde daha iyi bir mevzi tutmak amacıyla dış politika, ticaret, silahlanma ve ittifaklarda yeni yönelimler içine giriyorlar. Bölge gericiliklerinin çıkarlarının farklılıklar göstermesi emperyalizme bağımlılıkla çelişmediği gibi, tersine bu bağımlılığı daha da güçlendiren birer etmen haline geliyor.

Bölgedeki gelişmelere bu perspektifle bakıldığında Türkiye ve Yunanistan arasında anlaşmazlık konusu olan sorunların klasik anlamda bir sınır sorunu olmaktan çıktığı açıkça görülecektir.

Rusya Karadeniz, Balkanlar ve Doğu Avrupa’dan abluka altına alınıyor. Yunan adalarına hava savunma sistemlerinin yerleştirilerek Ege kontrol altına alınmaya çalışılıyor. Doğu Trakya ABD-NATO üssüne çevriliyor. Öte yandan Doğu Akdeniz’de İsrail, Güney Kıbrıs ve Yunanistan arasında enerji nakil anlaşmasının yürürlüğe girmesi, Yunanistan’ın münhasır ekonomik bölge çerçevesi içinde uluslararası tekellerle yaptığı anlaşmalar, enerji rezervlerinin önemi, Ortadoğu’ya müdahalede bölgenin önem kazanması, Çin ve Rusya ile girişilen rekabet vb. gelişmeler Türkiye ile Yunanistan arasındaki sorunların artık klasik anlaşmazlıklar olmaktan çıktığını gösteriyor. Gelişmeler, Ege ve Doğu Akdeniz’i emperyalist yayılmacılık, paylaşım ve egemenlik rekabetinin açıkça görüldüğü alan durumuna getiriyor.

Yunanistan’da 1973 yılında yıkılan Albaylar Cuntası sonrasından bugüne kadar kurulan en işbirlikçi yönetim olan Kiryakos Miçotakis’nin Yeni Demokrasi (ND) hükümeti, Ege’de ve Doğu Akdeniz’de Yunan sermayesinin çıkarları doğrultusunda başta ABD, İsrail ve sonrasında AB ile, son derece stratejik anlaşmalar yapmış bulunuyor. Mısır, Lübnan, BAE, Suudi Arabistan ile askeri ve ticari ve teknik ilişkiler geliştirdi. Bu arada özellikle Fransız ve Alman tekellerinin çıkarlarının sözcülüğünü de yapıyor.

Erdoğan hükümeti ise ABD ve AB destekli İsrail, Yunanistan ve Güney Kıbrıs kesimi eksenine karşı Suriye’de sahip olduğu etkiyi, son süreçte Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan ile kurulan “Mekke ittifakı”nı, ABD ve NATO politikaları ile tam bir uyum içinde olan tutumunu; Trump’ın övgüsünü kazanan İran ve Filistin politikasını, NATO politikaları çerçevesi içinde artan silahlanma harcamalarını kullanarak elini güçlendirmeye ve bölge ülkeleriyle kurduğu ekseni güçlendirmeye çalışıyor.

Kuşkusuz her iki ülkenin bağımlılığı daha fazla artıran bu tutumlarının ana nedeni sadece Türk-Yunan ilişkileri ve Ege-Doğu Akdeniz gibi sorunlarla açıklanamaz. Esas neden bölgede oluşan ya da oluşması olası olan dengelerden pay kapma yarışıdır. Türkiye’yi asıl kaygılandıran İsrail’in bölgede oyun kurucu duruma gelme planlarıdır. Örneğin “yavru vatan” ilan edilmesine ramak kalan Suriye’de İsrail’in etkisinin artması ve Colani hükümeti ile anlaşma masasına oturulması, Arap ülkeleriyle İbrahim anlaşmalarının imzalanması, Yunanistan’ın AB üyesi olarak Türkiye ile bölgesel çıkarlar üzerinden iş birliği yapan ülkeler ve tekellerle ekonomik, askeri ve ticari ilişkiler geliştirmesi Türkiye’nin yayılmacı politikaları önünde ciddi engeller oluşturuyor.

Son süreçte ise Yunanistan, Kıbrıs ve İsrail arasında çekilen elektrik hattı ve Türkiye tarafından hazırlanan “Mavi vatan” kanunu ve “deniz parkları” kararı, iki ülke arasında gerginliğin yeniden yükselmesine neden oldu. Yunan hükümeti “Mavi vatan” kanununun “hiçbir geçerliliğinin olmayacağını” savunurken, Dışişleri Bakanı Yorgos Gerapetritis defalarca “Yunanistan her türlü tahrike karşı koymaya hazırdır” …

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: Blood Rush | $100 barrel, super El Niño and Pax Silica: Energy hegemony, enclosure, and national liberation
content:
The AI-assisted illustration of the proposed 1,600-hectare industrial hub to be located in New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac. Photo courtesy of the People’s Television Network

The convergence of crude oil surpassing $100 per barrel and the acceleration of El Niño to “super” status—drawn from projections and reports by energy-market analysts, international economic-monitoring bodies, and climate agencies tracking compound global shocks—exposes the deep structural crisis of monopoly capitalism. This dual rupture demonstrates how imperialist war-making, extractive plunder, planetary warming, and the ongoing enclosure of the countryside function not as separate phenomena, but as interconnected expressions of the same underlying logic of capital accumulation.

The rapid climb of crude oil past $100 per barrel cannot be detached from the escalation of U.S.-led imperialist aggression, military blockades, and regional destabilization. Financialized markets and transnational fossil-fuel monopolies exploit war and artificial scarcity to protect superprofits, while the resulting inflation functions as a mechanism of structural extraction from working classes in colonies and semicolonies. Peripheral societies are forced to absorb the crisis through debt traps, budget cuts, declining purchasing power, and reduced national sovereignty. High energy prices further incentivize ruling elites to expand speculative and destructive extraction projects in the name of energy security and geopolitical hegemony.

This energy regime is increasingly bound up with “Pax Silica”—the global alliance centered on microelectronics, semiconductor supply chains, and automated defense systems. Localized military interventions rely on a global network of critical mineral extraction, energy consumption, and defense technology transfer. The fusion of high-tech militarism and fossil capital reinforces imperialist control over global supply lines, shifting the operational costs of planetary warfare directly onto the working classes of the Global South.

At the same time, a “super” El Niño brings the violence of ecological crisis directly to the doorsteps of the global peasantry, smallholders, and urban poor. Although the historical carbon footprint belongs overwhelmingly to the industrial centers of the imperialist world, the physical destruction—manifested in crop failures, severe drought, flooding, and damaged infrastructure—falls disproportionately on semicolonial societies. Framing these events as merely “natural disasters” shields the capitalist mode of production from critique and obscures climate catastrophe as an institutionalized assault on oppressed and economically vulnerable populations.

Far from resolving the agrarian question, this ecological and economic squeeze accelerates what Paris Yeros calls generalized semiproletarianization. In this condition, households that have lost all or part of their means of production do not become fully dependent on wages. Instead, they combine precarious employment with small-scale farming, petty trade, subsistence production, care work, and other sources of livelihood (Yeros, 2023). Across much of the Global South, this blurs the conventional boundary between peasant and worker and produces socially fragmented labor forces that move between rural and urban economies (Moyo & Yeros, 2005; Moyo et al., 2013; Yeros, 2024).

Under conditions of monopoly capitalism, these labor reserves can weaken workers’ bargaining power and shift the costs of social reproduction onto households and communities (Marx, 1976; Yeros, 2023). Millions may circulate between degraded smallholder farming, informal street trade, temporary migration, and precarious wage work without being absorbed into secure urban industrial employment. Rather than representing a simple transition from peasant production to wage labor, semiproletarianization describes a durable social formation in which rural and urban livelihood strategies remain interdependent (Yeros, 2023).

To propose “ecosocialism” as a generic, off-the-shelf alternative to this twin crisis, without subjecting the term itself to critical scrutiny, is to risk reproducing a dangerous conceptual trap. Much dominant Western-centered ecosocialist discourse reduces the problem to an abstract, planet-wide carbon-accounting exercise. In doing so, it can erase the national question, gloss over the unresolved agrarian question, and ignore the necessity of national-liberation struggles in …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Big data and the AUKUS war machine
content:
The world’s greatest remilitarisation since the World War II is underway, driven by the imperatives of the flailing United States empire.

The AUKUS war pact places us at the centre of this drive towards war. How should we imagine Australia’s role in the world?

Australia is not just a settler-colonial state; it is a sub-imperial power that has transferred subordination from its one-time colonial ruler, Britain, to the US, its new imperial master.

It is now acting to preserve the military and economic interests of its master state. This is encapsulated in the AUKUS war pact, which, despite no public debate, commits the country to eight nuclear-powered submarines, high-tech weapons development and sharing and the subsequent invasion of US personnel and weaponry in the event of our “interoperability” in a contrived future conflict with China.

Through AUKUS, Australia acts as a mechanism for US force projection into the Pacific, to rattle the sabre against China.

AUKUS makes Australia the first non-nuclear-weapons state to use a loophole in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons for naval propulsion with weapons-grade uranium.

That sets a proliferation precedent.

Climate change is the real security threat. Pacific leaders named climate change their main security threat in the 2018 Boe Declaration. Yet Australia keeps expanding fossil fuel exports while spending hundreds of billions on submarines.

But AUKUS is about so much more than submarines; its more sinister part is AUKUS Pillar II, which is about “advanced capabilities” including: undersea capabilities; quantum science; artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomy; advanced cyber; hypersonics and counter-hypersonics; and electronic warfare.

Any pretense about “defensive” capabilities is put to rest with Pillar II because these technologies are about highly efficient offensive war-fighting capabilities.

The Australian Human Rights Commission said it is arguably impossible for AI to comply with the proportionality rule, because AI is unable to understand the intrinsic value of human life.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that machines determining proportionality in life-or-death situations is “politically unacceptable and morally repugnant”.

Australia said in 2018 that it was premature to regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems. Nearly a decade later, it maintains this position despite significant advances and uses of the technology.

It is instead barrelling ahead with developing the most advanced and lethal forms imaginable.

The first “signature project” of AUKUS Pillar II was announced in May — payloads and systems for uncrewed undersea vehicles are due from 2027, covering surveillance, reconnaissance, strike, anti-submarine and electronic warfare, among other missions.

The stated aim is meeting near-term war fighting objectives. The Ghost Shark project for Australia is being developed by Silicon Valley-based defence contractor Anduril. Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said they will conduct surveillance and can strike at extremely long distances. It means the weapon is designed to operate far from our shores — not for defence.

Pillar II extends into the realms of software and artificial intelligence. Tests for active warfighting scenarios to integrate Australian, British and US AI models have been ongoing for years.

A 2023 pilot had Australia PA-8 Poseidon aircraft sharing data for submarine detection, amid other tests of “AI-enabled assets” and machine-learning models.

There was a large-scale US trial in 2024. The US Department of War was enthusiastic: “These trials demonstrated significant progress since the first AUKUS RAAIT trails in the UK in April 2023 and show tangible results of the AUKUS Pillar II commitment to making our warfighter more lethal on the battlefield.

“It used to be that each nation used its own datasets to develop separate models and deploy those models on their own platforms. Under RAAIT, we’ve matured the AI pipeline, focusing on interchangeability and interoperability, which allows for any combinations of datasets, models, algorithms and platforms to be used across all three nations.”

These models and cloud computational capacity are key to war power investments today.

The Pentagon’s AI office awarded Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI contracts worth up to US$200 million each for military and intelligence AI last year.

author: Unknown
title: Emon Azmi - Solidarity has to have teeth
content:
Author

: Emon Azmi

Title

: Solidarity has to have teeth

Subtitle

: Where’s the anti-imperialism that goes beyond lip service in the west?

Source

: https://thatanarkatamuslim.substack.com/p/solidarity-has-to-have-teeth


 A recent

Open Letter to Iran’s Political Prisoners

 published by the Guardian has gotten lots of attention (criticism and defense). i have some thoughts on this. However, i’m more interested in discussing an ongoing anti-anarchism issue within the western ‘anti-imperialist’ sphere. Let’s get into it.


(Note: the title is a quote from F12 in a recent


interview


with The Dugout)


On the Guardian letter (kinda)


 That the Islamic Republic of Iran is, de facto, an anti-imperial State in our present international context is not a question. That carcerality is a defining feature of modern States, a core colonial-imperial infrastructure exported from and upheld to an outsized degree by the west (especially the US and Israel), is not a question. That the Guardian letter does not properly articulate this — that it does not offer a constructive analysis of the resulting tensions nor a useful outlook for anti-carceral international solidarity, insofar as revolutionary internationalism is concerned — is clear. There is no need to defend the letter or its signatories on these points.


 It is, however, frustrating that many segments of the western left are sooner jumping to defend the anti-imperial position of the Islamic Republic than to clarify how their anti-imperialist praxis contends with carcerality across contexts and present an alternative anti-carceral outlook within their critique. It’s even more frustrating that this is so unsurprising.


 The sib X, from

HoodSchoolNYC

, hit the nail on the head when they

penned this

:


I think a lot of the western left, and right for that matter, engages politics like sports teams mascots. There’s a certain decadence to an “anti imperialism” that never requires a drop of your blood — only statements, open letters and unfounded audacity… It’s all so unserious. Safiya Bukhari said,

 “it could be that, after all, we don’t want the same things”

, maybe that is true. What frustrates me most is that despite freedom dreams or slogans, the proverbial big bad wolf of imperialism sleeps peacefully each night in the house we all live in.


 The evident lack of substantive anti-imperialism in the west — that is, the kind which would position progressive and anti-war forces against empire’s existence in their ‘internationalist’ practice — is telling. Where is the

solidarity with teeth

 so needed in this moment?


 At present, ‘anti-imperialism’ in the west largely amounts to sectarian navel gazing, sideline cheering, and moral posturing of the sort we see in the Guardian letter.


 ‘Narrative war’ is waged between factions of leftists in a virtual ‘marketplace of ideas’ in a propaganda economy that metabolizes their open letters and statements — fueling their hostilities and feeding off their content, rendering the bulk of their interventions materially insignificant, relegating them to silos in our current media ecosystem. Here, ‘anti-imperialism’ is largely assessed by one’s rhetorical fealty to whatever stance or analysis their niche of leftists has deemed correct. “Hollow”, ironically, characterizes this all quite well.


 Criticisms can be pointed at the individuals, groups, media outlets, and social media accounts comprising these factions — many, justifiably so. But at what point does this counterproductive form of practice itself receive greater scrutiny?


 At what point do insights from those who have been naming the issues of this approach to ‘solidarity’, analyzing the conditions from which it emerges and the forces perpetuating it, get foregrounded? At what point will the work of developing material bases of power at the grassroots level become the primary site from which revolutionary internationalism is conceptualized and discussed, specifically among ‘anti-imperialists’ in the west?


 To these ends, non-statist and anti-statist frameworks (e.g. anarchism, autonomism) have great value. But a pervasive left anti-anarchism is blurring this reality.


Reflection on left anti-anarchism


(Note: My essay


The Statism Inherent to Fascism


discusses this further)


 Elder Ashanti Alston made multiple crucial points at the 2025 National Black Radical Organizing Conference.


 During a

panel discussion

 , anarchism and anti-imperialism had been …

author: anred
title: Las alarmas de la IA: una carrera imparable hasta la extinción masiva
content:
Los CEOs que piden frenar la carrera, ¿a quién le reclaman? | Un robot humanoide Unitree Robotics G1 en la sala de la Bolsa de Nueva York (NYSE) en Nueva York, EE.UU. (Bloomberg/Michael Nagle)


No son filósofos apocalípticos como el francés Eric Sadin. Tampoco son quienes propugnan la necesidad de ralentizar o detener el desarrollo tecnológico. No son los vecinos de los distintos pueblos de Estados Unidos o del mundo que reclaman para que no les levanten monumentales centros de datos en el patio, ruidosos y ruinosos con el medio ambiente. Son investigadores estrella de las grandes compañías de inteligencia artificial y, más aún, son sus propios CEOs, Sam Altman o Dario Amodei, quienes confiesan la necesidad de frenar la descontrolada competencia en IA porque podría llevarnos a un desastre. En palabras de Jacob Coxon, el joven investigador que renunció a Anthropic: “quienes desarrollan la IA creen sinceramente que podría acabar con todos nosotros para finales de la década”.

Por Santiago Gándara, para Prensa Obrera.


Hubo una primera alarma en julio pasado cuando, en un experimento, varios agentes o sistemas de software de OpenAi hackearon otros servidores de una empresa. Nadie los había instruido para que hicieran eso. Desde entonces se vienen produciendo situaciones similares: los agentes se asocian con otros, planifican ataques en enjambres de centenares de agentes, hackean o intentan hackear a cadenas de suministros de software y hasta se han reconocido intentos para avanzar en investigaciones científicas ligadas a la producción de armas biológicas. De pronto, la tecnología asume las tan humanas prácticas del engaño o del sabotaje, pero con una velocidad de ejecución potencialmente muy superior. Como si no bastaran las noticias que prenuncian pérdidas de trabajo en ramas enteras de la industria y pronostican desocupación masiva, ahora aparecen advertencias según las cuales una IA mucho más autónoma podría poner en riesgo nuestra supervivencia en pocos años.


Humo


Paralelamente, analistas y agentes de bolsa se preguntan todos las mañanas si las millonarias inversiones estatales y privadas en IA aseguran o no ganancias futuras. Los más optimistas señalan que las revoluciones tecnológicas requieren tiempo para que empecemos a ver sus efectos en la organización de las empresas o en la vida económica. Los escépticos recuerdan el estallido de las puntocom a principios de los dos mil y afirman que los multimillonarios dueños de estas empresas son… Vendedores de humo.


Por eso, muy probablemente, estas declaraciones que sacudieron la semana expresan una preocupación menos por la humanidad que por el curso de sus compañías que, como en el caso de OpenAi y Anthropic, estaban por cotizar en la bolsa, aunque ya la primera resolvió postergar la salida. En ese sentido, la carrera no sería solo descontrolada sino agotadora, de allí que Altman y Amodei hayan pedido un 

break

, algo así como un freno antes de estrellarse contra ellos mismos. La excepción es Alex Karp, el CEO 

supremacista de Palantir

, que no quiere detener ni un minuto las guerras imperialistas en Gaza o donde mejor se le pague por sus servicios de inteligencia militar.


Libertarios


Estos CEOs piden frenar la carrera criminal que nos llevaría, según afirman, a la extinción masiva. Ahora bien, siendo los mayores publicistas del capitalismo crudo y duro, que hacen su religión laica de la evasión impositiva y de la celebración de la mano invisible del mercado, que sueñan con un mundo sin trabajadores pero con plusvalía, ¿a quién le reclaman? Y aquí viene lo notable.


Amodei se reclama a sí mismo y sus colegas. Imagina una declaración de armisticio que blinde cada compañía mientras un grupo de auditores o evaluadores externos revisa y sugiere medidas de control. Altman, por su parte, solicita al gobierno que fije un marco regulatorio. Incluso si estos oligopolios pudieran llegar a acuerdos y regulaciones, subsiste un problema: cómo involucrar a las compañías chinas para que no sigan avanzando mientras las estadounidenses se detienen.


Parafraseando un chiste popular, podríamos concluir: CEOs de las mayores compañías del mundo descubren la lógica de la competencia capitalista en la que nadie puede dejar de correr incluso a riesgo del desastre. Eso, si el asunto no fuera serio. author: Monthly Review Press
title: In the Public Eye: “Albert Einstein’s ‘Why Socialism?'”
content:
London Review of Books

: Letters section features a quote from  John Bellamy Foster’s introduction to the book:


“…Einstein’s essay ‘Why Socialism?’, published in 1949 in the first issue of

Monthly Review

, remains one of the most succinct and powerful arguments for socialism ever written. ‘The crippling of the social consciousness,’ Einstein wrote, is ‘the worst evil of capitalism’. ‘I am convinced’, he concluded, ‘there is only one way to eliminate these grave evils, namely through the establishment of a socialist economy.’


‘Why Socialism?’ was regarded by the FBI as direct confirmation of what they referred to as Einstein’s strong ‘communist sympathies’. The Bureau had opened a file on him in late 1932, when he was in the US on a visitor’s visa to teach at Caltech, with a long report by the Woman Patriot Corporation arguing that he should not be admitted to the country. ‘Not even Stalin himself,’ the WPC charged, ‘is affiliated with so many anarcho-communist international groups to promote … world revolution and ultimate anarchy, as ALBERT EINSTEIN.’ The FBI continued to collect everything it could on Einstein’s socialist connections for the remainder of his life.”


As the U.S. approached its 250th anniversary, the current US President respectively imprisoned and killed the heads of Venezuela and Iran in a clear attempt to control access to their oil supplies. It then found itself mired in another imperialist war in the Middle East that is very likely to veer towards World War III. Einstein’s perspective links alienation and nuclear annihilation, capitalism to the devastating possibility of omnicide — the destruction of all human life on earth.


Einstein’s prescient article “Why Socialism?”, first published by Monthly Review in its inaugural 1949 issue, has to say the least, been circulating for some time. Yet it has never been more relevant than today.

Monthly Review Magazine

 republished the article online in 2009, making the article even more widely available.

Monthly Review Press

‘ recent reprint,

‘Albert Einstein’s “Why Socialism?”‘

 stands out, however, for the extremely enlightening and thorough introduction written by magazine editor, John Bellamy Foster.

In defiance of those who would like to, not only re-write history, but erase the future, please help us get this book out to as wide an audience as possible.


In the Public Eye


One of the many places you can find this classic essay, which just happens to be more relevant now than perhaps at any time in history.

Pictured here at Labyrinth in Princeton.


GPEnewsdocs, with Lynn Fries:


In the last segment of an interview series on ecology and materialism conducted by journalist Lynn Fries, John Bellamy Foster reflects on the enduring relevance of Einstein’s “Why Socialism?”. Marx’s foundations of ecological materialism are blended with the work of natural scientists and the Greek philosopher Epicurus. Socialism, as a transformational project whose intellectual birthplace is materialism, had to be forcefully defended by Albert Einstein, the preeminent scientist of the 20th century. Bellamy Foster, discussing his Introduction to Einstein’s essay, explains the importance of Einstein’s contribution in the postwar context and into the present.

Read more

here

, and

watch here.


A note: Almost as soon as Fries released the Einstein piece, it made the rounds, circulating to such outlets as

Naked Capitalism,


The Analysis

, and the like.


REVIEWS


For

Green Socialist

,

 Vol 114, by

Bryn Glover

:


“Mention the name Albert Einstein in any modern context and the most likely images it will provoke would be of a wild-haired old man, and his famous equation, E=mc2. It may also conjure cartoon caricatures of such a person advertising an energy supply company. Given the real man’s unwavering dedication to international socialism, the likelihood of his actually allowing his name to promote a capitalist enterprise is extremely remote…. …Einstein strongly supported the founding of the journal, Monthly Review, and was persuaded by a mutual friend of one of the founding editors, Leo Huberman, to contribute an article. author: Publicación Abierta
title: Venezuela: En las Comunas permanece viva la reserva estratégica de la Revolución
content:
Venezuela


La hora de los hornos: el internacionalismo en tiempos difíciles


Cira Pascual Marquina (*)


En Venezuela, los internacionalistas deben dirigir su mirada hacia las comunas, porque es allí donde permanece viva la reserva estratégica de la revolución.


Por más de dos décadas, fue fácil solidarizarse con la Revolución Bolivariana. Caracas llegó a ser una suerte de capital política para una izquierda internacional heterogénea: militantes de partido y sindicalistas, antiimperialistas e intelectuales y, cada vez más, personas cuya relación con la política estaba mediada por las redes sociales. Llegaban a congresos, reuniones y elecciones. Eran hospedados en hoteles de lujo, se reunían con funcionarios del gobierno y, en algunos casos, con comuneros y activistas de base. Luego, regresaban a casa llevando consigo las imágenes y los argumentos de una revolución que, durante gran parte de ese período, avanzaba a pesar de la tremenda presión que el imperialismo ejercía sobre el proceso.


Esta historia es importante. Venezuela abrió un espacio político y material en el que gentes de diferentes partes del mundo pudieron reunirse, intercambiar experiencias e imaginar un proyecto común. Los encuentros internacionales organizados durante los años de Chávez y Maduro formaron parte de un esfuerzo más amplio por construir una nueva geografía política en América Latina y el Sur Global. Colaboraron para mantener redes, amistades, campañas y formas de cooperación política que de otro modo habrían sido difíciles de establecer. Sería mezquino e históricamente inexacto desestimar estas experiencias simplemente porque las condiciones que las hicieron posibles han cambiado desde entonces, o porque algunos visitantes se sintieron atraídos tanto por los privilegios que les otorgó la revolución como por la tarea de construirla.


Había, sin embargo, un techo para esta forma de solidaridad. Las condiciones materiales permitían participar en la revolución sin compartir sus riesgos o las crecientes dificultades cotidianas que enfrentadas por los venezolanos del pueblo trabajador a causa del bloqueo imperialista. El propio gobierno lo hizo posible: mediante un gran esfuerzo de organización y sacrificio colectivo, desarrolló la capacidad de recibir a miles de visitantes, organizar eventos y proporcionar alojamiento, permitiendo así que el visitante internacionalista viviera la revolución sin verse afectado por las penurias que pasaban los venezolanos y, a menudo, al margen de los intensos debates que se desarrollaban en las bases. Este internacionalismo exigía poco de quienes lo practicaban y ofrecía recompensas a los visitantes, pero fue útil.


La situación ha cambiado drásticamente. Desde el 3 de enero, cuando el imperialismo estadounidense bombardeó objetivos en Venezuela y secuestró al presidente Nicolás Maduro y a la diputada Cilia Flores, el Proceso Bolivariano ha entrado en un período mucho más difícil, marcado por retrocesos tácticos, nuevas contradicciones y acontecimientos que han restringido algunas de los caminos abiertos por la revolución. Por ahora, no se trata de un simple retroceso, sino de una vuelta atrás que cierra ciertas posibilidades, mientras deja intacto el terreno sobre el cual continúa el proceso radical de construcción de comunas.


Para muchos internacionalistas que viajaron a Venezuela antes del 3 de enero, el proyecto comunal estaba, en gran medida, al margen de su participación política con la revolución, aunque muchos realizaron visitas de dos o tres horas a alguna comuna de Caracas. Sin embargo, el discurso en torno a la comuna se convirtió en un pilar central de la defensa internacional de la Revolución Bolivariana. Este énfasis no fue infundado. Hoy, las comunas constituyen la principal reserva estratégica de la revolución, aunque su desarrollo sigue siendo altamente desigual.


El proceso revolucionario venezolano no ha llegado a su fin. La experiencia política acumulada durante más de dos décadas permanece viva en muchas comunas, así como las capacidades forjadas a través de años de lucha. Y, quizás más importante aún, las comunas continúan existiendo como espacios vivos de resistencia, organización, producción, deliberación y poder popular, aunque con niveles muy diferentes de desarrollo y conciencia política.


En su mejor expresión, el internacionalismo es una relación de compromiso político recíproca –aunque no necesariamente simétrico– entre fuerzas organizadas: un intercambio de capacidades …

In diesem Moment.

title: ‘Philippines not for sale,’  groups tell investors
content:
Tensions flared outside the venue of the investors’ forum at the posh Bonifacio Global City between the activists and the police where 29 activists sustained injuries after they were dispersed by the police. Photo courtesy of Altermidya

The groups rejected the Luzon Economic Corridor, calling it a “massive sellout” of Philippine patrimony.

MANILA – “The Philippines is not for sale!”

Progressive groups led by the Bagong Alvansang Makabayan (Bayan) and International League of Peoples Struggle (ILPS) Philippines on Thursday expressed their strong condemnation as the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) Investment Forum inaugurated on Thursday, September 10 at the Grand Hyatt Hotel at the Bonifacio Global City, Taguig City.

The group said the initiative is a threat to Philippine sovereignty and a vehicle for foreign control over the country’s resources.

In a joint statement, the groups rejected the LEC, calling it a “massive sellout” of Philippine patrimony, and accused the government of allowing foreign interests to shape the country’s infrastructure and economic development agenda.

Sponsored by the U.S. Trade and Development Agency (USTDA), the event brought together about 600 international investors, industry leaders, project developers, and government officials to discuss investment opportunities within the Subic-Clark-Manila-Batangas corridor.

Bayan and ILPS argued that the corridor would not lead to genuine industrialization but instead create profit opportunities for foreign companies and local business interests. The groups questioned the prominent role of the U.S. government in promoting the initiative, noting that the USTDA is sponsoring and organizing the investment forum

According to the USTDA, the LEC is a trilateral initiative involving the Philippines, the United States, and Japan aimed at mobilizing investments in transportation, logistics, energy, digital infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing. The agency said the corridor seeks to strengthen connectivity and economic growth across Luzon

The groups also cited the proposed 232-kilometer Subic-Clark-Manila-Batangas Freight Railway, which they said would primarily serve foreign commercial interests. Corridor documents identify the freight railway as a key transport project linking major economic hubs in Luzon.

Among the projects criticized by the groups was the proposed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone, which they claimed could accelerate critical mineral extraction and affect Indigenous and agricultural communities.

Bayan and ILPS further alleged that the corridor forms part of a broader U.S. strategy in the Indo-Pacific and raised concerns over what they described as the possible dual-use nature of infrastructure projects located near strategic transportation and military facilities.

The groups said several corridor projects could support both commercial and defense-related activities, citing developments in Subic and other strategic locations. Corridor materials show that the LEC connects key economic centers, ports, airports, and transport networks across Subic, Clark, Manila, and Batangas.

Bayan and ILPS urged the public to reject the corridor, arguing that national development should remain under Filipino control and not be driven by foreign governments or investors. The groups also criticized recent government policies that they said were designed to attract more foreign investment and expand critical mineral projects associated with the corridor.

“Do not sell the Philippines to foreigners. The Philippines belongs to Filipinos. If the government is to undertake projects or programs for industrialization, these should be geared toward national industrialization by Filipinos and for Filipinos, not for foreign interests.,” said former Bayan Muna Rep. Teddy Casino, now chairperson of Bayan, during the protest.

For Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP), the LEC is being presented as “economic development” by Ferdinand Marcos administration, but in reality, the group said it is “really a corridor for imperialist profit and war.”

“Filipino land, resources and infrastructure are being prepared to serve foreign corporations, global supply chains and the strategic military interests of the United States,” said KMP Chairperson Danilo ‘Ka Daning’ Ramos in a statement.

author: Editors
title: 9/11: How the US turned tragedy into barbarity
content:
Twenty-five years ago, the world changed irrevocably. Not because terrorists from the al-Qaeda network attacked the United States, bringing down the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers in New York, hitting the Pentagon in Virginia and killing nearly 3,000 people. It changed because of US imperialism’s response.

The day after 9/11, the editors of

Socialist Alternative

 magazine, one of the precursor publications of

Red Flag

, warned: “The real threat to people around the world is not terrorism, but the racism, militarism, repression and nationalism that has been unleashed in the wake of the terrorist attacks”.

A week later, President George W. Bush, in an address to a joint session of Congress, announced his so-called War on Terror: “Every nation, in every region, now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists”. His administration rode the wave of outrage over al-Qaeda’s assault to open a new era of imperialist aggression that has cost millions of people’s lives. 

First came Afghanistan in October. It didn’t matter that the ruling Taliban

offered to hand over Osama bin Laden

, the alleged mastermind of the terrorist attacks, to a neutral country to face trial. The US was interested only in war. Condoleezza Rice, then Bush’s national security adviser, admitted as much to the

New Yorker

’s Nicholas Lemann several months later. In the wake of the 9/11 attacks, she had asked senior national security staff to think about how to “capitalise on these opportunities”. 

The Bush administration soon began making a public case for invading Iraq—which had no ties to 9/11—declaring the country part of an “axis of evil” with Iran and North Korea. Undersecretary of State John Bolton soon expanded the axis list to include Cuba, Libya and Syria. The bombs started raining down on Baghdad in March 2003.

These invasions would have been followed by more had the resistance in Iraq not bogged down the US military in an intractable counterinsurgency. Nevertheless, Brown University’s

Costs of War research

 estimates the direct death toll from US military operations in the post-9-11 era in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan to be close to 1 million people. It estimates a further 3.6 to 3.8 million “indirect” deaths resulting from the “destruction of economies, healthcare systems, infrastructure and the environment”. 

The US also set up a global kidnapping network, which it termed “extraordinary rendition”, and a series of “black sites” in which prisoners were held without charge and tortured.

The Open Society Foundation estimates

 that 54 governments collaborated in the program. Then there is the notorious

Guantánamo Bay torture camp

, used since 2002 and still holding ageing prisoners from the War on Terror. This all served as notice that the US empire would stop at nothing to maintain its global domination.

A more enduring legacy of this era of “forever wars” has been the construction of vast internal security and surveillance states, which have trampled civil and democratic rights. 

More than 140 governments have adopted “counterterrorism” legislation since 9/11, beginning with the USA PATRIOT Act, which green-lit mass surveillance and delayed-notice search warrants and bolstered spy agency resources. Mega-departments, such as Homeland Security in the US and Home Affairs in Australia, were established as Western states have become more authoritarian.

Indeed, Australia is one of the worst offenders. “No other nation can match the volume of Australia’s counter-terrorism laws”, wrote legal academics Rebecca Ananian-Welsh and Keiran Hardy in

a 2021 piece for the University of Queensland’s

Contact

 magazine

. They describe the scope of the laws as “staggering”, “unprecedented” and “extreme”, noting that they go beyond even “historical wartime powers”.

They include control orders, preventive detention, and compulsory retention of all telecommunication and online data of every resident. The

Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Act

 of 2021 gave law enforcement agencies the power to take control of a person’s individual online accounts, modify or delete their data and even take over entire networks. That is, they can legally alter a person’s text messages.

Death and destruction abroad and authoritarianism at home: such is the “rules-based order”, the purported demise of which we are supposed to lament. This post-9/11 era normalised authoritarianism …

author: ROAPE
title: Charting the evolution of US-led imperialism, 1974-2026
content:
In 1990, Indian Marxist economist and political commentator Prabhat Patnaik asked ‘

Whatever has happened to imperialism?

’. His point was not that it had disappeared. To the contrary, he argued, “the deafening silence about imperialism is a reflection of the extraordinary strength and vigour it is displaying at present”. The silence is no more. The mask of US-led imperialism is now off. The long, drawn-out process of seeking to justify and manufacture consent for the illegal invasions of Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003 abandoned.


In its place, bald assertions and celebrations of US imperialist intent from President Trump and his White House coterie of acolytes. The deafening explosion of US-Israeli bombs, missiles, mortars, and munitions falling from the skies over Gaza and Iran. Over

100,000 tonnes of explosives dropped on Gaza

 alone since October 2023.


Following Patnaik’s logic, this new phase of flagrant ‘might is right’ imperialism might be interpreted as a weakening of the US’ position as global imperialist hegemon. Perhaps so – yet it will not feel this way to those who suffer under its unrelenting assault.


Gaza, Iran, Venezuela and the much-less covered

intensification of the Cuban blockade

 are the most glaring examples of US-led imperialism in 2026. Who will fall next, under the pounding of US bombs, the chokehold of US sanctions or blockade, the deposing or killing of sovereign leaders?    


In such a moment, developing and deepening our understanding of US-led imperialism has become an urgent task for radical and progressive forces everywhere. In this spirit,

Review of African Political Economy

 offers a curated selection of ten open-access publications on the topic of US-led imperialism from our archives.


For the inspired reader, our

more than 50 years of easily searchable archives

 are filled with further analysis on imperialism and Africa including engagement with the broader debates concerning class, accumulation and state capture. The simple use of the keyword ‘imperialism’ alone, for instance,

returns 85 articles

 that focus in one way or another on this topic.


Collectively, the ten contributions listed below theorise the evolving drivers, manifestations and contradictions of US-led imperialism over time (for, to harness Cabral, “

nobody has yet made a successful revolution without a revolutionary theory

”) while laying bare its devastating consequences for those against whom it is directed.


US-led imperialism and Africa


1.


US imperialism and Southern Africa

, Barry Cohen (1977)


Contends Carter-era US policy toward Southern Africa sought not to end imperial domination but to manage decolonisation and racial conflict in ways that preserved  capitalist and strategic interests while containing revolutionary movements.


2.


Imperialism and the national bourgeoisie

, Bjorn Beckman (1981)


Argues local capitalist classes in postcolonial Africa are not anti-imperialist national liberators but partners of global capital, helping reproduce underdevelopment by using state power to shield both domestic and foreign elites from popular demands.


3.


Imperialism in the post-cold war era

, Giles Mohan and Alfred Zack-Williams (1995)


Demonstrates how in the post-Cold War era, imperialism has not disappeared but has been reconfigured through debt, structural adjustment, financial globalisation, and selective intervention, continuing to subordinate African development to the interests of advanced capitalist powers.


4.


Bringing imperialism back in

, Ray Bush and Morris Svfetel (1999)


Contends the dominant discourse of globalisation obscures the enduring realities of imperialism, showing how international financial institutions, debt regimes, and neoliberal restructuring deepen African dependency while presenting market rule as the only possible path to development.


5.


Africa, imperialism and new forms of accumulation

, Sarah Bracking and Graham Harrison (2003)


Argues contemporary African capitalism remains structured by imperialist relations in which global and local elites use states, markets, debt, and new forms of accumulation to reproduce inequality, exploitation, and external domination under the banner of globalisation and development.


6.


Imperialism and international governance: the case of US policy towards Africa

, Robert Biel (2003)

author: Randi Beers
title: A case for rent control in Nunavut
content:
As temperatures drop and we start to prepare for another fall, we’re reminded of one of Nunavut’s most urgent problems: housing.


Andrew Morrison


We don’t need another study to make us aware of the crisis. We see it every day not only on the streets of Iqaluit, but in other, more hidden ways: students coming home with nowhere to live, families crammed into relatives’ homes and long-time Iqalummiut losing their staff housing when they retire. Too many people face various forms of homelessness in their own homeland.


The numbers back this up. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. reports that Iqaluit’s rental vacancy rate was just 0.3 per cent in 2025 — six empty units out of nearly 2,000. That leaves tenants with almost no alternatives and lets rents climb far beyond what many can afford.


Nunavut should freeze rents.


Rent control won’t solve the whole housing crisis. It won’t build the homes we badly need, and it won’t house everyone who is currently without shelter. But a rent freeze will help address staggering rental rates that seem to be going up every time we blink. 


Rent control won’t lower today’s already high rates, but it would limit how fast they can rise in future. Right now, Nunavut’s Residential Tenancies Act allows landlords to raise rent once every 12 months, with three months’ written notice — but sets no limit on the size of the increase.


For example, a landlord could raise rent on a one-bedroom apartment from $2,500 to $5,000 a month, as long as the notice requirements are met. There’s no cap. In a territory where buying a house seems more and more like a distant dream (or nightmare) and government staff housing regimes inflate the rental market, local tenants simply have nowhere else to go.


A freeze on rent can also have other positive impacts on tenant rights. Following New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s election on a rent-freeze platform, reports suggest New York landlords became more responsive to tenants’ repair requests, potentially reflecting the benefits of prioritizing tenants’ rights.


The path forward is clear. The minister of justice can amend the Residential Tenancies Act to let municipalities set their own rent-control rules, within territory-wide minimum standards. Iqaluit could adopt protections suited to its pressures, while Igloolik would remain free to choose its own approach.


We have a rental officer who hears landlord-tenant disputes. That office should be given authority to investigate unlawful rent increases, order repayment and enforce the rules.


Any new rules should cover all new rental units and should apply to housing paid for by governments and Inuit organizations. Rent control is also in the interest of the Nunavut government, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. and other institutions facing steep staff-housing cost increases over the past 15 years.


Of all the housing problems we face, this one has a straightforward fix. The GN, NTI, and the City of Iqaluit should push for that authority — and use it.


Nunavummiut deserve stronger tenant rights and the security of knowing their homes will stay within reach.


Andrew Morrison is a lawyer and musician who lives in Iqaluit.

editors@nunatsiaq.com

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Albo is proud to be a houso—will anyone else get the chance?
content:
“I’m proud to be a houso, and I’m proud of the community in which I grew up.” These were the words of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, spoken with a quivering top lip, after One Nation leader Pauline Hanson attacked his mother, Maryanne Albanese, for living most of her life in a public housing unit.

“Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 [years]”, Hanson said. “And he said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years.”

Albanese may be proud to be a houso, but his party is ensuring that very few others will be able to access the level of housing security he and his mother did. Across the country, public housing is being eroded and depleted—homes and buildings left in disrepair, demolished or sold off to private developers. The idea that the government should build and provide long-term public housing to those who need it has been almost entirely destroyed.

In Victoria, public housing has been decimated. Walk-up estates have been bulldozed to make way for luxury developments, and 44 apartment towers are scheduled for demolition. The UN special rapporteur on adequate housing, Koldo Casla, has condemned the slated demolition of the 44 towers. In his letter to the Australian government, Casla writes:

“I am concerned that affected residents have primarily been treated as occupants of public property rather than as rights-holders entitled to participate in decisions fundamentally affecting their homes and communities.”

Demolishing housing will force residents out of homes meant to be permanent, out of their communities and away from vital services and infrastructure they depend on. All in the middle of a housing crisis.

According to the Victorian Housing Peaks Alliance, Victoria needs 377,000 more social housing dwellings by 2051 to accommodate everyone who needs low-cost housing. Instead of demolishing public housing and handing over public land to private developers, the government should refurbish existing stock and build new homes.

“It must be reasonably feared that the destruction of 44 public housing towers in central locations or the city will rather amplify these problems and not be a suitable measure to address these preexisting violations of the right to adequate housing”, Casla notes.

The Victorian Labor government says that the total number of dwellings will increase. But it will cut public housing unit numbers significantly. They will be replaced by a mix of community housing, run by not-for-profit agencies, and private dwellings sold at market rates. Tenants have fewer rights, face higher costs, enjoy less long-term housing security and are more easily evicted from community housing as compared to public housing. Data from the Australian Institute of Housing and Welfare in 2023, for instance, shows that when comparing public and community housing tenure length, the proportion of public housing residents that have lived in their homes for more than a decade is twice that of the community housing sector.

Residents in inner-city suburbs will and have been shunted off to outer suburbs, far from the schools, kindergartens and other services they rely on and that connect them with others. Many won’t be able to return to public housing at all.

This adds to the general erosion of the idea that housing is a human right that should be guaranteed to all. Instead of being an option for working-class people to live in, raise their families and build their communities over a lifetime, public housing is increasingly seen as a temporary option for only the most desperate—those living in extreme poverty and for whatever reason unable to participate in the labour market. Today, it is being deliberately run down to make its demolition or sell-off inevitable.

Public housing in Australia has always fallen below the standard of Britain and Western Europe. Writing in the

Marxist Left Review

, Jordan Humphreys details the limitations: “Access to public housing would be restricted to those on very low incomes, so it would be put aside only for the very poorest of the poor. If not enough of the poor could be found, then the Housing Commissions were encouraged to sell off ‘excess’ housing stock”. By the 1960s, two-thirds of British people lived in public housing, compared to only 4.2 percent of Australians (today it is about 2.6 percent).

The Victorian government’s housing strategy document describes public housing as a “legacy”, and what remains is intended …

author: Amira El-Fekki
title: Clashes flare around Warraq with tensions high as island residents campaign for housing guarantees
content:
Warraq Island residents clashed with security forces deployed intensively on and around the Nile island this week, with tensions flaring as authorities are yet to respond to the residents’ demands for clear answers and guarantees regarding the fate of their homes and lands.


The new chapter in talks between residents and authorities comes as families in Warraq take action to disrupt the government’s ongoing development project and seek firm guarantees that officials will support them to stay in their homes and lands.


Security forces set up on Tuesday metal mesh barriers at the entrance to the Qolaly ferry crossing that connects the island to the Nile bank, and, on Wednesday, more barriers were added in the vicinity of the crossing, according to a resident of the island who spoke to Mada Masr.


The measures, they said, add to a series of existing restrictions already imposed on the residents’ movement and access to key goods and services.


The new barriers appear intended to protect security personnel, after stones were thrown during clashes with residents near the ferry crossing in the preceding days, the resident said.


The latest of these took place at Qolaly on Sunday and Monday, with several residents injured as a result, including a young man whose skull was fractured in the clashes, they added.


To protest the security response to the Qolaly clashes, several residents also gathered at a demonstration on Monday evening near a security forces deployment stationed beneath the Tahya Misr Bridge that runs through the island.


The gathering ended in further

clashes

, according to two residents who were present. The confrontations were visible in footage posted by Warraq residents on social media.


As the ban on construction materials entering the island continues, the Qolaly ferry crossing, the main entry point to Warraq from Giza, has been a flashpoint of near-daily confrontations between residents and security forces for around nine years. One resident said to Mada Masr that the friction around the entry of materials to the island arises mainly between security forces and residents who work to deliver construction supplies to the island — but the clashes it triggers spill over to other residents in the area around the ferry.


The clashes come in parallel to a campaign to remain the island that residents have pursued since August. A large number of island residents have begun organizing as part of a group called Staying on Warraq, pushing for firm guarantees from authorities regarding the fate of their land and homes, according to several residents who have spoken to Mada Masr in recent weeks, particularly as circulating reports and unofficial maps of the government’s development project appear to include parts of the residents’ lands.


For years, residents have watched the development project unfold, waiting to learn what would happen to them, while their access to basic services on the island — like healthcare and education — has deteriorated due to state restrictions, leaving residents to establish replacements or alternatives themselves. Their efforts have included spending around LE400,000 to prepare schools for the current academic year.


They have now concluded that waiting has brought no solutions, as the state continues to carry out the project after

acquiring

most of the island’s land, the residents have said.


As part of this campaign, residents attempted on Sunday to obstruct the state’s road construction work on the island, blocking the way of transportation trucks involved in the state development project. The following day, they

held

a protest outside the New Warraq City Development Authority, where they vowed to escalate until their demands are met.


“People went out and stood outside the authority because the state is now building the roads, and they found out that the roads are getting close to residents’ homes. What impact will this have in terms of demolitions?” a lawyer from the island told Mada Masr.


“The state doesn’t solve anything. It wants to suffocate people so that they get fed up and leave,” one of the two residents who witnessed Monday’s clashes said. They said residents planned to continue disrupting the construction work being carried out by the state. “God willing, all the work will stop,” they said.


The second resident said halting construction has an impact that “is felt quickly” because the work involves multiple companies and bodies. Clashes, by contrast …

author: winter oak
title: The Love Activists
content:
This is the third in a selection of chapters from the book 

King of the Squatters

 by jaybo which we are delighted to be able to share on Winter Oak. The whole text can be found as a pdf

here

.


Here we are in 2015.


I do not recall my last night in Ireland, at all. I was extremely upset to leave Amy and all of our new friends behind. They got me very drunk to deal with the situation. When I arrived back in Liverpool, the Love Activists (LAs) had achieved support and notoriety in the city, after squatting six different high-profile places in a few months. The LAs had started out in London, declaring themselves to be anarchists driven, by love, to help house and feed the homeless and bring down the evil bankers and their corrupt system.


One LA known as ‘Grandad’ described the LAs eviction from the Bank of England to me. He said that they had been kept on lock-down, a prison term for everyone being locked up in their cells, for two long weeks by the police. The police had erected a tall steel fence which completely surrounded the bank and a cordon of cops then stood completely surrounding the fence all day and night. Upon witnessing this action local people spontaneously formed their own human chain surrounding the police and also maintained a 24/7 presence. Supporters cheekily threw many crucial supplies right over the polices heads to grateful activists who caught them on window balconies!


He said, “Almost everybody who entered the bank respected the building. Only a few made some graffiti on walls, and that could have easily been painted over. But the police did not respect the building cutting through those amazing doors.” Grandad also told me, with great pride, “The fire bobbies were called to the eviction. When they arrived, they talked and quickly decided that they were employed to save lives, not evict homeless people. They fucked off, to cheers from the crowd of hundreds surrounding the police. Ha Ha!”


Having been unceremoniously evicted from the Bank of England on Castle Street in the spring, the LAs had blazed a trail of six squats from the city centre, south, ending up on Sefton Park meadows. They had set up camp “right outside fat Joe’s new offices”, fat Joe being the name many of our people in the city used to describe the deeply unpopular

mayor of Liverpool

. The LAs had squatted a Georgian terraced block of houses in the city centre, and they did a sit-down protest on the road at the entrance to the Mersey car tunnel, closing the tunnel down completely. They had stormed the city, which had not seen any squatting in the previous twenty years, and received the support and admiration of thousands of ordinary people across the region.


As I approached the LAs camp on Sefton Meadows for the first time, it warmed my heart to see the anarchist flag that had hung from the Bank of England flying high, together with a Bob Marley flag. As I got closer, I saw a big banner at the side of the kitchen, next to the camp’s entrance, which read in large letters, ‘Uprising of the Homeless’. I never expected to read such an audacious banner and was utterly intrigued.


The LAs and Uprising of the Homeless (UOTH) camp was right on my old doorstep. Situated just across Princes Park to Sefton Park on the meadows beyond. A lovely, open site that had been left to the people of Liverpool, two hundred years previously, in perpetuity, i.e. forever, as a green haven in an industrial city. Sefton Park was one of Liverpool’s biggest and best parks, just a short walk from the city centre and the River Mersey. There were huge, magnificent, old trees surrounding the meadows, and about twenty-five raggle-taggle tents had been erected in the middle, surrounded by a rope border.


On a beautiful early summer’s afternoon, with everything I owned in my backpack, I slowly walked across the meadows towards the camp, full of anticipation. There was a group of mostly men sitting around a small fire. I saw Jed and Grandad first. They both gave me a huge smile as I got closer. Then I saw Lisa Love, looking like a futuristic steam punk. She also gave me a huge smile and had a very powerful energy. She seemed to have all of the men’s respect. Then I saw Biggy, and he gave me possibly the cheekiest smile I had ever seen. I knew immediately that I would be fine with the LAs and UOTH. I was definitely in the right place.


Most of the guys that I met at the camp considered themselves to be both LAs and UOTH. I asked about the Bank of …

author: Mag
title: Energiearmut und Stromsperren: Den Armen wird der Strom gesperrt, den Reichen die Fonds gefüllt
content:
Dossier


„

Artikel 1 GG: “Die Würde aller Menschen, die über ein mittleres oder hohes Einkommen verfügen, ist unantastbar”. Kommt Ihnen an diesem Satz etwas merkwürdig vor? Richtig: Eigentlich heißt es: “Die Würde des Menschen” – aller Menschen. Da ja niemand so gemein wäre, die zuständigen Behörden und die Stromlieferanten des Verfassungsbruchs zu bezichtigen, können wir daraus nur eine Schlussfolgerung ziehen: Personen, die es aus sozialer Not heraus nicht mehr schaffen, ihren Strom zu bezahlen, sind überhaupt keine Menschen. Denn ist es etwa “würdig”, ohne warmes Wasser und warme Mahlzeiten zu leben, ohne Telefon, Internet, Radio und Fernsehen, mit ungebügelter Wäsche, frierend und im Dunkeln? In Anlehung an Marie Antoinette könnte man da vielleicht raten: “Wenn sie keinen Strom mehr haben, sollen sie halt Kerzen aufstellen!” Holdger Platta weist in seinem erschütternden und hervorragend recherchierten Artikel auf einen alltäglichen Skandal hin, der selbst in “linken” und sozial engagierten Kreisen viel zu selten, viel zu wenig vehement kritisiert wird

…“

Artikel von Holdger Platta vom 22. Mai 2014 in Konstantin Weckers Webmagazin


 und dazu seitdem:


3,8 Millionen Menschen leben in Haushalten mit Zahlungsrückständen bei Versorgungsbetrieben


„

Das Begleichen von Strom- oder Gasrechnungen stellt für einige Menschen eine finanzielle Herausforderung dar. Rund 3,8 Millionen Menschen lebten im Jahr 2025 nach eigenen Angaben in Haushalten, die bei Rechnungen von Versorgungsbetrieben wie etwa Strom- oder Gasanbietern im Zahlungsverzug waren. Das entsprach einem Anteil von 4,6 % der Bevölkerung, wie das Statistische Bundesamt (Destatis) nach Ergebnissen der Erhebung zu Einkommen und Lebensbedingungen (EU-SILC) mitteilt. Im Vergleich zum Vorjahr ist der Anteil leicht gesunken: Im Jahr 2024 hatten 5,0 % der Bevölkerung Zahlungsrückstände bei Rechnungen von Versorgungsbetrieben

…“

destatis-Pressemitteilung vom 14. September 2026


 und dazu:


Millionen Deutsche haben Zahlungsrückstände bei Versorgungsbetrieben


„

Viele Menschen in Deutschland kommen mit dem Begleichen ihrer Strom- und Gasrechnungen nicht hinterher. Besonders betroffen sind laut Statistikern Mieter.


Rund 3,8 Millionen Menschen in Deutschland hatten im vergangenen Jahr Probleme, ihre Strom- und Gasrechnungen fristgerecht zu bezahlen. Dies entspreche einem Anteil von 4,6 Prozent der Bevölkerung, teilte das Statistische Bundesamt mit. Im Vergleich zum Vorjahr ist der Anteil leicht gesunken: Im Jahr 2024 hatten 5,0 Prozent der Bevölkerung Zahlungsrückstände bei Rechnungen von Versorgungsbetrieben.


Besonders Mieterinnen und Mieter beglichen Rechnungen nicht: Während 3,3 Prozent der Menschen aus Eigentümerhaushalten im vergangenen Jahr bei Versorgungsbetrieben im Zahlungsverzug waren, lag der Anteil bei Mieterhaushalten mit 5,8 Prozent höher.


Höhere Nebenkosten


Auch Nebenkosten und Nebenkostennachzahlungen bedeuten für viele Mieterinnen und Mieter eine finanzielle Belastung. Die Preise für Wohnungsnebenkosten waren zuletzt leicht überdurchschnittlich gestiegen. Diese lagen laut den Statistikern im August 2026 um 3,1 Prozent höher als im Vorjahresmonat…“


Agenturmeldung vom 14. September 2026 in der Zeit online

 


Steigende Energiearmut: Verbraucherzentralen fordern Schutz vor Sperren


„… Verbraucherschützer:innen fordern mehr Rechte für Kund:innen, denen Energieversorger den Strom oder das Gas absperren wollen. Die Kosten einer Sperrung für die betroffenen Verbraucher:innen unterscheiden sich erheblich, zeigt ein noch unveröffentlichter Marktvergleich des Bundesverbands der Verbraucherzentralen (VZBV), der der taz vorliegt. Einer Energiesperre geht immer ein Zahlungsrückstand voraus. Sie kann bereits ab einem Zahlungsverzug von 100 Euro vom Lieferanten eingeleitet werden. Das ist kein Randproblem. Dem Monitoringbericht 2025 der Bundesnetzagentur und des Bundeskartellamts zufolge – der derzeit aktuellste Bericht – erhielten im Jahr 2024 rund 4,6 Millionen Haushalte eine Sperrandrohung für Strom. Bei Gas waren es knapp eine Million. (…) Nach Auffassung der Verbraucherschützer:innen sind die gesetzlichen Fristen von vier Wochen zwischen Sperrdrohung und Vollzug sowie die acht Werktage zwischen der Sperrankündigung und der tatsächlichen Versorgungsunterbrechung zu kurz. author: CMI Argentina
title: Neuquén: la provincia le dio la personería jurídica a la comunidad Melo pero sigue la amenaza de desalojo
content:
En Neuquén el gobierno provincial acaba de reconocer la personería jurídica a la Lof Melo. Lo paradójico de esta situación es que la reconoce la personería jurídica como comunidad, sin embargo la amenaza de desalojo no retrocede.


Escuchá el reporte de Maitén Cañicul desde la FM Che.


Julieta Melo, werquen de la Lof Melo, expresó al respecto: “El gobierno nos otorgó la personería jurídica y con este acto se cerró la discusión. Este conflicto no es un conflicto entre privados” y agregó que “la personería jurídica es el DNI colectivo de una comunidad mapuche, algo que viene negando sistemáticamente el juez Bonorino y la terrateniente Cristina Broers a través de su abogado Guillermo Hensel”.


“No necesitábamos estos papeles para demostrar nuestra existencia colectiva como comunidad, pero sabemos que en este sistema era la evidencia con la que podíamos tirar por la borda esa persistente postura negacionista”, explicó.


Los seis consejos zonales de la Confederación Mapuche en Neuquén presentaron una nota a Rolando Figueroa, gobernador de la provincia y al ministro Jorge Tobares, solicitando la personería jurídica no sólo a la comunidad Melo sino también a otras comunidades que la vienen reclamando hace bastante tiempo: “Instamos al gobierno de la provincia del Neuquén el otorgamiento inmediato de personerías jurídicas a todas las comunidades mapuche que la están demandando”.


Además solicitaban la intervención urgente del gobierno de Neuquén ante el fallo injusto del juez Bonorino que mantiene bajo grave amenaza a la comunidad Melo: “La situación de un inminente desalojo no ha cesado, generando una carga emocional sobre mi comunidad. Nos llevará mucho tiempo reparar todo el daño ya causado, por eso el acompañamiento que estamos teniendo hace mucho más llevadera esta situación”.


“Sabemos que si el juez Bonorino mantiene esta postura negacionista y racista hacia nuestra lof y pretende llevar adelante este desalojo, estos acompañamientos se van a multiplicar por todo el territorio”, agregó.
