author: Unknown
title: Merve Asya Özgür: If Kurdish artists are free, Turkish artists also gain - Part Two
content:
Actress Merve Asya Özgür, one of the lead actresses in Pelin Esmer’s latest film And the Rest Will Follow, in which she plays the character Aliye, spoke to ANF about the relationship between art and peace.


Part one of this interview can be read

here

.


You seem to be saying that artists need freedom in order to find the courage to speak. Wouldn’t positive progress in this process help create that freedom?


We were quite critical of the artistic community earlier, but there are also people who genuinely have something to say and cannot express it because of the pressure they face. There is, first of all, a major problem of censorship. These conditions inevitably create their own artistic language. People often say, ‘Art somehow finds a way and creates a new form.’ There is some truth in that, of course. But repression and the inability to speak under that pressure eventually turn into a collective silence, beginning with the self-censorship of those who would otherwise speak out. Then a new generation emerges within that collective silence. They enter the creative process, quietly settle into a corner and fall into line with that silence. The spiral of silence expands to include the new generation, while subdued forms of artistic expression remain trapped within the same vicious cycle.


You know how popular movements are often discussed: repression creates an accumulation of discontent within people, makes contradictions visible and awakens feelings of resistance. Anger grows and accumulates until, eventually, it develops into a mass movement. There is often such an expectation in periods when conditions are particularly harsh. That accumulation can, of course, also help movements mature.


But if you look at the history of struggles, radical changes have generally taken place during more moderate periods. Change occurs in an environment where people still have some room to breathe and act, where everything has not yet become completely blocked and entrenched. So if we approach this issue with the hope that a more moderate and democratic atmosphere can emerge, then the silence I mentioned earlier will naturally begin to evolve into something different. People may find the courage to say something new rather than simply repeating the same words in muted voices.


It is quite clear. Artists in the west of the country who have acted as though an issue that has been visible in this region for years simply did not exist may perhaps turn and look at it. Maybe it will become popular; I don’t know. Something that becomes popular can suddenly have a completely different impact and acquire a certain appeal. People want to gravitate towards it. In my view, we should not separate art from the conditions in which it is produced and place it on some idealised pedestal. Art is something created by people; it is a way of seeing. It is influenced by circumstances, its surroundings and the political climate, and it takes shape accordingly. If the more moderate environment we are talking about can be created, I imagine such tendencies will emerge.


We always talk about the artist’s responsibility towards society and their role in ‘showing the way’. But how are artists themselves nourished by society, and what do they learn from it?


Everything an artist knows, sees and creates, everything that nourishes their creative work, comes from society, from the people who make up the society into which they are born and first open their eyes. Even our sense of self is established through another person, through the existence of someone else. I can only be me because I am not you, isn’t that so?


Ultimately, it is society that shapes your entire world of images. Its culture, its stories, the richness of its language, the pain behind it, its folk songs and dances… All this accumulated heritage, the conflicts within it, the political tensions, everything shapes people and the way they live. You grow up within it. You speak its language and try to tell something through that language. Everything from the words you use and the way you think to the laughter and humorous traits of the characters you portray or create comes from the society in which you live. Which sections of society all that we take is ultimately given back to is another, rather neglected question. 


Unfortunately, the art world in Turkey often operates within a closed circle. Under these economic conditions, people are already struggling simply to get through everyday …

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Naujaat’s $19M solar project comes online
content:
From her cabin just outside Naujaat, resident and former Kivalliq Inuit Association director Helena Malliki can see the solar panels she spent years pushing to bring to her community.


“I get a feeling that I’ve done something for the community,” she said in an interview Friday.


Malliki served as the KIA director for Naujaat while plans were developed for the Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link, a proposed 1,200-kilometre transmission line that would carry hydroelectric power north from Manitoba. 


Naujaat and Coral Harbour were not included in the planned route, which was designed to connect five mainland communities: Arviat, Baker Lake, Chesterfield Inlet, Rankin Inlet and Whale Cove.


Malliki said that inspired her to push for another option for Naujaat.


“I was asking if we can get a windmill or a solar panel, and I fought for that,” she said. “And it happened.”


The Ikayuut Solar and Energy Storage Project began supplying electricity to the community’s grid Aug. 20, ahead of a ribbon-cutting ceremony the project partners held Wednesday.


The project was developed by Kivalliq Alternative Energy, a partnership between Sakku Investments Corp. and Vancouver-based Northern Energy Capital. Construction began in 2024.


It operates under Qulliq Energy Corp.’s Independent Power Producer program, which allows independent renewable-energy developers to generate electricity and sell it to QEC.


The Ikayuut Solar and Energy Storage Project is the first to operate under the program.


The solar array is located at a reclaimed municipal scrapyard about 400 metres from the nearest homes in Naujaat, James Griffith, Northern Energy Capital’s director of development said in an email.


The project, which includes 1.4-megawatts of solar power and a one-megawatt-hour battery storage system, is expected to generate roughly 30 per cent of Naujaat’s annual electricity demand, according to a joint release from Sakku and Northern Energy Capital.


Over its expected 25- to 30-year lifespan, it is expected to replace about 400,000 litres of diesel fuel, the release said.


It cost about $19 million to build, Griffith said.


Most of the funding came from federal programs, including the Clean Energy for Rural and Remote Communities program, the Low Carbon Economy Fund, Indigenous Community Infrastructure Fund and the Indigenous Off-Diesel Initiative.


The Government of Nunavut also contributed another $250,000 through its Sustainable Energy Support Policy, he said.


“The most important

 thing about this project was to reduce the cost of energy bills, and for using clean energy, instead of diesel, for the environment,” Malliki said.


Under its Independent Power Producer program, QEC purchases renewable electricity at a price equivalent to the cost of generating electricity with diesel, the corporation told Nunatsiaq News in an email.


Naujaat residents filled all eight to 12 construction jobs that the project created, said Griffith. Two residents will be employed during

 the project’s operations.


QEC says the project is still undergoing testing and is expected to reach its full renewable-energy production capacity in spring 2027, the email said.

title: "Inequality Emergency": Ahead of U.N. General Assembly, Oxfam Urges Action on Climate, AI & Gaza
content:
As world leaders prepare to head to New York for the United Nations General Assembly and Climate Week,

Democracy Now!

 speaks with Amitabh Behar, executive director of Oxfam International. “We live in a very different world from 1945,” when the U.N. was formed, says Behar. “You cannot continue with the veto power.” And with António Guterres soon stepping down, Behar stresses that the United Nations’ next secretary-general must be a woman — “a fundamental shift we need to make.”


He also argues that while the world is “torn apart” by inequality, “there are real possibilities of change.” Behar cites the G20’s International Panel on Inequality and “movements across the world” aimed at “changing regimes,” including in Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh and India.

author: winter oak
title: The Blind Mirror
content:
by

Mike Driver


Humanity is trapped in the space between peace and flow: a permanent agitation. The main culprit is in front of your face right now. The blind mirror, a mirror that only reflects half of reality. The dead half. A mirror that can only present what is constructed, forced, labelled, modelled, politicised, propagandised, manufactured, verified, certified, credentialed, seductive, selective, sensationalised, tampered, re-represented, reified, reduced, separated, digitised, financialised, corporatized, sexualised, compartmentalised, decontextualised, formalised, processed, objectified, artificial, hollow, desacralized, corrupted, depraved, perverted and unfeeling.


A mirror reflecting only the past or an absent future but never now. All the time, every day. A blind mirror that only reflects half of you: the restless, tense, anxious half. The addict. What is propagandised as connection is disconnecting the contextual, grounded, present, relational, quiet, calm, loving half. The half that hosts that feeling of peace we all crave. The half that lives in the reverie of flow. 


There are two states to wish for in this life: peace and flow. The trouble is you can’t aim yourself right at them, they arise as a side effect of doing something else. Agitation on the other hand is an easy target to hit. Just turn your phone on and let the algorithm manipulate your synapses. 


So, what is peace and where do we find it? The recently deceased Wendell Berry (RIP),

pictured

, answers that question for us here:


The Peace Of Wild Things


When despair grows in me

and I wake in the night at the least sound

in fear of what my life and my children’s lives may be,

I go and lie down where the wood drake

rests in his beauty on the water, and the great heron feeds.

I come into the peace of wild things

who do not tax their lives with forethought

of grief. I come into the presence of still water.

And I feel above me the day-blind stars

waiting for their light. 

For a time, I rest in the grace of the world,

and am free.


Where do we ‘rest in the grace of the world’ today? If we were visited by particularly cultured aliens, might they consider annihilation of grace to be the purpose of our modern society? We inhabit environments where the aesthetics are relentlessly ugly and utilitarian, what the architect Chris Alexander describes as ‘these faceless things’’. Where would we go to live what Alexander called ‘the sanctified life’?


Consider the difference between a library and a data centre. The library contains life, warmth, wholeness and beauty, it is connected to history and tradition, it has a quality you struggle to name. A peace you can access. The data centre on the other hand is dis-harmonious, ugly, voracious, atomised, the noise unnatural, the electronic howl of something from the depths of madness.


We’re draining the resources of the planet to build the latter while the former becomes a museum of our lost minds.


McLuhan famously said ‘the medium is the message’ – are we the medium and if so have we become the message? Have we lost ourselves? Has something removed our internal life and replaced our minds with an artificial imposter? What effect does the method of storage and accessibility of knowledge have on us? What happens if we outsource the processing of this knowledge? What is the consequence of the loss of unmediated experience? What is left?


Denise Levertov steps in to explain the problem here: 


Contraband 


The tree of knowledge was the tree of reason.

That’s why the taste of it

drove us from Eden. That fruit

was meant to be dried and milled to a fine powder

for use a pinch at a time, a condiment.

God had probably planned to tell us later

about this new pleasure.

                                  We stuffed our mouths full of it,

gorged on

but

 and

if

 and

how

 and again

but

, knowing no better.

It’s toxic in large quantities; fumes

swirled in our heads and around us

to form a dense cloud that hardened to steel,

a wall between us and God, Who was Paradise.

Not that God is unreasonable – but reason

in such excess was tyranny

and locked us into its own limits, a polished cell

reflecting our own faces. God lives

on the other side of that mirror,

but through the slit where the barrier doesn’t

quite touch ground, manages still

to squeeze in – as filtered light,

splinters of fire, a strain of music heard

then lost, then heard again.


The storage and instant …

author: Redazione_web
title: Stiamo freschi – Il taccuino della crisi climatica. La fisica condanna il capitale
content:
Premessa


La carenza, in primo luogo di chi scrive, di approfondite conoscenze di antropologia biologica e sociale, nonché di termodinamica, induce ad operare delle semplificazioni che, però, ben si addicono ad un articolo che non è destinato ad una pubblicazione su una rivista scientifica ma, semplicemente, si inserisce nella rubrica “Stiamo freschi” come spunto di riflessione e stimolo al confronto sulle tematiche connesse alla crisi climatica.


Prima d’iniziare, vorrei segnalare all’attenzione di chi segue questa rubrica l’opuscolo: “

CRISI CLIMATICA Critiche e prospettive da un punto di vista anarchico

”, curato da un gruppo di lavoro della Federazione Anarchica Italiana. Un documento che inquadra ed approfondisce in maniera più strutturata


il tema dei cambiamenti climatici

che, per il suo carattere globale e per le molteplici implicazioni inerenti a questioni ambientali, sociali ed economiche, non solo assume un interesse riferibile all’intero pianeta Terra, ma permette di sviluppare un’analisi che, inevitabilmente, si riferisce alla complessità della società in cui viviamo.


https://umanitanova.org/crisi-climatica-critiche-e-prospettive-da-un-punto-di-vista-anarchico/


Energia per l’Homo sapiens


Il fenomeno vita, anche nelle sue forme più semplici, gli organismi unicellulari, ha bisogno di energia per svolgere le proprie funzioni fondamentali. Le fonti da cui ricavare energia sono diverse:

 i vegetali sfruttano direttamente l’energia del sole con il processo di fotosintesi; noi umani dipendiamo dall’energia ricavata dalle sostanze nutritive prodotte da altri viventi, apparteniamo cioè alla categoria degli eterotrofi. Se la necessità di alimentarci è, in primo luogo, legata alla sopravvivenza, non possiamo dimenticare che la storia della specie Homo sapiens e della sua evoluzione non solo in termini quantitativi, come numero di individui, ma anche in termini sociali, economici e culturali è strettamente legata allo sfruttamento di diverse risorse energetiche.


Se scorriamo i passaggi più significativi del percorso del genere Homo, dando per scontata l’importanza dell’utilizzo del fuoco (a partire da 1,5 milioni di anni fa), dobbiamo di certo considerare il passaggio

 dai piccoli gruppi di raccoglitori-cacciatori, che usavano solo la propria energia muscolare per la raccolta di vegetali o per la cattura delle prede, all’uomo agricoltore-allevatore, che riesce a ricavare dal lavoro agricolo (fotosintesi controllata) e dallo sfruttamento degli animali addomesticati un surplus alimentare. Tale eccedenza

ha contribuito al primo salto, in termini di disponibilità ed accumulo di energia nella forma delle derrate alimentari. La gestione di forme aggregative più complesse, che ne derivavano, ha favorito una diversa strutturazione dei rapporti sociali, con la definizione di nuovi ruoli e funzioni con la parallela imposizione dei rapporti gerarchici. Se per millenni la fonte di energia per eccellenza è stata rappresentata dal legno, attraverso la sua combustione, e dall’utilizzo degli animali come forza lavoro che in parte sostituisce l’attività muscolare umana, dobbiamo ricordare che a partire dal XVII secolo la domanda di legname, sia per la costruzione di abitazioni, navi, ponti, sia come combustibile, sia per la produzione di carbonella, divenne così elevata da non essere più sostenibile. Dal momento in cui la richiesta superò la capacità di rigenerazione delle foreste, una fonte già conosciuta, il carbone, andò via via aumentando la propria importanza in tutto il corso del XVIII secolo. Un’altra innovazione tecnologica, l’invenzione e il perfezionamento della macchina a vapore (James Watt 1765), determinò un’ulteriore svolta permettendo di sfruttare il carbone su larghissima scala. Il carbone divenne la fonte di energia che rese possibile la prima rivoluzione industriale, con tutte le conseguenze che ben conosciamo: urbanizzazione, accelerazione dello sfruttamento delle risorse umane ed ambientali, rapido sviluppo del sistema capitalista, solo per citarne alcune.


L’inclinazione dell’umanità all’assoggettamento e alla rapina delle risorse naturali non nasce con la rivoluzione industriale né con la nascita delle prime gerarchie proto-statali.

 Homo sapiens

 tende ad ampliare la propria nicchia ecologica dissipando energia residua ogni volta che ne trova l’opportunità tecnica, ma il suo impatto diventa imponente a partire dalla rivoluzione industriale. Infatti,

author: rti_admin
title: Bablai Mata Yatra: How Does Development Politics Affect Madia Culture?
content:
For the Madia Adivasi community in the Bhamragad region, the Bablai Mata Yatra (pilgrimage/fair) is not just a religious pilgrimage but a living symbol of cultural, environmental, and constitutional rights.

However, in recent times, the politics of development, religious conversion, the administration, and Naxalism have begun to significantly impact the Bablai Yatra.

For the Madia Adivasi community in the Bhamragad area, the Bablai Mata Yatra is not merely a religious fair but a living symbol of their cultural, environmental, and constitutional rights. Every year, thousands of Madia Adivasi people from the Bhamragad tract come together to worship Bablai Mata and to renew their generations-old culture, traditions, and relationship with nature. Yet, in the name of development, the pilgrimage of Bablai Devi is slowly disappearing.

According to Adivasi tradition, Bablai was the sister of a man named Morka. Bablai was married to Thakur Dev, who is still worshipped at a shrine on Surjagad today. After their marriage, Thakur Dev went to Surjagad for a second wife, but Bablai did not go away with her people. She stayed in this region, remained among the people here, and became one with this land and forest.

The locals say that their faith was born from this sacrifice:

She left her husband for us, but she never left us, and that is why she is a goddess for us.

Today, Bablai Mata is the presiding deity of Adivasis across the Bhamragad region. This story is not found in written form, but this tradition has been carried forward from generation to generation through the words of the ancestors.

Traditional Governance: Bhoom Perma, Bhoomiya, and Kathdi

The Bablai Yatra is not only about worshipping the deity; it is also where the traditional self-governance system of the Adivasis becomes visible. The highest position in this system is “Bhoom Perma” (in simple terms, the “President” of this traditional system). The Bhoomiya (or Bhoom Bhoomiya) is considered the owner and protector of that place. There are also traditional office bearers like Bhoom, Kotwal, and Kathdi (village-level customary officials). This group consists of around 22 members and includes active participation of women. Together, they handle the worship of Bablai Mata, management of the Yatra, decision-making processes, and the entire religious and cultural programme. In essence, this structure is the local expression of the gram sabha (village assembly), self-governance, and collective decision-making. The Adivasi community believes that Bablai Mata protects all the water, forests, and land in the region. Therefore, the central focus of the Yatra is not only religious rituals but a spiritual relationship with nature.

People from many villages in the Bhamragad area come together to clean the sacred groves in the forest, consider trees, water bodies, and hills as deities, and follow a code of conduct that ensures no harm to nature.

Law, Constitution, and Cultural Protection

Before 2013, the Bablai festival was not celebrated in this form. Even after Independence, the influence of the princely state remained here. After India became independent, the kings of the Aheri State used to visit this tract. People here worshipped them like Brahma Dev — falling at their feet, washing their feet, and serving them through performances like dancing by women performers. The kings would come once or twice a year and enjoy such festivities. This practice continued until about fifteen to twenty years ago. People used to come to Bejur village only for Bablai Mata’s darshan (sacred viewing/audience with the deity).

Later, local scholar-youth took the initiative and made people aware that before Independence they were subjects of the British, and that after Independence the Constitution abolished the princely order. They formed a traditional Kuthul committee (customary coordinating body) in the Bhamragad belt and, by bringing all gram sabhas together, decided that they would gather right here and organise Bablai Mata’s traditional worship and a traditional convention in a proper way. Along with this, all the gram sabhas in the Bhamragad area began discussing the Forest Rights Act and PESA. The Yatra thus became not only a cultural symbol for the Madia community but also a space for public awareness.

Social activist Chinu Mahaka from Bhamragad says that “when the Bablai Yatra began in this way, all the gram sabhas started coming together, and they began discussing the …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: New! Chris dePloeg’s “The Exterminating Empire”
content:
REVIEWS:


Counterpunch

, “

Capitalism is Waging War on Palestine While Creating a Burning Planet

” by Daniel Falcone:


Daniel Falcone:

What is the central argument of

The Exterminating Empire

 and how is the book structured? It looks as though the book serves as an intervention as well as an addition to current scholarship.  


Chris Kaspar de Ploeg:

 I open the book with some jarring facts that seem paradoxical at first sight. We need about 30 percent of our productive capacity to

give everyone on the planet a good life

. Not just the basics like housing, clothing and healthcare, but also modern appliances like refrigerators, laptops, access to the internet and more. At the same time, that standard of living is denied to about

80 percent of the world population

. Green energy has been cheaper than fossil fuels for years, yet climate breakdown is only accelerating. We could

solve world hunger

 with about 0.03 percent of global GDP, but hunger is only increasing.


That looks like an extraordinarily wasteful system, and it is. The point, however, is that under capitalism, these are not paradoxes at all. In fact, they are signs of capital’s success. Under our current economic system, the primary goal, ruthlessly pursued, is

profit maximization

. That profit maximization is reached through pushing down costs–and we are those costs, our labour, our environments, our lives–and by conquering markets, often through a mix of military and economic warfare. That essentially puts

capitalism on a warpath against life

. The system is working exactly as it is supposed to.


We see, for example, that profit rates are higher in the fossil fuel industry because it essentially

functions through monopolies

, despite the higher costs. We see that the military-industrial complex is growing exponentially, targeting any vestiges of resistance against

US-led global hegemony

, which globalized harsh budget cuts in social welfare, healthcare and education. These very conditions of

structural impoverishment

 then create the conditions of desperation necessary for people and countries to accept their status as sources for cheap labour, resources and land for global corporations, mostly centered in the Global North.


In the book I write about a dialectic between slavery and genocide, and between structural genocide and active genocide. A good way to understand that relationship is by going back to the

We Charge Genocide petition

, which was presented in 1951 at the United Nations by William L. Patterson, on behalf of the

Civil Rights Congress

. He estimated that, since the abolition of slavery, some 10,000 black people had been lynched, often for something as small as looking a white woman in the eyes. These lynchings were not hidden affairs, but were a

public spectacle

, for which neighbors came together, and pictures were spread on postcards across the country.


Patterson

 goes on to argue that this kind of active violence serves a deeper purpose. It was meant to intimidate the black masses to accept lower living standards, functioning as a dehumanized workforce for corporations. At the time, this led 32,000 excess deaths every year among Black Americans compared to white death rates. Patterson charges this as a ‘genocide for profit’, based on the article in the UN convention that lists “

deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction

.” Combining two studies that were done since that time, I show that between 1940 and 2020 the total excess death toll of African Americans is 6 million.


Nowadays, scholars tend to call this ‘

structural genocide

’. And I argue that this is a global phenomenon under capitalism. In a sense, the active genocide in Palestine is a lynching aimed at intimidating the Global South into accepting its role as devalued lives for Western profits. The blatant, live-streamed and openly announced nature of that genocide is exactly the point, just as the lynchings of the American South were broadcast widely. It is aimed to intimidate people, because the active genocide serves the broader, structural genocide.


The histories of

genocide and slavery

 are deeply intertwined. In fact, almost every genocide in history also deployed slave labor–even in the archetypical death camp, Auschwitz – and chattel slavery also contained genocidal dynamics of cheapened lives and heightened death rates. In a sense, even in Gaza the …

author: Petala Ironcloud
title: Big Tech Is Trampling Native Treaty Rights to Build Data Centers
content:
Tribal consultation isn’t optional, but the corporations building data centers in New Mexico are acting like it is.

Tribal consultation isn’t optional, but the corporations building data centers in New Mexico are acting like it is.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

In 2004, Microsoft’s future chief sustainability officer, Melanie Nakagawa, co-edited a law journal issue on Indigenous peoples’ right to prior informed consent. This month, as a data center developer routed around exactly that standard in New Mexico, she didn’t answer whether it applies to her own company’s work.

Ask Google, Amazon, and Microsoft whether they consult Native nations before building a data center, and you’ll get the same answer: silence dressed up as sustainability commitment — as if the law here were unsettled, rather than two centuries old. Chief sustainability officers operate by ESG (environment, sustainability, governance) principles that imply tribal consultation, typically executed either to pacify objecting community members or to comply with an environmental review process. ESG reports are meant to define a company’s community impact but instead serve as shields for deals structured to sidestep responsibility.

Project Jupiter, a 1,400-acre Oracle and OpenAI hyperscale data center under development in Santa Teresa, New Mexico, is leased by these tech titans from BorderPlex and Stack: two companies handling physical infrastructure, simultaneously distancing the lessees from responsibility for their environmental and tribal impacts.

ESG (environment, sustainability, governance) reports are meant to define a company’s community impact but instead serve as shields for deals structured to sidestep responsibility.

On August 23, the New Mexico Supreme Court temporarily halted construction for air quality review and ordered a state engineer to diminish water use. Oracle has forecast its use of 11 million gallons of water for an initial fill, plus roughly 168,000 gallons per year in ongoing maintenance. Sen. Melanie Stansbury has separately put the figure at “over a million gallons a day” — a gap neither company nor state officials have reconciled. Lisa Henne, general counsel for the Interstate Stream Commission, told Truthout the water used for construction is purchased from an existing water right holder, not a new appropriation, and that New Mexico’s Pueblos — all located upstream of Elephant Butte Reservoir — aren’t affected, since Jupiter sits in the Lower Rio Grande, a separate hydrological zone.

That leaves an open question: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, based across the state line in Texas, sits in the same Lower Rio Grande stretch, closer to the site than any New Mexico Pueblo. Asked whether the Commission had been in contact with the Pueblo, Henne confirmed it had not. She added, though, that the Commission “would not expect” the project to affect it, based on the same reasoning she applied to New Mexico’s own Pueblos. In other words: no contact, but a conclusion about impact reached anyway.

Even that thin standard assumes someone’s title implies responsibility. OpenAI has no chief sustainability officer at all. The closest approximation would have been the company’s Head of Data Centers Chris Malone, who just left the company in August amid a wave of executive departures, leaving infrastructure decisions split across engineers with no explicitly named party responsible for considering environmental or community impact.

Zephyr Jaramillo of Isleta Pueblo, speaking for Youth United for Climate Crisis Action at the Santa Fe County hearing, put it plainly: “Communities are already considering considerable harm … We look forward to engaging with communities throughout this process.” Whether that engagement extends to Project Jupiter and the Pueblos with senior water rights along its stretch of the Rio Grande, remains an open question that no one — not Oracle, not OpenAI, and not the state — has yet answered.

Amazon is the sole data center builder that appears to uphold a minimal standard of tribal consultation. Teara Farrow Ferman, the program manager for the Department of Natural Resources’ Cultural Protection Program, says, since 2019, the company has held monthly meetings with the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation (CTUIR), signing a memorandum of understanding with the tribes in 2023, and …

author: groundxero
title: Activists Targeted in Mumbai Over Kites Flown in Solidarity with Children in Gaza
content:
Kites flown by activists in solidarity with Palestinian children in Gaza have become the latest reason for police crackdown in Mumbai.


 


Groundxero Desk


19 SEP 2026


 


Even as the government of India under Narendra Modi publicly supports

Palestinian sovereign statehood

 and calls for an immediate halt to violence and forced displacements in Gaza, the BJP ruled state governments across the country are criminalizing acts of solidarity to Palestine.


 


The Mumbai Police allegedly raided a woman activist’s home and detained two other after they participated in a global kite-flying campaign in solidarity with Gaza’s children, This came days after India hosted a BRICS summit that reaffirmed support for Palestinian statehood and opposed the forced displacement of Palestinians.


 


The Indian People in Solidarity with Palestine (IPSP) has alleged that Mumbai Police on Friday riaded the home of a pro-Palestine and IPSP activist, Harshada Borade — a student and an artist — for flying kites in solidarity with Palestinian children, as part of the Global Gaza Kite Weekend 2026. The organisation said plainclothes police personnel entered the home of the volunteer, Harshada, and subsequently conducted a search without producing a warrant, written notice or other authorisation.


 


The search continued for more than 9 hours, and the police officials only left the premises after 2:30 AM on September 19, Saturday. In the ensuing period, they searched and photographed her books and literature, posters, and personal belongings.


 


“More than nine hours – and counting – for ‘searching’ a person’s place of residence

without a warrant

 merely for flying kites in solidarity with Palestinian children!” the Palestine solidarity group said in a social media post on Saturday.


 


According to IPSP, earlier in the week, Mumbai Police had identified two other volunteers who had participated in IPSP’s Kite Campaign, harassed them and forced them into “complying” with their demands, without providing any notice stating the said need for compliance. They also used intimidation tactics to threaten them and their families.


 


As per the panchnama, the action was undertaken in response to a September 15 pro-Palestine Kite campaign that Harshada had participated in, which the police referred to as a “protest”. Among the list of items found inside the house, as per the panchnama, were books and quotations by Bhagat Singh and Savitribai Phule. The panchnama also states that the search was authorised by senior police officials only after the police personnel found Harshada’s behavior to be “suspicious” in nature.


 


The crackdown came days after activists across the world participated in the Global Gaza Kite Weekend, a campaign intended to express solidarity with children in Gaza. The global campaign followed Israeli warnings over kites and balloons being flown by children from Gaza. The Israeli military has said that it would treat kites and balloons flown from Gaza as a security threat on par with drones and act accordingly.


 


The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry has documented the enormous toll of the Israeli military assault on Palestinian children in Gaza. Its June 2026 report recorded at least 20,179 Palestinian children killed and 44,143 injured between 7 October 2023 and 7 October 2025. The Commission concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had deliberately targeted Palestinian children and said such acts formed part of the genocide it had previously found to have been committed by Israel against Palestinians in Gaza.


 


The Mumbai police action on Palestine solidarity activists has acquired a sharper political significance because of the timing.


 


On September 12–13, India hosted the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi. The New Delhi Declaration, adopted by the BRICS countries, expressed concern over continuing violence in Gaza, called for an end to policies aimed at forcibly displacing Palestinians from Gaza, opposed demographic or geographical changes to the territory, and reaffirmed support for the establishment of a

sovereign, independent and viable State of Palestine

 within the internationally recognised 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. The declaration also backed Palestine’s full membership of the United Nations.

Palestinian people’s rights to self-determination

author: M.P
title: “Voces de las artesanas”:  80 relatos audiovisuales que tejen memoria
content:
80 cápsulas (microdocumental) entretejen memoria, territorios y cosmovisión en torno al arte del witral, de la textilería Mapuche.

“Voces de las artesanas” es una serie de 80 microdocumentales diseñados para redes sociales formato Reels, que dan vida al proyecto “Artesanas textileras de Los Ríos”, impulsado durante 2026 por la Fundación Universo en 6 Colores.

Desde Valdivia, esta organización trabaja en la investigación, rescate y difusión del arte y oficio del witral (arte textil Mapuche) y las memorias, historias de vidas y saberes de mujeres Mapuche en La Araucanía, Los Ríos y Los Lagos.

Se trata de una iniciativa financiada por el Fondo Nacional de Desarrollo Cultural y de las Artes, Fondart Regional de Los Ríos, 2025, del Ministerio de las Culturas, las Artes y el Patrimonio.

Al respecto, la investigadora responsable, Paulina Olivares Ramírez, explica sobre Universo en 6 Colores: “Es la comprensión de una forma de vida que se basa en el ecosistema circundante a cada territorio que habla del arte textil Mapuche. Es hablar de botánica, historias de vida, ética del trabajo, vida social y religiosa, y de todos los rasgos culturales que revelan la profundidad y amplitud de la cosmovisión”.

En tanto, sobre la iniciativa audiovisual, menciona: “En apenas 90 segundos de video, abordamos diversas temáticas vinculadas a la experiencia de vida de las mujeres que ejercen el oficio del tejido Mapuche y toda la cadena productiva que su trabajo implica. Son relatos que hablan de sus trayectorias, técnicas, reflexiones y territorios, además del daño ecológico y problemáticas que existen en los lugares en que habitan y que afectan a su oficio.”

“Cada una de las mujeres tejedoras entrevistadas mostró sus distintos quehaceres en torno a la lana, desde productoras, agrupaciones de hilanderas y tejedoras de telar Mapuche. Uno de los grandes desafíos fue adaptar sus narrativas al formato de micro cápsulas formato Reel, por lo que tuvimos que construir guiones atractivos y ágiles, capaces de captar la atención de las audiencias y transmitir lo que hemos observado durante años de trabajo en terreno”.

Así, finalmente destaca: “Ha sido una experiencia profundamente enriquecedora, porque logramos el objetivo inicial que es visibilizar la realidad de las mujeres Mapuche, “mujeres de la tierra” a quienes admiro profundamente. Como Fundación, comprendemos que el arte textil trasciende su materialidad: es un sujeto activo que nace, se transforma y toma forma en las manos de las tejedoras. En cada pieza habita una cosmogonía viva que relata el origen del mundo, entretejida con una conciencia profunda capaz de traducir los diseños de la naturaleza en hilos que reproducen sus patrones, ritmos y saberes. Nuestro propósito es difundir este arte desde la voz de sus creadoras, visibilizando el vínculo entre la memoria comunitaria, las técnicas tradicionales y los ciclos de producción.”

Desde marzo de 2026, la campaña en línea ha consolidado una estrategia de contenido digital de alto impacto, alcanzando la publicación de más de 50 reels en Instagram y Facebook. Este hito refleja la importancia de integrar nuevos medios de difusión para ampliar el alcance del proyecto y conectar con audiencias cada vez más diversas.

Como resultado, la campaña ha superado 1,4 millones de visualizaciones, generado 20.000 interacciones (comentarios, compartidos y guardados), sumando así 2.000 nuevos seguidores/as en redes sociales y registrando 45.000 visitas al catálogo web, lo que evidencia un crecimiento sostenido en la visibilidad, el compromiso de la comunidad y el interés por los objetivos del proyecto.

El witral en la cosmovisión Mapuche

El witral se fundamenta en el kimün —el saber ancestral Mapuche— en el equilibrio del itrofilmongen —la biodiversidad— y en la mapu, la tierra y el territorio. Este conocimiento, transmitido principalmente por mujeres de generación en generación, se vincula con la identidad, cultura, cosmovisión y espiritualidad, preservando la memoria colectiva y reafirmando la profunda vinculación del Pueblo Mapuche con su entorno natural y espiritual.

Para trabajar el witral, las ngerekafe (tejedoras) siguen un proceso integral que comienza con el cuidado y la alimentación de las ufisha (ovejas), hasta llegar a la esquila. En tanto, se recolectan los elementos necesarios para el teñido, entre ellos cortezas, raíces, flores, barros, barbas de árboles y cenizas. Se utilizan asimismo cáscaras y hojas de árboles como el tineo, pillo …

author: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
title: She governs a US territory. But she has no say in who mines its waters.
content:
Lou Leon Guerrero, the governor of Guam, learned about the government’s plan to mine her people’s waters the same way everyone else did: by reading the news.


It was November 12, and her advisor had sent her an article link — apparently, a journalist had inquired about it. She opened the page, and was stunned by what she read. The Trump administration planned to lease millions of acres of seafloor around the island to mining companies. 


“I’ll never forget the date,” Leon Guerrero said from her office overlooking Agaña Bay. “I had not heard anything about it.”


She immediately called David Apatang, the governor of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, a neighboring U.S. territory.

“We were both very upset that we didn’t get any kind of warning,” she said. Shortly after, she rang Bill Hague, an official in the Department of the Interior, an agency that handles federal relations with territorial leaders and tribal nations. 


“I know we are a U.S. territory,” Leon Guerrero recalls saying to him. “I know that you as the federal government can just come in and say, ‘I don’t care about what you guys say. We’re going to do it anyway.’” But still, she said, “I want you to know I don’t support this.” Hague reassured her, she said, that mining would never proceed without the community’s support. 


Nearly a year later, that’s exactly what’s happening. 


Read Next


American Samoa says no to deep-sea mining. The Trump administration might do it anyway.


Anita Hofschneider


The Trump administration is moving forward with plans to lease vast swaths of seafloor to mining companies. It is part of a broader push to secure critical minerals and counter China, which dominates the global supply. These resources — including copper, manganese,

nickel

, and

rare earth elements

 — are essential to military technologies and batteries.


First up are America’s Pacific island territories. In July, the Marine Minerals Administration

said

 that it would auction access to 31 million acres of the continental shelf

around American Samoa

 in mid-November. A month later, the agency

announced plans to do the same in December across

 more than 67 million acres

on either side

 of the Marianas archipelago, which includes the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam. About half of those acres

border a national marine monument

 established by President George W. Bush.


Local leaders and environmentalists staunchly oppose these plans. Recently, Earthjustice, an environmental law nonprofit, filed lawsuits against the Trump administration on behalf of conservation groups in

American Samoa

 and the

Mariana Islands

, arguing that the government does not yet know if seabed mining would harm animals that are protected by the Endangered Species Act, like whales and sea turtles.


The Marine Minerals Administration declined to comment on the ongoing litigation. Brent Lawrence, a spokesperson who responded to Grist’s questions, said that the department would continue “to closely coordinate with territorial leadership” as well as community members in American Samoa, Guam, and the Mariana Islands.


Unlike neighboring Pacific nations, which can decide for themselves whether to allow mining, Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands are subject to federal decisions often made without their approval. Under international law, the Indigenous peoples of these islands have the right to free, prior, and informed consent to projects affecting their lands and waters. The Trump administration, however, says it has the authority to proceed under U.S. law.


That decision is the latest example of how the United States has for more than a century denied the residents of these islands a meaningful voice in decisions that affect them, said Adi Martínez-Román, co-director of Right to Democracy. They cannot vote for president, have no voting representation in Congress, and their right to self-determination is generally ignored, she said.


“The territories are practically invisible to the general U.S. society and to public officials,” said Martínez-Román. “It is an insidious result of the colonial framework.”

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: On The Fringes | Mentally surviving the rotten healthcare system
content:
Flower blooming outside the state mental health facility. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

I refer to the force pinning me down to the sofa. For hours, I negotiated with my own body and mind, trying to gather enough courage to leave the house and go to the public mental health facility.

The last time I was here, the queue was so long that it took seven hours to see the doctor. As the body ached in intense abdominal pain, I tried not to cave in. Today, I arrived at past seven in the morning and I was No. 40. I managed to get a seat. That is already a small victory for the expected long day.

Most patients need to be accompanied. I am fortunate that I can still do this on my own.

There is a certain kind of fortitude required to spend an entire day waiting in a public hospital. But this “strength” is a product of a decaying public healthcare, of a system designed to make people used to surviving what should never have been normal. When the system designed to care for us is also pulling us down, this “strength” is dangerous.

In this hospital, only one psychiatrist is assigned for all patients. This explains the hours of long lines of patients every day.

Based on a 2026 study of University of the Philippines, there are 409 PhilHealth-accredited psychiatrists in the country, translating to 0.38 psychiatrists per 100,000 population. It also noted that the country’s ratio of psychiatrists and population has been decreasing since 2016. This shortage is not only about numbers but also about people’s access to health services.

If people struggling with their mental health opt for private consultations, the average cost ranges from P1,500 ($23.89) to P5,000 ($79.63) per session.

For the poor who are forced to join the long lines, the cost of psychiatric care is not an incidental expense. It can deprive families of food for several days, not to mention money allocated for utility bills, transportation, and rent.

The situation is much worse for minimum wage earners or contractual employees living from paycheck to paycheck. Sacrificing one whole day to get immediate psychiatric care means income loss.

Think tank Ibon Foundation said that around 70 million Filipinos belong to the poorest and low-income classes, earning between P10,000 ($159.27) and P22,000 ($350.39) monthly.

The high cost of consultation left poor patients to rely on a rotten public mental health system. Of course, the shame and stigma tend to prevent people from seeking psychiatric help.

The 2023 data from the Department of Health (DOH) showed that more than 3.6 million Filipinos suffer from mental health conditions, neurological and substance use disorders. Among the most prevalent conditions are major depressive disorder (affecting more than 1.1 million people); bipolar disorder (520,000 people); and schizophrenia (more than 213,000 people).

Behind all these numbers is the long line right now, with me sitting on a worn out chair in the waiting area. Someone is constantly checking the clock. Someone is wondering if the doctor will see him before the day ends. And someone is trying not to give up in this dreadful wait.

I had the privilege to take a leave at work to prioritize my consultation. But an average Filipino worker does not have this privilege, especially minimum wage earners and the contractual workers trapped in a no-work-no-pay system.

It’s already 3:00 pm. The two bottles of water and three pieces of bread are gone. The cellphone battery is running low.

A first-time outpatient tells another that it took her a long time to finally bring herself here. “Because of shame,” she said.

Behind her, a woman in her 50s told her, “You shouldn’t be ashamed. We are all survivors.” Sitting in the waiting area for half a day, most of us heard several stories of survival.

We pretended not to listen. But we heard such stories. This explains why the waiting area is difficult to forget. I spent more hours here than in my consultations. Most of my conversations with the doctor took only 15 to 30 minutes.

It’s 4:00 pm now, almost nine hours of waiting. I am already next in line. I may not be a doctor and I may be struggling but it is clear that the public healthcare system is dying from decay. (RTS, DAA)

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Warren Introduces Bill to Ban Private Equity From Owning Medical Practices
content:
More than 80 percent of doctors are employed by corporate entities — a massive increase from 62 percent seven years ago.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

A group of Democrats has introduced bicameral legislation to ban private equity from owning medical practices as increasingly widespread corporate ownership continues driving up health care costs each year.

The bill was introduced Wednesday by Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) with the support of 12 other members of the Senate and House. The legislation was based on a law in Oregon aimed at beating back the corporate takeover of health care providers that took effect this year. The law has already been successfully used by physicians in Eugene to prevent a corporate takeover.

Warren’s bill would ban for-profit corporations like private equity funds and insurance companies from owning medical practices, while also prohibiting entities known as management services organizations, which conduct business operations for practices, from controlling such offices.

Such a prohibition could help stanch the rapid rise in health care costs. Between 2000 and 2004, KFF found, costs for medical care far outpaced costs for goods and services at large, increasing by 121 percent compared to 86 percent for the rest of the consumer price index.

The growing grip of private equity on health care, like in other sectors, has played a major role in this rise in costs. In 2000, private equity invested $5 billion in health care; by 2024, this had risen to $104 billion. Since private equity firms are focused not on patient care, but on maximizing profits, research has found that private equity ownership is associated with worse outcomes for patients as well as higher costs, particularly in nursing homes.

In large part due to rising costs for care, health coverage costs are slated to rise precipitously next year. A recent survey found that employers expect health care plan costs to rise by an average of 11 percent per worker in 2027, unless benefits are cut. This could translate to higher costs for workers and patients on job-based insurance if employers shift the burden onto them; costs for plans through the Affordable Care Act are also expected to rise significantly due to Republicans’ massive slashes via the One Big Beautiful Bill.

“Patients want to know that decisions about their health are being made by their doctors, not by Wall Street investors,” said Warren. “If we’re going to lower costs and un-rig the health care system, we need to stop the corporate takeover of medicine.”

The passage of the bill could also help allow physicians to retain control in their practices, including in their medical decisionmaking, at a time when private equity and other corporate actors are close to gobbling up almost the entire field of medical providers.

As the lawmakers point out, research has found that, as of this year, 82 percent of physicians are employed by hospitals or other corporate entities as the industry shifts away from private practices. This is a 20-point increase from 2019, when 62 percent of physicians were employed this way.

The legislation has been backed by numerous health and advocacy groups, who say that private equity must be barred from standing between patients and receiving good health care.

“A prohibition is only as strong as its enforcement, and this bill backs its corporate practice of medicine prohibition with three enforcement paths: the FTC, state attorneys general suing on behalf of residents, and physicians themselves through a private right of action with treble damages,” said Marco Fernandez, president of the Association for Independent Medicine. “That layered enforcement, paired with mandatory divestment, is what gives this bill teeth that earlier [Corporate Practice of Medicine] laws have often lacked.”

title: The Saddle Lake Cree Nation, located northeast of Edmonton near St. Paul, says health care is a…
content:
The Saddle Lake Cree Nation, located northeast of Edmonton near St. Paul, says health care is a right under Treaty 6 and falls under its inherent jurisdiction. The First Nation has invoked the “medicine chest clause” provision from the treaty signed in 1876, which Indigenous Peoples interpret as a promise to provide comprehensive health care. “All children, including trans and two-spirit children and their family, will have safety under our treaty,” Saddle Lake Chief Dale Steinhauer said on Wednesday.

author: Unknown
title: Şiddetten kaçan engelli kadın için sığınma evine ulaşmak daha zor: Erişilebilir bina yetmez, erişilebilir sığınma hizmeti ihtiyaç
content:
Şiddete maruz bırakılan bir kadın evinden ayrılmaya karar verdiğinde güvenli bir yere ulaşabilmek için çoğu zaman polis, Şiddet Önleme ve İzleme Merkezi (ŞÖNİM), belediyelerin danışma birimleri veya destek hatlarıyla iletişime geçmek zorunda. Ancak bu süreç, her kadın için aynı ölçüde erişilebilir değil. Kadın engelliyse şiddetten uzaklaşmanın önündeki engellere; erişilemeyen binalar, iletişim kanallarındaki sorunlar, işaret dili desteğinin bulunmaması, kişisel bakım ihtiyacının karşılanmaması ve ayrımcı kabuller de ekleniyor.

Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanlığının 2025 Yılı Faaliyet Raporu’na göre Türkiye’de bakanlığa, yerel yönetimlere, bir sivil toplum kuruluşuna ve Göç İdaresi Başkanlığı’na bağlı toplam 151 kadın konukevi bulunuyor. 3 bin 726 kapasiteli bu kuruluşlar, aynı yıl kadınlar ve beraberlerindeki çocuklar dâhil 62 bin 698 kişiye hizmet sundu. Türkiye genelindeki 86 ŞÖNİM’e yapılan başvuru sayısı ise 310 bin 136 olarak kayda geçti.

Ancak Bakanlığın raporunda kadın konukevlerine başvuran veya bu kuruluşlardan yararlanan engelli kadınların sayısı, engel grupları, kabul ve yönlendirme süreçleri ayrı ayrı açıklanmıyor. Dolayısıyla kritik sorular yanıtsız kalıyor: Kaç engelli kadın sığınma talebinde bulundu? Kaçı kabul edildi? Kaçı öz bakım veya iletişim desteği sağlanamadığı için başka bir kuruma yönlendirildi? Avukat Deniz Yazgan’a göre veri eksikliği, ayrımcılığın boyutunu da görünmez hâle getiriyor: “Hangi engel gruplarında ret veya yönlendirme yoğunlaşıyor? Hangi makul düzenlemeler talep ediliyor ve bunların ne kadarı karşılanıyor?”

Mor Çatı Gönüllüsü Kübra Karagöz ise engelli kadınların karşılaştığı sorunların çoğu zaman sığınağın kapısından içeri girmeden başladığına işaret etti. Mevcut sistemde kadınlar konukevine doğrudan başvuramıyor. İl müdürlüğü, ŞÖNİM, ilgili kamu birimleri veya kolluk aracılığıyla yönlendirme yapılıyor. Bu nedenle ilk temas kurulan görevlinin yaklaşımı, doğru bilgi vermesi ve süreci geciktirmeden yürütmesi büyük önem taşıyor.

Karagöz, kadınların bu süreçte zaman zaman şiddetin nedenine ilişkin sorgulayıcı yorumlar, küçümseme, caydırıcı ifadeler ve sığınaklar hakkında yanlış bilgilendirmeyle karşılaştığını belirtti. Engelli kadınlar söz konusu olduğunda ise bu tutumların daha da ağırlaşabildiğine dikkat çekti. Ayrıca kadınların “engelli bir kadın olarak sığınakta kalmasının zor olacağı” yönünde bilgilendirilebildiğini, hatta bazı kadınlara sığınaklara engelli kadın kabul edilmediğinin söylendiğini aktardı.

Bu tablo, erişilebilirliğin yalnızca sığınak binasının girişindeki rampadan ibaret olmadığını gösteriyor. Bir kadın yardım hattına ulaşamıyor, telefonda iletişim kuramıyor, kendisine sunulan bilgiyi anlayabileceği biçimde alamıyor veya güvenli ulaşım desteği bulamıyorsa, bina fiziksel olarak erişilebilir olsa bile koruma zinciri daha ilk aşamada kopuyor. Bazı kadınlar ise engeller nedeniyle destek alamayacaklarını düşünerek hiçbir mekanizmaya başvurmuyor.

Mor Çatı’ya ulaşan kadınların anlatımları, sığınaklar arasında da ortak ve yerleşik bir standardın bulunmadığını gösteriyor. Koşulların yalnızca kentten kente değil, aynı kentteki farklı sığınaklar arasında dahi değişebildiği belirtiliyor. Bazı kadınlar saat ve telefon kullanımına ilişkin kısıtlamalar ile bina içindeki düzenlemeler nedeniyle sığınakları “hapishaneye” benzetirken, bazıları iyi koşullarla karşılaşabiliyor.

Oturmuş bir standart olmadığı için ana dilde destek, işaret dili desteği ya da erişilebilirlik konusunda kapsayıcı bir çalışma olmadığını ifade eden Karagöz, bununla birlikte olumlu örneklerin de bulunduğunu aktardı. Bazı durumlarda engelli kadınların ilk kabulde daha kısa sürede yerleştirildiğini ve çocuklarıyla tek başına kalabilecekleri bir odaya yerleştirildiklerini söyleyen Karagöz, “Ancak bu uygulama tüm sığınaklarda yok” dedi.

Avukat ve Engelli Kadın Derneği Yönetim Kurulu Üyesi Özlem Kara’nın anlatımına göre; engellilik ve destek ilişkisi fail tarafından yeni kontrol araçlarına dönüştürülebiliyor. Tekerlekli sandalye, beyaz baston, işitme cihazı veya iletişim aracının saklanması; ilaç, beslenme, tuvalet, hijyen ve kişisel bakım desteğinin kasten engellenmesi; engelli aylığına veya banka hesabına el konulması bu şiddet biçimleri arasında. Telefon, internet, işaret dili tercümanı, Braille (görme engelliler için alfabe) veya kolay okunur bilgiye erişimin engellenmesi de kadını ihbar ve destek mekanizmalarından koparabiliyor. Failin aynı zamanda bakım veren kişi olması ise şiddet ortamından …

author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: No Girls and women in Classrooms. No Women in Health Clinics. Afghanistan’s Healthcare Crisis Deepens by the Day.
content:
It has been five years since women and girls in Afghanistan have been among the primary targets of the Taliban regime. Their rights to go to school, go to work, and even leave their homes have been taken away. A direct consequence of these restrictions is a crumbling health system, under pressure from a lack of female medical professionals, Taliban restrictions, and funding cuts that threaten to keep health facilities open.

One of the first Taliban orders was to ban women from pursuing higher education and to ban all girls from attending school beyond grade six. According to UNICEF, more than 2.6 million girls do not have access to education as a result of the Taliban’s ban. Other edicts target women’s freedom of movement, including restrictions that prevent women from leaving their homes or going to health clinics without a male family member. These edicts have built on one another to the point where Afghanistan’s education and health systems are being systematically dismantled. The pipeline that once supplied the workforce with trained and skilled professionals is disappearing, creating major long-term consequences for the health system and the country’s workforce.

Due to this dismantled pipeline, Afghanistan is facing one of the worst shortages of female medical professionals. In Helmand, Zabul, and Uruzgan provinces, it is reported that there are no female medical professionals. There are only three female specialists in Kandahar, a neighboring province to Helmand. In addition to specialists, other female healthcare workers that Afghanistan’s health system depends on, such as midwives and nurses, have been forced out of their jobs because of Taliban restrictions. And because of restrictions on movement, Afghan women are also unable to visit health facilities and obtain treatment, according to a February 2026 report by UN Special Rapporteur Richard Bennett.

The cost of the ban on education and the removal of women from the workforce also has a deep and lasting economic impact. It is estimated that this will cost Afghanistan $84 million per year. But beyond the economic impact, the immediate human consequences are even more urgent. Infant and maternal mortality have risen back to some of the highest levels seen since the Taliban took over.

The lack of specialists, and in some areas any female healthcare workers at all, means that women are facing a painful reality. An Afghan from Helmand shared, “We take patients from one doctor to another without success and eventually have to go elsewhere.”

Manizha, a medical doctor whose name has been changed for her safety, is part of one of the few medical teams still providing care to Afghan women. She sees women who would otherwise have no access to healthcare, with her team traveling to them. Her team originally started with fourteen members, but has since decreased to seven, as many of her colleagues were unable to find male guardians to accompany them to work, compounded by financial hardships.

With decreasing staff and an increasing health burden, the situation is dire. Even as Manizha faces enormous challenges, she remains hopeful: “Whenever I remember the smiles, the tears, and even the deprivation of the women I have visited over the years, I tell myself that I must not give up. They need even the little that I can do for them.”

Afghanistan’s healthcare system is collapsing because the foundation of a skilled labor force including women is collapsing. By excluding women from education, employment, and public life, the Taliban are not only denying women their rights today; they are dismantling the pipeline needed to train the healthcare professionals Afghanistan will need tomorrow. The result is a health system that is losing its existing female workforce while failing to produce the next generation of women professionals to serve their communities.

Sources: Feminist Majority Foundation, Afghanistan International, United Nations, UNICEF, Rukhshana

title: İstanbul Barosu’ndan engelli çocukların eğitim hakkı için veli rehberi
content:
İstanbul Barosu Engelli Hakları Merkezi, yeni eğitim-öğretim döneminde engelli çocukların ve ailelerinin okullarda karşılaşabileceği hak ihlallerine karşı 

“Eğitimde Sağlamcılığa Hayır! Engelli Çocukların Eğitim Hakkı İçin Veli Rehberi”

 başlıklı bir çalışma yayımladı.


Eylül 2026 tarihli 68 sayfalık rehber; okul kaydı, sağlık raporu talepleri, “gölge öğretmen” dayatması, başka okula ya da sınıfa yönlendirme, Bireyselleştirilmiş Eğitim Programı (BEP), destek eğitim odası, erişilebilirlik, yardımcı cihazlar, akran zorbalığı, ayrımcılık ve mahremiyet gibi başlıkları ele alıyor. Ailelerin sorun yaşaması halinde başvurabileceği idari ve hukuki yollar ile örnek dilekçeler de rehberde yer alıyor.


“Çözüm çocuğu eğitim ortamından uzaklaştırmak değil”


Rehberde öne çıkan sorunlardan biri, engelli çocukların okul kaydı sırasında karşılaştığı doğrudan ya da dolaylı ret uygulamaları.


Baro, bir çocuğun engelli olmasının tek başına okul kaydının reddedilmesi için gerekçe oluşturamayacağını hatırlatıyor. Okulların “Bu okul çocuğunuza uygun değil”, “Sınıf çok kalabalık”, “Öğretmenimiz bu konuda eğitimli değil” ya da “Başka okul daha iyi olur” gibi gerekçelerle çocuğu eğitim ortamından uzaklaştırmasının eğitim hakkını ortadan kaldırmadığını belirtiyor.


Engelli Odaklı Habercilik Atölyesi sona erdi: "Kafamızdaki sağlamcıyı öldürmeliyiz"


25 Haziran 2026


“Gölge öğretmen tutamazsanız okula alamayız” denilemez


Rehberin dikkat çektiği uygulamalardan biri de bazı ailelerden çocuklarının okula devam edebilmesi için kendi imkanlarıyla “gölge öğretmen” ya da destek personeli sağlamalarının istenmesi.


İstanbul Barosu, çocuğun sınıf içinde desteğe ihtiyaç duyması halinde öncelikle BEP, destek eğitim ve sınıf içi uyarlamalar gibi kamusal yükümlülüklerin değerlendirilmesi gerektiğini vurguluyor.


Ailenin ekonomik gücüyle özel bir personel çalıştırabilmesi ile çocuğun anayasal eğitim hakkının birbirine karıştırılamayacağını belirten rehber, okul kabulünün ailenin ücretini ödeyeceği bir personel bulmasına bağlanmasının eğitim hakkı ve ayrımcılık yasağı bakımından ciddi hukuki sorun doğurabileceğine dikkat çekiyor.


Okul yönetimi tek başına “Bu çocuk bu sınıfta yapamaz” diyemez


Baro ayrıca, engelli bir öğrencinin başka okula veya özel eğitim sınıfına gönderilmesine yalnızca öğretmenin ya da okul yönetiminin karar veremeyeceğini hatırlatıyor.


Çocuğun eğitim ortamının değiştirilmesinin eğitsel değerlendirme ve tanılama sürecine bağlı olduğu; değerlendirmelerin Rehberlik ve Araştırma Merkezi (RAM) bünyesindeki kurul tarafından yapılması gerektiği belirtiliyor.


Yerleştirme kararında velinin yazılı talebinin de dikkate alınması gerekiyor. Bu nedenle öğretmenin ya da okul müdürünün “Bu çocuk burada yapamaz” şeklindeki değerlendirmesinin tek başına yerleştirme kararı sayılamayacağı ifade ediliyor.


Engelsiz Erişim Derneği: Otizm “farkındalık” değil, kabul ve eşit erişim meselesi


2 Nisan 2026


Destek eğitim odası çocuğu sınıftan uzaklaştırmanın aracı değil


Rehber, tam zamanlı kaynaştırma/bütünleştirme yoluyla eğitim gören öğrenciler bakımından destek eğitim odalarına da geniş yer ayırıyor.


Destek eğitim odasında verilecek eğitimin öğrencinin haftalık toplam ders saatinin yüzde 40'ını aşamayacağı; temel olarak bire bir yürütüleceği, BEP geliştirme biriminin kararıyla en fazla üç öğrenciden oluşan gruplarla da eğitim yapılabileceği aktarılıyor.


Ancak rehber özellikle bir noktaya dikkat çekiyor: Destek eğitim odası, öğrenciyi akranlarından soyutlamak veya genel eğitim sınıfından uzaklaştırmak için kullanılamaz.


Okul yönetiminin “odamız yok” ya da “öğretmenimiz yok” demesinin de tek başına öğrencinin ihtiyaç duyduğu desteğin karşılanmamasını hukuken haklı hale getirmeyeceği belirtiliyor.


Zorbalığa karşı önlem almak okulun yükümlülüğü


Çalışmanın “Güvenli okul, ayrımcılık ve mahremiyet” bölümünde engelli çocukların karşılaşabileceği akran zorbalığı da ele alınıyor.


Alay etme, hakaret, tehdit, dışlama, fiziksel şiddet, çocuğun eşyalarına veya kullandığı yardımcı cihazlara müdahale ve dijital ortamda rahatsız etme zorbalığın farklı biçimleri arasında sayılıyor.


Rehber, Milli Eğitim Bakanlığı'nın ilgili genelgelerine işaret ederek okul yönetimlerinin zorbalığa yol açabilecek riskleri belirlemek, önleyici tedbir almak ve rehberlik hizmetlerini işletmekle yükümlü olduğunu hatırlatıyor.


Ailelere her bir olayı tarih, yer ve gerçekleşme biçimiyle ayrı ayrı kaydetmeleri öneriliyor.


Çürük


7 Eylül 2026

title: Nurses Across US Demand Hospitals Cut Ties With Palantir, Citing ICE and Gaza
content:
National Nurses United is expanding its campaign against Palantir in a global week of action starting on September 28.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

National Nurses United (NNU), the largest union of registered nurses in the U.S., is demanding that hospitals cut ties with Palantir, with nurses citing the firm’s role in developing technology used to surveil immigrants in the U.S. and target civilians in Gaza.

The union – which represents more than 225,000 nurses in all 50 U.S. states — has announced a global week of action against Palantir, set to begin on September 28.

Palantir’s “AI-powered tools for large-scale data collection and mass surveillance… threaten human rights globally,” the union said in a press release announcing the campaign.

The global week of action is aimed at pushing all public institutions — including hospitals and other health care providers — to end contracts and partnerships with Palantir, and to divest from the company, the union said.

The global week of action builds on a national day of action, also led by the union, which saw demonstrations in eight cities across the U.S. on August 27, including in Portland, Maine; Washington, D.C.; Chicago; Austin; and Los Angeles.

The global week of action is also coordinated with health care workers in the U.K., where National Health Service (NHS) workers and activists will protest Palantir’s use in health care on October 1. Other organizations, like Amnesty International and the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) Movement, are also part of the global week of action.

“Palantir has no place in patient care, no place in our communities, and no place in our society,” a NNU nurse said in a video from the August 27 day of action.

The nurses have outlined Palantir’s complicity in human rights violations both nationally and internationally, from detentions of immigrants by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to the genocide in Gaza.

“We think that a company that specializes in mass surveillance, kidnappings and killings, has no place in patient care,” one nurse explained in a video posted by the California Nurses Association.

During the August day of action, nurses placed 50 pairs of baby shoes in the street in each city – to represent the 500 babies and toddlers who have been detained in immigrant jails since President Donald Trump started his second term. The nurses also brought letters written by children in ICE detention.

“Palantir, we know, helps ICE identify people to kidnap off of our streets,” another nurse said during the day of action.

The company also has “their hands in the genocide and murders of civilians in Gaza,” another nurse present at the protests said. “They’ve [helped with the targeting of] hospitals, schools, mission workers taking food and aid….”

In a statement shared with Truthout and read at the August 27 day of action, Chicago-based nurse and NNU member Elizabeth Lalasz said that “nurses, health care workers, our patients, immigrants, and allies from every walk of life stand united here in Chicago and all across the country to demand an immediate end to the violence inflicted by Palantir technologies and the Trump administration.”

“As we speak, Palantir’s AI is enabling atrocities and human rights abuses: ICE killings, mass deportation, and concentration camps with no access to health care – even the imprisonment of more than 500 babies and 6,200 children – and Palantir is providing the technology for Israel’s U.S.-funded genocide in Gaza, the cruel and illegal war in Iran, and mass surveillance at home and abroad,” she went on.

Lalasz also noted that Palantir has partnered with the world’s largest health care corporations “to suck more and more profit from our broken health care system, causing untold suffering in our hospitals.”

“This country could fund health care for 12 million children with the money spent on ICE detention alone,” she said.

João Paulo Connolly, an activist in the Bay Area who has organized protests against Palantir, explained in a webinar that “Palantir’s profit model is data extraction and surveillance,” and then “giving employers new, powerful ways to monitor and spy on their workers at all times and track their behavior,” while also selling the health care industry and the federal government “unprecedented levels of access” to this data.

title: Zayıflama iğneleri tehlikeli mi? Bilim ne diyor, sağlıkçılar ne öneriyor?
content:
Kilo kaybı sağlayan ilaçlar, obezite tedavisinde önemli bir seçenek haline geldi. Ancak “zayıflama iğnesi” olarak bilinen bu ilaçlar masum birer kilo verme ürünü değil. Bilimsel çalışmalar etkili olduklarını gösterirken, ciddi yan etkiler ve yanlış kullanım riskleri de bulunuyor. İlaçların hekim değerlendirmesi ve yaşam tarzı değişiklikleriyle birlikte kullanılmasının ise önemi büyük.

Son yıllarda sosyal medyanın da etkisiyle kilo vermek isteyenlerin gündemine giren GLP-1 temelli ilaçlar, aslında başlangıçta özellikle tip 2 diyabetin tedavisinde kullanılan ilaçlar arasında yer alıyordu. Semaglutid ve tirzepatid gibi etken maddeler iştahı azaltıyor, tokluk hissini artırıyor ve kan şekeri düzenlenmesine yardımcı oluyor. Bu etkiler, obezite tedavisinde de kullanılmalarının önünü açtı.

Ancak bu ilaçları “hızlı kilo verme iğnesi” olarak görmek önemli bir yanılgı. Dünya Sağlık Örgütü (DSÖ), 2025'te yayımladığı kılavuzda semaglutid, tirzepatid ve liraglutid gibi GLP-1 ilaçlarının yetişkinlerde obezitenin uzun süreli tedavisinde kullanılabileceğini koşullu olarak önerdi. DSÖ, bunun yanında uzun dönem güvenlilik, tedavinin bırakılması sonrası ne olacağı, maliyet ve sağlık sistemlerinin bu tedavilere hazırlığı konusunda belirsizlikler bulunduğuna dikkat çekti.

Evet. Bu ilaçların kilo kaybı konusunda güçlü bilimsel kanıtları bulunuyor. Özellikle semaglutid ve tirzepatid, iştah ve enerji alımı üzerinde etkili olarak kişilerin daha az yemek yemesine yardımcı olabiliyor. Ancak alınan sonuç kişiden kişiye değişiyor ve ilaçların etkisi, tedavinin süresi ve kişinin yaşam tarzıyla yakından ilişkili.

Bu nedenle sağlık otoriteleri ilaçları diyet ve fiziksel aktivitenin alternatifi olarak değil, obezitenin kapsamlı tedavisinin bir parçası olarak değerlendiriyor. DSÖ de GLP-1 ilaçları kullanan obezitesi olan yetişkinlere yapılandırılmış sağlıklı beslenme ve fiziksel aktivite programlarının eşlik etmesini öneriyor.

Doğru hastada, uygun dozda ve hekim gözetiminde kullanıldığında bu ilaçların yararları ve riskleri klinik olarak değerlendirilmiş durumda. Ancak ciddi yan etki potansiyelleri nedeniyle gelişigüzel kullanılmaları güvenli değil.

En sık karşılaşılan sorunlar arasında bulantı, kusma, ishal, kabızlık, karın ağrısı, hazımsızlık gibi şikâyetler bulunuyor.

Bunların yanı sıra ilaçların resmi güvenlik bilgilerinde pankreatit, safra kesesi hastalıkları, böbrek hasarı ve ciddi gastrointestinal reaksiyonlar gibi daha önemli riskler de yer alıyor. Bazı hastalarda kan şekeri düşüklüğü ve diyabetik retinopati komplikasyonları da önem taşıyor.

Bu nedenle “yan etkisi sadece biraz mide bulantısı” şeklindeki yaklaşım doğru değil.

İlaçların etkili olabilmesi kadar doğru dozda kullanılması da önemli. Özellikle doktor kontrolü dışında kullanılan ürünlerde doz hataları ciddi problemlere yol açabiliyor. ABD Gıda ve İlaç Dairesi (FDA), onaysız veya bileşik olarak hazırlanan semaglutid ürünlerinde yanlış doz kullanımına bağlı olarak hastaneye yatış gerektiren vakalar bildirildiğini açıkladı.

Bildirilen sorunlar arasında şiddetli bulantı ve kusma, karın ağrısı, susuz kalma, pankreatit ve safra taşı bulunuyor.

Uzmanların en önemli uyarılarından biri de ilacın nereden temin edildiği. FDA, onaylanmamış semaglutid ve tirzepatid ürünlerinin güvenlilik, etkinlik ve kalite açısından piyasaya çıkmadan önce kurumun değerlendirmesinden geçmediğini belirtiyor.

Daha da önemlisi, kurum sahte semaglutid ve tirzepatid ürünleri tespit edildiğini; bazı ürünlerin etiketlerinde gerçekte bulunmayan eczanelerin isimlerinin dahi kullanılabildiğini bildiriyor.

Bu nedenle sosyal medya üzerinden, internet sitelerinden veya doktor değerlendirmesi olmadan satılan ürünler ile ruhsatlı ilaçların aynı şey olmadığı unutulmamalı.

Bu ilaçların temel kullanım alanı obezite veya belirli koşullarla aşırı kiloluluk gibi tıbbi durumların tedavisi. Sırf birkaç kilo vermek isteyen sağlıklı bir kişinin sosyal medyada gördüğü bir ilaçla kendi kendine tedaviye başlaması doğru değil. Tedavi kararı verilirken kişinin kilosunun yanı sıra boyu, vücut kitle indeksi, eşlik eden hastalıkları, kullandığı ilaçlar, beslenme alışkanlıkları ve diğer sağlık koşulları birlikte değerlendirilmeli.

Ayrıca gebelik söz konusu olduğunda GLP-1 tedavileri kullanılmamalı; DSÖ'nün obezite kılavuzu da hamile kadınları kapsam dışında bırakıyor.

Burada da önemli bir ayrıntı var. GLP-1 ilaçlarının iştah üzerindeki etkisi tedavi sürdüğü sürece devam eder. Tedavi bırakıldığında iştahın yeniden artması ve …
