title: Bayık: As long as Öcalan is not physically freed, the state’s law will not be implemented
content:
In an extensive interview with NÛÇE TV’s Hevpeyvîn program, Cemil Bayik, co-chair of the KCK (Kurdistan Communities Union) Executive Council, answered a wide variety of questions regarding the progress of the Peace and Democratic Society Process in Turkey, as well as developments in the region. Bayik particularly emphasized the crucial role played by the situation of the Kurdish people’s leader, Abdullah Öcalan, and offered insights into various aspects of the struggle.


What stage is the Peace and Democratic Society Process at?


The law passed by the Turkish Parliament does not meet our demands. The Turkish state enacted this law not in accordance with our demands, but rather in line with its own interests. The primary purpose of this law is the disarmament and disbandment of the guerrillas. Some articles have been included in the law that are not very important from our perspective. This is their law; we have our own laws as well. Neither their laws nor our laws are being enforced. There is a struggle between us and the Turkish state over this law.


What is important to us is ensuring that the necessary conditions and circumstances are in place for Rêber Apo [Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan] to carry out this process and bring it to a successful conclusion. This newly enacted law contains no principles regarding the resolution of the Kurdish issue. Rêber Apo wants the Kurdish issue to be resolved at the negotiating table. Bahçeli made some assessments in this regard. This was and is important in terms of giving the issue official recognition. This is important to us. If they clear the way for Rêber Apo and provide him with the opportunity to work freely, he can bring this process to a successful conclusion.


Were your views sought before the law was submitted to parliament?


Rêber Apo does not take any steps without us. He seeks our views. We may not be holding direct talks with the Turkish state or Imrali, but we find our ways to convey our views to Rêber Apo. When Rêber Apo wishes to take a step, he takes our decisions and views into account. Messages are sent and received through the delegation of the DEM Party. Rêber Apo did not make the decision to dissolve the PKK as a result of a meeting with the Turkish state – he took this step of his own volition. Rêber Apo trusts himself, his movement, and his people. He has no other guarantee beyond this.


Will the state take any steps regarding the Kurdish issue?


Just as the state acts in its own interests, we and our people also have our own interests. The law can act as a foundation. We can work on this basis and achieve certain results. If democracy does not advance in Turkey, the Kurdish issue will not be resolved. But still, our movement and Rêber Apo view this law as insufficient. We are taking steps with a patient, conscious, and strategic approach. Kurds are a force in the Middle East. Certain powers want to use this force for their own interests. However, we want to put this power at the service of the Kurdish people.


Amid the developments taking place in the world, will the Kurdish issue be resolved?


When the Third World War began in the Middle East, the Kurdish issue came to the forefront. The time and conditions for resolving the Kurdish issue have been created. What happens next depends on Kurdish unity. Resolving the Kurdish issue is possible only through Kurdish unity.


Did the state ask you to visit Imrali?


Certain efforts were made before the framework law reached Parliament. Rêber Apo, in particular, spearheaded these efforts. Rather than just talking, practical steps need to be taken in the political and legal spheres. Journalists and advisors have to be able to travel there to meet with Rêber Apo. Politicians and academics also need to be enabled to go to Imrali. This needs to happen in the near future. There is a great deal of skepticism in both the Kurdish and Turkish societies. Rêber Apo’s address dispels these doubts. Turkey’s approach also creates doubts among us. The KCK also needs to visit Imrali, and we will go to Imrali. This step is necessary for Turkey more than for the Kurds. Because the Turkish state is in a bad situation. The war being waged around the world is putting Turkey in a very difficult position. Turkey wanted to defeat the PKK using all the means at its disposal, but it failed to achieve this goal.

title: Organizaciones preparan el Primer Festival Dignidad Migrante
content:
Foto: Alejandra Malcorra – Archivo Marcha Noticias


Se realizará en el Parque de la Estación, en la ciudad de Avellaneda el día 27 de septiembre. La actividad busca mostrar la diversidad y aporte de lxs migrantes a la cultura y economía. Pero también denunciar las políticas antimigratorias impulsadas por el gobierno nacional.

Por César Saravia, para ANRed. 


Como suele ocurrir en contexto de crisis y ajuste neoliberal, los gobiernos que impulsan medidas empobrecedoras encuentran en los migrantes un chivo expiatorio a quien culpar. Estigmas e ideas como que los servicios de salud y educación se encuentran saturados por culpa de la migración, son rápidamente difundidas e instaladas como sentido común.


Pero en un contexto de avance de ultraderechas y fascismos este discurso se internacionaliza de una manera que incluso resulta forzado. La «trumperización» de la política migratoria en Latinoamérica asume elementos performáticos y marketineros que poco o nada resuelven los problemas de las grandes mayorías, pero que sí que impactan en la vida de las minorías.


Estos discursos adquieren una dimensión territorial cuando se traslada a redadas como las que llevó a cabo la

 Policía Federal y la Dirección Nacional de Migraciones a inicios de este año

 en Villa Celina, en el partido de La Matanza. Se trata de operaciones con una fuerte carga mediática y detenciones que rápidamente remitieron a las redadas estadounidenses llevadas a cabo del ICE de Trump.


Según datos de organizaciones migrantes, solo en lo que va de 2026 se han llevado a cabo más de 20 redadas en zonas donde la población migrante tiene fuerte presencia. Para Lila Baez, migrante paraguaya organizada en la Secretaría de Trabajadores Migrantes,

«este tipo de mecanismos constituyen un relato en que se configura una lógica de migrantes buenos y migrantes malos»

. Pero el migrante malo, siempre es el que vive en barrios populares y no otros como Peter Thiel que descansa en una mansión.


¿Qué cambios ha impulsado el gobierno?


En mayo de 2025 el gobierno emitió el Decreto de Necesidad y Urgencia (DNU) 366/2025. Este decreto tiene como efecto una restricción a los derechos a la salud, educación, radicación y a la ciudadanía. Entre los principales cambios que contempla es que los servicios de salud pasan a tener un costo para personas que cuentan con residencia temporaria, transitoria o precaria. Anteriormente la Ley garantizaba el derecho a la salud sin importar el estatus migratorio. Cabe mencionar que los casos de emergencia fueron excluidos dentro de estos cambios.


En lo que refiere a educación, se mantiene el acceso gratuito en los niveles iniciales, primaria y secundaria. Pero se limita el acceso gratuito a las universidades a personas sin residencia permanente. Si bien el decreto no obliga a las universidades a cobrar este arancel, deja abierta la posibilidad.


El cambio además señala que las personas que hayan ingresado de forma irregular, ya sea por motivos no declarados o puntos ciegos,

podrían ser expulsadas

. Este mecanismo de alguna manera desincentiva a las personas a acercarse a regularizar su situación. En este sentido, el Estado cambia su perspectiva de la migración como derecho, hacia una que restringe y criminaliza.


Imagen: swissinfo.ch


Este decreto, además de ser criminalizador y tener tintes xenófobos y racistas, es inconstitucional. Pues la Constitución de la República, en su artículo 4, establece que la migración es un derecho humano. En este sentido viola la Declaración Universal de Los Derechos Humanos, que establece que los derechos son siempre progresivos y no regresivos.


En relación a la obtención de la ciudadanía, el gobierno modificó el procedimiento, que a partir del 2025 pasa a ser potestad de la Dirección Nacional de Migraciones, en lo que siempre fue un trámite de tipo civil. Con esto el mensaje que envía el gobierno es de que su política migratoria está bajo el ala de su política de seguridad. Por otro lado, elimina contrapesos institucionales y deja el proceso a discreción del gobierno nacional. 


En 2026, con la entrada en vigencia del DNU 681/2026 el gobierno estableció que serán expulsadas o se negará el ingreso a aquellas personas que «expresen mensajes de odio contra Argentina». Sin embargo, no aclara a qué se refiere con mensajes de odio, ni tampoco justifica la necesidad de un decreto de este tipo. Esto abre un camino enorme hacia arbitrariedades, y restringe la libertad de expresión de personas …

title: DİSK’ten 18 Eylül Uluslararası Eşit Ücret Günü açıklaması: Eşdeğer işe eşit ücret yasal güvenceye alınmalı
content:
Devrimci İşçi Sendikaları Konfederasyonu (DİSK), 18 Eylül Uluslararası Eşit Ücret Günü kapsamında yaptığı açıklamada, Türkiye’de erkeklerin gelirlerinin kadınlardan yüzde 30 daha yüksek olduğunu vurguladı. Açıklamada, çalışma hayatındaki cinsiyet temelli gelir eşitsizliğinin son bulması ve "eşdeğer işe eşit ücret" ilkesinin yasal güvenceye kavuşturulması talep edildi.

DİSK'in açıklamasında, bakım emeğinin tek taraflı olarak kadınların üzerine yıkılması nedeniyle kadın işçilerin çifte mesai yaptığı ve buna rağmen erkeklerden daha düşük gelir elde ettiği belirtildi.

Açıklamada, Uluslararası Çalışma Örgütü (ILO) verilerine dikkat çekilerek küresel düzeyde kadınların ücretli istihdamda erkeklerden yüzde 20 daha az kazandığı, mevcut koşullarda bu uçurumun kapanmasının 257 yıl sürebileceği aktarıldı.

Türkiye'deki tablonun daha ağır seyrettiğine işaret edilen açıklamada, kadınlar 100 lira kazanırken erkeklerin ortalama 130 lira gelir elde ettiği kaydedildi. Bu gelir farkının ücretli çalışanlarda yüzde 19, yevmiyelilerde ise yüzde 89 düzeyine kadar çıktığı vurgulandı.

İş gücüne katılım oranlarındaki eşitsizliğe de değinilen açıklamada, Türkiye'de erkeklerin iş gücüne katılım oranının yüzde 70,6, kadınların ise yüzde 35,3 olduğu paylaşıldı. 5,5 milyon kadının ev işleri ve bakım sorumlulukları nedeniyle iş gücü piyasasına dahil olamadığı belirtilirken, 33,9 milyon kadından sadece 6,7 milyonunun kayıtlı ve tam zamanlı istihdamda yer aldığı, 27 milyon kadının ise kayıt dışı ya da yarı zamanlı işlere mahkum bırakıldığı ifade edildi.

İktidarın Orta Vadeli Program hedeflerinde yer alan esnek çalışma modellerine tepki gösterilen açıklamada, kadın istihdamını artırma gerekçesiyle sunulan esnek çalışmanın kadınları ucuz iş gücü haline getirdiği kaydedildi. Çözümün esnekleşmede değil, insanca yaşanabilecek ücret, sendikal haklar ve güvenceli istihdamda olduğu hatırlatılarak Türkiye'nin 1966'da imzaladığı ILO'nun 100 No'lu Eşit Ücret Sözleşmesi'nin gereklerinin yerine getirilmesi istendi.

DİSK, açıklamanın sonunda taleplerini sıraladı:

Eşdeğer işe eşit ücret politikası yasal güvence altına alınmalı ve iş yerlerinde etkin denetim mekanizmaları kurulmalıdır.

Yetki ve karar mekanizmalarında kadınların eşit temsiliyeti sağlanmalıdır.

Kadın istihdamında esnek çalışma dayatmasından vazgeçilmeli, tam zamanlı ve güvenceli iş olanakları yaratılmalıdır.

Bakım yükünü kadınların üzerinden almak için ücretsiz ve kamusal kreş, gündüz bakımevi ile hasta ve yaşlı bakım merkezleri yaygınlaştırılmalıdır.

İstanbul Sözleşmesi'nin feshinden vazgeçilmeli; 6284 sayılı Kanun etkin uygulanmalı ve ILO'nun 190 sayılı Şiddet ve Taciz Sözleşmesi derhal onaylanmalıdır

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Deckmantel „Bürokratieabbau“ für Angriffe auf soziale und ökologische Standards
content:
Dossier


„Unter dem Deckmantel „Bessere Rechtssetzung“ oder „Bürokratieabbau“ werden seit Jahrzehnten Angriffe auf soziale und ökologische Standards gefahren. (…) „Demokratische Regulierung der Wirtschaft und Verwaltungsmodernisierung im gesellschaftlichen Interesse“ könnte der Arbeitstitel für theoretische und praktische Projekte der konkreten Auseinandersetzung und Alternativen sein. Dabei geht es um nicht weniger, als um die Reflexion der politischen Funktionen des Staates und seiner Administration zum Schutz einer demokratischen sozial-ökologischen und rechtsstaatlichen Wirtschaftsordnung. Die Bedeutung dieser Frage wächst erkennbar, denn politische Regulierung, demokratische Legitimation und gesellschaftliche Akzeptanz fallen auseinander und finden einen Ausdruck in Verdrossenheit gegenüber zentralen Elementen der Regierungspolitik sowie in den Erfolgen nationalistischer und rechtspopulistischer Kräfte…“


Beitrag von Uwe Wötzel vom 13. Juni 2016 bei annotazioni.de

 

 („Bürokratieabbau: Regulierung im gesellschaftlichen Interesse statt „Better Regulation“) – mittlerweile ist jede Branche und jeder Aspekt der Politik von Sparmaßnahmen unter dem Label Bürokratieabbau tangiert…


[Bürokratieabbau im Arbeitsschutz] Arbeitssicherheit: Kritik am Arbeitsschutzabbau durch das BMAS


„… Das vom BMAS vorgelegte »Konzept für einen effizienten und bürokratiearmen Arbeitsschutz« beansprucht, den Arbeitsschutz zu modernisieren, zu digitalisieren und stärker an der tatsächlichen Gefahrenlage auszurichten. Stellungnahmen aus Fachorganisationen der Arbeitsmedizin, von Fachkräften für Arbeitssicherheit (ihren Verbänden) und den Gewerkschaften zeigen demgegenüber eine weitgehend übereinstimmende Gegenposition: Der angekündigte „Bürokratieabbau“ betreffe nicht nur entbehrliche Formalien, sondern zentrale Elemente der Präventionsarchitektur wie die Sicherheitsbeauftragten (Sibe), die Verbindlichkeit der DGUV Vorschrift 1, die Selbstverwaltung der gesetzlichen Unfallversicherung und die betriebliche Beteiligung. (…)


Aus arbeitsmedizinischer Sicht ist die Skepsis gegenüber den BMAS-Vorhaben besonders nachvollziehbar, weil die Prävention systematisch als vorausschauende Erkennung, Bewertung und Begrenzung gesundheitlicher Risiken verstanden wird. Eine Orientierung des Arbeitsschutzes ausschließlich auf „tatsächliche Gefahrenlagen“ steht hierzu in Spannung. Arbeitsmedizinische Vorsorge ziele auf latente, kumulative und langfristig wirksame Belastungen ab, die frühzeitig erkannt abgebaut werden müssten. (…)


Die Stellungnahmen aus dem Bereich der Fachkräfte für Arbeitssicherheit und ihrer Verbände liegen in zentralen Punkten auf dieser Linie. Der Verband für Sicherheit, Gesundheit und Umweltschutz bei der Arbeit (VDSI) hebt hervor, dass insbesondere die Bestellung der Sicherheitsbeauftragte keine entbehrliche Formalie sei, weil diese betriebsnahe Gefährdungen wahrnehmen, die Sicherheitskommunikation förderten und als niedrigschwellige Ansprechpartner in den Arbeitsbereichen mit den Beschäftigten und Vorgesetzten im Verbund wirkten. Die Anhebung der Beschäftigtenzahl als Schwelle zur Bestellung von Sicherheitsbeauftragten stößt auf erhebliches Unverständnis, da in der Praxis Unsicherheiten und höhere Gefährdungen drohten, jedoch kaum mit Kosteneinsparungen zu rechnen sei. (…) Hinzu kommt die Kritik am geplanten politischen Zugriff auf das autonome Regelwerk der Unfallversicherung. Fachkräfte für Arbeitssicherheit und ihre Verbände sehen in der Selbstverwaltung einen wesentlichen Grund dafür, dass Unfallverhütungsvorschriften branchennah, fachlich fundiert und an realen betrieblichen Bedingungen orientiert entwickelt werden können. Ein staatlich forcierter Regelrückbau verschiebt dieses Gleichgewicht zulasten fachlicher Expertise. (…)


Die gewerkschaftliche Kritik am Abbau von Arbeitsschutzstandards bezieht auch die Perspektive der Interessenvertretungen ein, die etwa qua Betriebsverfassungsgesetz eine starke Position bei der Mitgestaltung im Arbeits- und Gesundheitsschutz innehaben. (…) Bereits heute sei der Vollzug des Arbeitsschutzrechts unzureichend. Nur etwa zehn Prozent der Gefährdungsbeurteilungen entsprächen den gesetzlichen Anforderungen (…) Besonders kritisch bewerten Stellungnahmen und Unterlagen die beabsichtigte Schwächung der DGUV Vorschrift 1 und den Eingriff in die Autonomie der Selbstverwaltung der gesetzlichen Unfallversicherung. Die branchennah entwickelten Unfallverhütungsvorschriften gelten als wesentliches …

title: Girne açıklarında batan gemiyle ilgili 9 kişi için 7 gün ek gözaltı süresi daha verildi:'Yakalama emri olan 5 kişi hâlâ aranıyor
content:
KKTC'de Türk Ajansı Kıbrıs'ın (TAK) haberine göre, Girne açıklarında batan yolcu gemisiyle ilgili soruşturmada gözaltındaki 9 kişi 4'üncü kez Girne Kaza Mahkemesine çıkarıldı.

Gözaltında bulunan 9 kişinin aleyhinde 7 gün daha gözaltı emri verilirken, ikisinin sağlık sorunları nedeniyle tam teşekküllü bir hastanede sağlık kontrolünden geçirilmesine karar verildi.

Polis Müfettiş Muavini Mehmet Mannaş mahkemede, soruşturma kapsamında kazayla ilgili bugüne kadar 300'ün üzerinde ifade alındığını, Türkiye ve KKTC'deki birçok kuruma yazı yazıldığını ve haklarında yakalama emri bulunan 5 kişinin hala arandığını belirtti.

Mannaş ayrıca, soruşturma kapsamında yardımcı kaptanın gönüllü olarak ifade verdiğini, bu ifadenin ardından zanlılardan alınan WhatsApp yazışmalarında geminin sol ön kızağının uç kısmında bulunan bir kırığın üstünkörü tamir edildiğine dair fotoğraflar tespit edildiğini söyledi.

Fotoğrafların 17 Haziran tarihli olduğunu belirten Mannaş, söz konusu tamiratın, kaptanın emriyle gemide çalışan bir mürettebat tarafından yapıldığının tespit edildiğini ve tamiratı gösteren fotoğrafların kaptana ve hakkında yakala emri bulunan bir şirket yetkilisine gönderildiğini ifade etti.

KKTC'deki Girne Limanı ile Mersin'deki Taşucu Limanı arasında sefer yapan "Filo Jet" isimli yüksek hızlı yolcu gemisi, 30 Ağustos Pazar günü öğle saatlerinde Girne'den hareket ettikten kısa süre sonra ön kısmından su almaya başlamış, Girne Limanı'na dönmeye çalıştığı sırada batmıştı.

Toplam 267 yolcu ve mürettebatın bulunduğu geminin batmasının ardından 239 kişi kurtarılmıştı. Girne açıklarında 554 metre derinlikte enkazı bulunan gemideki 14 yolcu hayatını kaybetmişti. Kayıp 14 kişinin bulunması için de çalışmalar devam ediyor.

title: Rusya'da Nestle ve Auchan varlıklarına kayyum atandı
content:
Rusya’da Nestle ve Auchan’ın ülkedeki varlıklarını yönetmek üzere kayyum atandı.

Rusya Devlet Başkanı Vladimir Putin’in imzaladığı yeni kararnameye göre iki şirketin varlıkları geçici süreyle devlet denetimindeki yerel şirketler tarafından yönetilecek.

Bu kapsamda Nestle’nin Rusya’daki varlıklarının idaresi Moskova merkezli LEV Management’a devredildi.

Rus medyasında yer alan haberlere göre, lojistik firması KS Logistika daha önce Nestle hakkında kayyum atanması için başvuruda bulundu.

Başvurunun, Nestle’nin Rusya’daki fabrikalarından ihracatı durdurması ve üretim kapasitesini artırmama kararıyla bağlantılı olduğu belirtildi. Kararın Nestle’nin beş farklı birimini doğrudan etkilediği aktarıldı.

Nestle ise kararnameye ilişkin yaptığı açıklamada hukuki seçeneklerini değerlendirdiğini bildirdi.

Şirket, çalışanlarının çıkarlarını gözetmek, haklarını korumak ve ticari operasyonların sürekliliğini sağlamak için gerekli adımları atacağını açıkladı.

Moskova yönetimi, Ukrayna savaşının başlamasının ardından yabancı şirketlerin Rusya’daki varlıkları üzerindeki denetimini aşamalı olarak artırdı.

2023’te çıkarılan kararnameyle Rusya hükümetinin “dost olmayan ülkeler” listesinde bulunan devletlere ait şirketlerin varlıklarına geçici yönetim atamasının önü açıldı.

Bu mekanizma daha önce Fransız süt ürünleri üreticisi Danone ve Danimarkalı bira üreticisi Carlsberg’in Rusya’daki iştiraklerinin kontrolünün devralınmasında kullanıldı.

Rus yetkililer, uygulamanın Batılı ülkelerin Rus varlıklarına yönelik yaptırımlarına ve Moskova’ya karşı “saldırgan” tutumlarına misilleme olduğunu savunuyor.

Analistlerin değerlendirmelerine göre ise geçici yönetim uygulaması, bazı durumlarda varlıkların Kremlin’e yakın şirket veya isimlere devredilmesi, zorunlu satış ya da kamulaştırma süreçlerinin başlangıcı olarak kullanılıyor.

Moskova yönetimi, Batılı şirketlerin Rusya’dan ayrılmasını da çeşitli koşullara bağladı. “Dost olmayan” ülkelerden ayrılmak isteyen şirketlerin varlıklarını en az yüzde 60 indirimle satması ve Rusya devletine özel bir “çıkış vergisi” ödemesi gerekiyor.

Danone, Rusya’daki operasyonlarını yaklaşık 1,2 milyar avro zararla satmak zorunda kalırken, Carlsberg’in Baltika iştirakinin 1,4 milyar dolarlık defter değerine karşılık 320 milyon dolara devredildiği aktarılmıştı.

Nestle, Rusya’da 1990’lardan bu yana faaliyet gösteriyor. Ukrayna savaşının ardından çok sayıda Batılı şirket ülkeden ayrılırken İsviçreli şirket, temel gıda ve bebek maması tedarikini sürdürmek amacıyla Rusya’daki faaliyetlerinin bir bölümünü korudu.

Şirket, temel olmayan ürünlerin ithalat ve ihracatı, reklam faaliyetleri ile yeni sermaye yatırımlarını askıya almıştı.

Nestle’nin verilerine göre şirket, savaş öncesi 2021’de küresel gelirlerinin yaklaşık yüzde 2’sini Rusya’daki 6 fabrikası ve 7 bin çalışanı üzerinden elde ediyordu.

Kiev Ekonomi Okulu'nun (KSE) araştırmasına göre, savaşın başlamasından bu yana 565 yabancı şirket Rusya’dan tamamen çekildi.

Buna karşılık yabancı şirketlerin yüzde 55’inin Rusya’daki faaliyetlerini sürdürdüğü belirtiliyor. PepsiCo ve Mondelez gibi büyük çok uluslu şirketler de Rusya pazarında faaliyetlerini sürdüren şirketler arasında yer alıyor.

KSE, Rusya’da faaliyet göstermeye devam eden yabancı şirketlerin 2025’te toplam 200 milyar avronun üzerinde gelir elde ettiğini tahmin ediyor. Araştırmaya göre yabancı şirketlerin yaklaşık üçte biri ise ülkeden ayrılmayı planlıyor veya operasyonlarını durdurmuş durumda.

Nestle ve Auchan’a ilişkin son karar, Moskova’nın savaş sonrasında yabancı sermayeye yönelik uyguladığı geçici yönetim mekanizmasının kapsamının genişlediğini gösteren yeni bir örnek oldu.

author: Unknown
title: Mızraklı: Society must shape its own future
content:
Selçuk Mızraklı, former Co-Mayor of Amed (Diyarbakır) Metropolitan Municipality, who was imprisoned after a government-appointed trustee took over the municipality in August 2019 and was released after completing his sentence, assessed the ongoing peace and democratisation process in Turkey.


Mızraklı said there is cautious hope within society alongside uncertainty about what lies ahead, stressing that lasting peace cannot be achieved simply by the parties shaking hands. He described the rule of law as the “first milestone” of the process and democratisation as the second.


In your first statement after your release, you emphasised “democracy, peace and a solution” and said the process needed to be transparent. How do you assess the process today? What do you observe in society’s approach to it?


Making observations about society genuinely requires a great deal of time and energy. It requires communicating and building relationships with different sections of society and creating spaces where more candid conversations and exchanges can take place. If you look at a city from a bus passing through it, you make judgements based on the buildings, the people walking along the streets, how they are dressed or what they are carrying. Yet none of these things may represent even one ten-thousandth or one hundred-thousandth of everything that city has produced and contains.


 


Society is waiting somewhere between hope and despair


For now, what I can offer are more like “surface observations”. They are not yet observations that reach the essence or the concentrated core of what is happening. But this is what I have seen: there is a sense of waiting. A mood of anticipation has taken hold across society, shifting back and forth between hope and despair. This hesitation exists alongside a sense that something is happening, particularly since 1 October 2024, followed by the declaration and manifesto of 27 February 2025, subsequent developments and, ultimately, the law passed by parliament.


Yet when I think about what is causing this doubt or anxiety, or when I occasionally ask people about it, I hear society trying to describe something like a car whose brake pads have jammed: no matter how hard you press the accelerator, it cannot pick up speed. Instead, the brake pads wear down and burn, and you can even smell them burning.


Another observation concerns why this trust or support remains cautious. The first responses I have heard reveal questions about sincerity. The second issue is a sense of not being able to see what lies ahead.


There needs to be clarity about what should happen next for the parties involved and how it should happen. Are we going to pave this road and make it easier to travel, or will we continue cautiously along the rocky and thorny path we are currently on, constantly worrying that something might be hurt or damaged? That needs to be determined.


I believe society needs a clearer picture of what lies ahead. The political actors involved need to put their future commitments genuinely on record, a language of mutual recognition needs to prevail, and the process needs to be built around a shared language rather than everyone speaking only in their own terms.


Peace is the well-being of the social body


I will once again draw on an example from my experience as a doctor. In my medical practice, before an operation I would explain to my patients what kind of surgery they were going to undergo, what difficulties they might experience afterwards, roughly how long those difficulties would last and how they could overcome them, the possible risks involved and the overall benefit we were trying to achieve. My patients would later tell me, “We are glad you explained all of this to us. Because you did, we were not afraid or anxious, and we were able to cope with our situation and overcome it.”


I cannot separate a peace process from a process of democratisation in this case either. Peace is the well-being of the social body.


What mistakes from the past must not be repeated if a new peace and solution process is to become lasting?


For the social body to be well, peace must develop fully and permeate every sphere of life. It must be experienced at every level, across every identity and gender. You need to gradually see the points of conflict in those areas begin to subside.


Peace has a memory of its own


But peace does not mean saying, “All right, we have made peace, joined hands and shaken hands …

title: KESK Women’s Conference releases final declaration
content:
The final declaration of the 3rd Women’s Conference, organized by the Confederation of Public Employees’ Trade Unions (KESK) under the slogan “Our legacy is resistance, our word is struggle,” was released.


The declaration stated that the struggle against inequalities and forms of domination over women’s labor, bodies, identities, cultures, nature, and right to life would continue. It called for childcare, eldercare, care for the sick, and care for people with disabilities to be removed from the specific responsibility of women and families and organized as a free and high-quality public service.


Women's participation in trade unions will be strenghtened


KESK stated that women’s councils and commissions should be strengthened so that women can have a voice and decision-making power in workplaces and trade unions. It said that meetings and events should be planned in a way that ensures women’s care responsibilities and time poverty do not prevent them from participating in trade union activities.


The declaration also emphasized that education should be organized on the basis of equality, free of charge, secular, democratic, scientific, in people’s mother tongues, and with an approach that upholds gender equality.


Call for action against violence


The declaration described violence against women as a structural problem and called for the implementation of the provisions of the Istanbul Convention, the effective enforcement of Law No. 6284, and the ratification of ILO Convention No. 190.


It stated that women’s access to justice in their mother tongues should be guaranteed and that effective legal and psychosocial support should be provided to survivors of violence.


Demand for free healthcare services


The declaration also drew attention to women’s right to make decisions about their bodies and fertility. It stated that abortion, HPV vaccination, contraception, and sexual and reproductive health services should be provided as free public services.


Women should be founding actors of peace


The final declaration of the KESK Women’s Conference stated that peace is not merely a matter of silencing weapons. It said that lasting peace requires eliminating inequalities and relationships of domination, as well as ensuring democratic participation, social equality, truth, and justice.


The declaration emphasized the importance of women taking part as founding actors, through their voices and decisions, in the processes of institutionalizing and socializing peace.


KESK said that women should strengthen equality, freedom, and organized struggle in all areas of life, from workplaces and trade unions to local governments and peace processes, and from culture and the arts to ecology and disaster policies.

title: Iran Human Rights publishes names of over 4,200 people killed in January protests
content:
Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO) has published the names of more than 4,200 people killed during the January 2026 protests in Iran, following months of collecting information, comparing sources, and verifying the identities of victims.


Rojhelat Info

 translated the main findings into English and said that according to the report, at least 420 women and 281 children under the age of 18 are among those identified. Twenty-five of the children were under 14, and the youngest recorded victim was only four and a half months old.


The organization says a large part of the killings took place on January 8 and 9. At least 3,356 people, or 91 percent of the cases where the exact date of death is known, were killed during those two days.


Deaths were documented in cities across 30 of Iran’s 31 provinces. The report also documents repeated patterns of deadly force, including direct fire at protesters, shots aimed at vital parts of the body, shooting people from behind or while they were fleeing, and the use of snipers.


The Iranian authorities have officially announced a death toll of 3,117 people, but Iran Human Rights says the government’s own lists are incomplete. The organization stressed that the figure of more than 4,200 represents only the minimum number of verified deaths and should not be considered the final toll.


Internet shutdowns, pressure on families, restricted access to hospitals and forensic records, and the lack of independent investigations have made it difficult to establish the full scale of the killings.

title: Family of Mazlum Rizgar Diyar: We will keep our martyrs’ legacy alive
content:
Mazlum Rizgar Diyar (Abdullah Karaviş), a guerrilla of the People’s Defence Forces (HPG) from Şırnak (Şirnex), whose martyrdom was recently announced, was martyred in İdil (Hezex) in 2015 during the struggle for the freedom of the Kurdish people and a democratic life. Diyar joined the guerrilla ranks at a young age and dedicated his life to the Kurdish people’s struggle for freedom. Following in the footsteps of family members who had been martyred before him, he took on responsibilities in different areas of the freedom struggle until his martyrdom.


His elder brother, Hakim Karaviş, spoke to ANF about his family’s history of struggle and the legacy left by the martyrs.


We are indebted to the martyrs until our last breath


Hakim Karaviş began by paying tribute to all the martyrs of the freedom struggle. He said the losses his family had suffered represented not only profound grief but also a responsibility to uphold the legacy of struggle left behind by the martyrs.


Karaviş said his family had been involved in the Kurdish people’s freedom struggle for many years and would continue to honour the martyrs and their struggle throughout their lives.


Karaviş also said: “We bow with respect before all our martyrs who lost their lives in the struggle for the freedom of our country. Until our last breath, we remain indebted to their efforts and their struggle. With great conviction, respect and reverence, we salute Abdullah Öcalan. We offer our condolences to Öcalan. Our family also has a long history in this struggle. My eldest brother, Lezgin Karaviş (Rizgar), was martyred in the 1990s. However, neither the location of his grave nor the details of his martyrdom have ever been established. Many years have passed, yet much about what happened to our brother remains unknown to us. As a family, this is a source of profound pain.


Many years later, my younger brother Abdullah Karaviş joined the ranks and took up the struggle of the martyrs. He dedicated his life to the freedom of the Kurdish people and embraced the legacy of struggle left by his elder brother and the comrades who had lost their lives before him. Another of our brothers was martyred in İdil during the urban resistance on 13 November 2015. Years later, in 2026, their martyrdoms were officially announced alongside those of many of our comrades who took part in the freedom struggle.”


We will remain part of this struggle for the rest of our lives


Karaviş said his family, known as “Mala Şêxo”, has lost 19 members as martyrs to date and added: “For the rest of our lives, we will remain indebted to this struggle, to the lands of Kurdistan and to Abdullah Öcalan. Had Öcalan not launched this struggle, perhaps today we would not even be aware of our Kurdish identity, our language or our history. For us, this struggle cannot be regarded solely as an armed struggle. It is also a struggle that has enabled us to reclaim our identity, our language, our culture and our existence as a people.


Our younger brother also followed the path of his eldest brother and took up his struggle. Our family, known as Mala Şêxo, has lost 19 martyrs to date. Many other members of our family have also become fighters. Some of our young people have been forced into exile and dispersed across Europe or other parts of Kurdistan because of the state’s policies of repression.”


The words of the martyrs are a testament to us


Karaviş said the bond the martyrs forged with the lands and peoples of Kurdistan carries great significance for the family. He described their approach to the struggle and the legacy they left behind: “Our brothers and comrades who sacrificed their lives for their land used to say, ‘If one day we are martyred, write on our gravestone: “We owe a debt to this country.”’ With the same conviction, we reiterate that we owe a debt to this country and to Abdullah Öcalan. They placed this land, this people and a free life above everything else. They sacrificed their own lives for the future of their people.


For us, it is not enough simply to mourn or commemorate them. We must uphold the effort, conviction and struggle they embodied. As a family, that is what we are trying to do. Keeping the memory of our martyrs alive, explaining why they struggled and passing that legacy on to future generations is a fundamental responsibility for us.


It should be understood that the martyrs are not ours alone. They are the martyrs of everyone who stands against oppression and …

author: Unknown
title: Merve Asya Özgür: If Kurdish artists are free, Turkish artists also gain - Part One
content:
Actress Merve Asya Özgür, one of the lead actresses in Pelin Esmer’s latest film And the Rest Will Follow, in which she plays the character Aliye, spoke to ANF about the relationship between art and peace.


Özgür said war creates “new distances and new forms of polarisation” between communities, stressing that the Peace and Democratic Society Process is important not only for Kurdish artists but also for Turkish artists, women and workers. She said the process could help bring social groups that have been driven apart closer together again.


Özgür also reflected on the way artists approach the Kurdish question and said: “Artists in the west of the country who have acted as though an issue that has been visible in this region for years simply did not exist may now turn and look at it.”


Özgür stressed that artists need to be more political and courageous, adding that art can play an important role in building broader social support for peace.


What can the relationship between art, prejudice and confrontation teach us when it comes to the issues facing this country?


If we look back at human history, we see that ‘everything’, what we call history itself, is in fact a collection of stories. Long before today’s sanitised spaces of art, the halls, stages and exhibitions, even before language existed, we were beings who somehow managed to tell one another our stories and communicate our troubles. We did it around the fire through sound and movement, or by carving into walls and shaping the earth.


Somehow, we learned to share what was happening to us, our fear, our pain, our laughter, with the ‘other’. All these accumulated narratives are part of one another’s stories; they are ‘our common story’. Perhaps it is only through this shared experience that we can find the courage to see and understand one another, including those we call the ‘other’.


Stories and by this I mean the entirety of the narratives we call art, have such an organic relationship with the past, with fear, with what we call foreign and what we call familiar. So when we ask, amid the fears and confrontations of today, ‘Will people be willing to look into the eyes of those they regard as enemies and see the stories behind their gaze?’, it seems to me that turning to art and asking what it can teach us is exactly where we should be looking.


But where does this potential to bring about confrontation actually come from? What do we call a story, and what is it about this ‘thing’ that gives it the power to bring us closer to one another?


What makes something a story is essentially the set of contradictions it contains. To put it very simply: Ali loves Ayşe, Ayşe loves Ali, they get married and live happily together. There is no story there. But if Ayşe’s father prevents them from marrying because Ali is Alevi, suddenly a story begins.


Ali is rich and Ayşe is poor. No one consents to their marriage. That gives us another kind of story.


Ali is actually in love with Ahmet. There you have yet another story, one that gives rise to entirely different contradictions and confrontations. It has been this way since the earliest narratives, since Adam. The trouble Adam and Eve bring upon themselves creates a conflict. A story comes and finds them, human beings. Humanity is therefore no longer in an infinite expanse but within life itself, with all its contradictions.


A narrative begins with conflict. Conflict is so fundamental to the very structure of a story that when you witness a story, you begin to see the contradictions of the person at its centre, and the entire narrative is essentially built around them.


You encounter someone you might simply walk past in the street without knowing who they are, but once you enter their story, you realise that they are actually not so different from you. That inevitably creates a confrontation.


In essence, every conflict gives rise to a story, and stories ultimately lead to confrontation. What we call art brings all these confrontations into a more contained space, presenting them in a more concentrated and perhaps more striking way, whether through tragic intensity or through humour. It seeks to create a confrontation and then leave an impact that can shape how people respond to it, potentially turning that response into thought or action. By ‘action’, I do not mean grand claims such as ‘art suddenly mobilises the masses and produces a radical impact’.


Rather, it seems to seek to leave people with a …

title: Osman: Kurds should pursue their struggle politically and diplomatically in the new period
content:
At a time when political balances are being reshaped in the Middle East, significant developments are also taking place in the regions where Kurds live. In Iraq, discussions are underway about the future of armed groups and the state’s role in security, while the region’s political and security balances are being reassessed. In Rojava, meanwhile, the future of the gains achieved by Kurds through years of struggle, education and language policies, and the integration process with the administration in Damascus have come to the fore. The political process underway in Turkey regarding a solution to the Kurdish issue is also bringing discussions about a new period, alongside regional developments.


Former Iraqi parliamentarian and Kurdish politician Muhsin Osman assessed the developments facing Kurds in the new period and the methods of struggle they should pursue. Addressing a range of issues, from the future of Sinjar and the gains in Rojava to the relationships Kurds have established with different states in the past and the importance of political and diplomatic struggle, Osman stressed that Kurds need to develop their own political strategy in the new period and protect the gains achieved in different areas.


Persistence on education in Kurdish in Rojava is necessary


Osman said that an important struggle has been waged for years in Rojava in the fields of education and language, describing the establishment of Kurdish as a language of instruction as one of the important gains of this struggle. Recalling that Kurds had fought for many years for the right to receive education in their own language and with their own identity, Osman stressed that the new political conditions emerging today also require a new form of struggle.


“A gain has been achieved, but this gain needs to be made permanent,” Osman said, emphasizing that recognition of Kurdish as a “national language” in the new Syria is important, but that this alone is not sufficient and Kurdish should be recognized as an official language. Osman noted that the limited inclusion of Kurdish in the educational curriculum has created a new debate regarding the education system developed in Rojava over the years, and said that the struggle must continue to protect and guarantee the gains that have been achieved.


Pointing out that this struggle now needs to be pursued not only in the field of education but also within the political and legal structure of the new Syria, Osman said that Kurds should develop political and diplomatic methods suited to the new circumstances while protecting the gains they have achieved in the past.


Osman said that Kurds had for many years been subjected to efforts to shape them around the question of “What is a Kurd, and what should a Kurd be?” and stated that education and assimilation policies had been important aspects of this struggle. Saying that the gains emerging in Rojava should not be viewed merely as the result of the struggle waged in the past, Osman stressed that securing these gains in the new period is also part of the struggle.


Warning against provocations


Osman said that developments in Rojava and the political process in Turkey affect one another, and stated that Kurds should be cautious about provocations in the new period and should not be drawn back into a period of conflict. Saying that discussions in Turkey concerning democracy and peace should be considered together with developments in Rojava, Osman stressed the importance of making use of the political space that has emerged, saying, “The struggle in the new period should be political and diplomatic.”


Osman said that Kurds need to reassess their methods of struggle in the new period, adding that it is important to make more effective use of political and diplomatic channels alongside armed struggle. Recalling that Kurds have developed relationships at different times with the United States, the Soviet Union, France, Turkey, and other regional powers, Osman said that states’ policies can change depending on circumstances and, therefore, Kurds should not shape their own policies according to the positions of other powers.


“It is necessary to correctly determine who is a friend and who is an enemy,” Osman said, adding that dialogue and negotiation are also part of the struggle. He stressed that Kurds should pursue a form of struggle suited to the conditions of the new period by making effective use of political and diplomatic channels.

title: Berwari: Kurds must develop a common will and strategy
content:
The Middle East is going through a new struggle over power and influence, placing Kurds at a critical juncture. A new wave of attacks is targeting the gains Kurds have achieved across different parts of Kurdistan, while regional balances of power are being reshaped.


Dr Kamuran Berwari spoke to ANF about developments in the region and said Kurds must build their own national policy, defence capacity and common political will rather than seeking a place within balances shaped by other powers.


There can be no disarmament without guarantees


Berwari said discussions over laying down arms and the future of the armed struggle in the process with Turkey should not be reduced solely to the question of “disarmament”. He stressed that the debate must also address how the national and political gains achieved through decades of struggle will be protected, what guarantees will safeguard them and how Kurds will defend themselves in the period ahead.


Berwari underlined the need to establish a constitutional and legal framework before any formal agreement is reached with Turkey, stressing that Kurdish interests must be guaranteed within such a framework. He said the necessary laws and regulations must be introduced, political mechanisms put into operation and a diplomatic dimension incorporated into the process, emphasising that the question of disarmament cannot be considered separately from these issues.


Berwari said the states concerned are pursuing discussions on the “disarmament” of the Kurdish Freedom Movement as part of a specific project and plan, which he said aims to eliminate Kurdish defence capabilities altogether. If this project is carried through as intended, he said, Kurds would be deprived of forces capable of defending them across Northern Kurdistan (Bakur), Southern Kurdistan (Başur), Rojava, Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan), Shengal and Maxmur. He stressed that the consequences would not be limited to the military sphere but would also directly affect the political position of the Kurds and the gains they have achieved.


Berwari said this strategy targets the national and political gains of the Kurdish people, adding: “There is a major plan against the Kurds. It is a plan targeting their national and political gains.”


Ending armed struggle is not the same as surrendering arms


Berwari said he is not opposed to a ceasefire, reconciliation, the pursuit of political solutions or the introduction of legal reforms, but stressed that seeking a political solution must be distinguished from Kurds relinquishing their capacity for self-defence. He noted that armed struggles in different countries have taken different forms over time and underlined the distinction between “ending the armed struggle” and “surrendering arms”. Methods of struggle may change, he said, but this should not mean completely eliminating the means through which Kurds can defend themselves.


The conditions that gave rise to the guerrilla must not be forgotten


Berwari said any discussion about the future of arms must take into account the conditions that gave rise to the guerrilla, stressing that the historical and social circumstances behind the armed struggle of the Kurdistan Freedom Movement cannot be ignored. He recalled that Kurds were deprived of freedom, the right to self-government and national rights when the guerrilla emerged, and said the armed struggle developed in an environment in which the political and social demands of Kurds living under the sovereignty of the Turkish state went unanswered. Treating the guerrilla merely as a military force, he said, would therefore mean disregarding both the circumstances in which it emerged and the decades-long struggle that followed.


Berwari said the guerrilla emerged within a broader struggle centred on the political, social and national demands of the Kurdish people, stressing that the current debate must also be approached with this historical background in mind.


Berwari pointed to decades of repression, military operations, attempts at political elimination, deception and plots involving different powers, arguing that the political and national gains achieved over the course of this struggle must be taken into account. He warned that dismantling Kurdish defence capabilities before those gains are secured would create new risks, stressing that the future of arms cannot be separated from guarantees for the political and national rights of the Kurdish people.

title: „Linke ausrotten“: Der neue ultrarechte Präsident Abelardo de la Espriella ist eine Gefahr (nicht nur) für Menschenrechte und Friedenspolitik in Kolumbien
content:
Dossier


„

Eine Gruppe von 21 internationalen Menschenrechtsorganisationen, darunter das Internationale Büro für Menschenrechte in Kolumbien (Oidahco), warnt vor der bevorstehenden Politik des ultrarechten gewählten Präsidenten Abelardo de la Espriella. Sie befürchten einen möglichen Abbau von Menschenrechten, Rückschritte bei der Umsetzung des Friedensabkommens von 2016 und der Friedenspolitik sowie eine Aushöhlung der Rechte von Frauen und LGBTIQ+-Personen. (…) Sein „Sofortplan“ sieht vor, den Einflussbereich bewaffneter Gruppen durch weitläufige Militäroperationen in den ersten 90 Tagen seiner Regierung zurückzudrängen. (…) Die unterzeichnenden Menschenrechtsnetzwerke fordern die Europäische Union und ihre Mitgliedstaaten sowie die Schweiz, Norwegen und das Vereinigte Königreich daher auf, die künftige Regierung De la Espriellas zur Einhaltung der Verpflichtungen des kolumbianischen Staates aus dem Friedensabkommen von 2016 zu bewegen

…“

Artikel von Pablo Schröder vom 26.06.2026 in amerika21

 und mehr zum Thema:


Präsident in Kolumbien stellt mit der Erlaubnis der Polizei zum Zugang zu Hochschulen die Autonomie der Universitäten infrage


„Der kolumbianische Präsident Abelardo de la Espriella hat angekündigt, dass die Polizei öffentliche Universitäten betreten darf, wenn es zu terroristischen Handlungen, Vandalismus oder Gewalt kommt. Ein entsprechender Einsatz soll auch dann legal sein, wenn nach Ansicht der Regierung entsprechende Taten vorbereitet werden. Die Maßnahme soll von einem landesweiten Protokoll begleitet werden, das friedliche Proteste von Handlungen unterscheidet, die die Regierung als gefährlich einstuft oder die öffentliche Ordnung in außergewöhnlicher Weise beeinträchtigen. (…)


Die Ankündigung hat bei den Hochschulleitungen Zweifel ausgelöst. Der Rektor der Universidad Nacional, José Ismael Peña, stellte klar, dass die Autonomie nicht bedeute, dass die Universität außerhalb des Gesetzes stehe. Wenn eine Straftat begangen werde, könne die Polizei ohne Genehmigung der Hochschulleitung eingreifen. Seine Sorge gelte vielmehr den Auswirkungen eines pauschalen Polizeieinsatzes. Ihm zufolge könnten sich diejenigen, die Gewalttaten verüben, unter Studenten mischen und die baulichen Gegebenheiten der Universitätsgelände ausnutzen. Er betonte jedoch: „Wir haben hier täglich 25.000 Menschen, und es kann kontraproduktiv sein, wenn ein Polizeipanzer auf den Campus fährt, weil dadurch viele andere Menschen verletzt werden können.“ Im Kern geht es um die Frage, was universitäre Autonomie bedeutet. Artikel 69 der kolumbianischen Verfassung erkennt sie als institutionelle Garantie an. Das bedeutet nicht, dass Universitäten außerhalb des Gesetzes stehen oder Gebiete mit Immunität sind. Öffentliche Universitäten sind Teil des Staates, unterstehen aber nicht der hierarchischen Leitung der Regierung. Ihre Autonomie soll die Unabhängigkeit von Lehre, Forschung und kritischem Denken gegenüber der politischen Macht schützen. (…)


Kolumbien hat historische Gründe, skeptisch zu sein. 1954 betrat die Polizei den Campus der Universidad Nacional. Im Rahmen des Einsatzes wurde der Student Uriel Gutiérrez Restrepo getötet. Am folgenden Tag schossen Soldaten des Batallón Colombia auf Demonstranten und töteten elf Menschen, darunter zehn Studenten. 1971 endete eine weitere Auseinandersetzung an der Universidad del Valle nach Angaben der Universität mit dem Tod von 15 Menschen. 1984 folgte auf einen Protest ein Einsatz der Sicherheitskräfte an der Universidad Nacional, der ebenfalls in einem Gewaltexzess kulminierte. Der Jurist Camilo Blanco ist der Ansicht, dass De la Espriella von der rechtlich korrekten Feststellung ausgeht, dass die Autonomie nicht über der Verfassung steht, daraus aber eine falsche Schlussfolgerung zieht. Laut Blanco „bedeutet das nicht, dass öffentliche Universitäten der freien Verfügung der Sicherheitskräfte unterliegen oder dass eine präsidiale Anordnung die verfassungsmäßigen Garantien ersetzen kann“.“

title: “STF em ponto de não retorno” – com Eloísa Machado de Almeida
content:
Não há saída rápida ou fácil para que o Supremo Tribunal Federal recupere sua capacidade de tomar decisões e volte a ser respeitado no Brasil. Essa é a avaliação de Eloísa Machado de Almeida, professora da FGV Direito SP e coordenadora do grupo de pesquisa Supremo em Pauta. No episódio do Pauta Pública desta semana, ela comenta as perspectivas para o

futuro da Corte

 após a Sessão Extraordinária do STF, que ocorreu na terça-feira.


Na conversa com Andrea Dip, Eloísa reforça a importância do jornalismo para esclarecer os acontecimentos envolvendo os ministros, mas alerta para os impactos que a imprensa pode causar na democracia quando adota interesses partidários, principalmente em ano eleitoral.

author: Simon Childs
title: Reform MP in Hypocrisy Row After Rightwing Think Tank Flies Him to Italy
content:
A Reform MP who rails against foreign influence in British politics was accused of “absurd hypocrisy” after accepting a trip to Italy paid for by a Dutch think tank.


In July, Danny Kruger took the all-expenses paid trip courtesy of the Center for European Renewal (CER), a pan-European rightwing organisation, based in the Netherlands, which says it is dedicated to “the Western ideal of a civilised, humane and free society”. The CER has ties to the former far-right, authoritarian government of Viktor Orbán, which ruled Hungary from 2010 until he was finally dislodged in an election in April this year.


The Dutch-based organisation spent £724.24 on his flights, hotel and meals over the course of the two-day trip from 8 to 9 July, according to the parliamentary register of members’ financial interests. He claimed the purpose of his visit was to “attend a day-long discussion of global affairs”.


The CER organises an annual meeting called the “Vanenburg conference”, named after the Dutch town in which it was first held. It is unclear whether this is the event Kruger attended – neither Kruger, Reform UK nor CER responded to a request for comment.


Only months before his jaunt to Italy,

Kruger spoke in the House of Commons

, alleging “glaring foreign interference” in the Gorton and Denton by-election.


In the March 2026 debate on the Representation of the People Bill, he claimed that votes had been cast under coercion through “family voting”. He went on to say that Asian voters in the UK were “taking their orders on how to vote from mosques and from clans – often directly from Pakistan.” The Green party’s Hannah Spencer won the 26 February byelection with 40.7% of the vote, compared with 28.7% for Reform’s Matthew Goodwin. A police investigation into claims of family voting

found “no evidence”.


On 28 August, Kruger tabled a series of proposed amendments to the bill, saying: “Recent changes in the makeup of Britain now jeopardise our democracy.”


Kruger’s amendments include removing the right to vote from Commonwealth citizens who are not British, limiting postal voting to diplomats and members of the Armed Forces and restricting election material to English, Welsh and languages “native to the British Isles”.


But Kruger appears to be more relaxed about some forms of so-called foreign influence than others.


CER is a Dutch non-profit organisation which “seeks to nurture in successive generations of Europeans an understanding of and devotion to the truth and wisdom embedded in the Western intellectual and moral tradition.” A key part of its programme is its Vanenburg conference, at which conservatives are encouraged to gather to exchange views and discuss the issues of the day.


CER also has a significant historical connection with the European Conservative, a rightwing magazine based in Budapest. The publication is funded by the Batthyány Lajos Foundation (BLA),

a non-profit through which

the former Hungarian government under Orbán used to channel funds to favoured projects. In 2021, its editor, Albino Mario-Fantiti,

said the magazine

 “grew out of the activities” of the CER. In 2022, it was

pulled from

 WH Smiths after it published a description of LGBT Pride month as “an opportunity to publicly parade some of the more dissolute aspects of human experience”.


Good Law Project policy advisor Cat MacLean said: “It’s not the first time Reform has been caught up in a foreign influence story and once again, the hypocrisy here is truly absurd.


“Kruger will happily allow a Dutch think tank with links to the Hungarian far-right to fly him out to Italy, and meanwhile, he refers to British citizens exercising their democratic rights as ‘foreign influence’, simply because they are Muslim.”


The revelation comes after a summer of scandal for Reform. The Metropolitan Police is investigating the party after a

Channel 4 News exposé

 showed two senior party figures discussing ways to take £500,000 and donations in kind from an actor posing as a wealthy American businessman. Foreign donations are illegal under electoral law. Nigel Farage’s senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy James Orr stepped down pending the outcome of an internal investigation.


There have also been questions over Farage’s personal finances, including an

undeclared gift of £5m

 from Thailand based crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne.

author: Ash Sarkar
title: Can’t Persuade Voters? Tom Watson’s New Palantir Job Shows You Can Just Buy Their Democracy
content:
Back in the halcyon days of Corbynism, I spent a lot of time thinking about Tom Watson. The then-deputy leader of the Labour party was

the right’s man on the inside

; either a noble fighter in service of the moderate cause, or a committed wrecker, who weaponised antisemitism allegations to 

undermine his own party

. He resigned from the post, and stepped down from the House of Commons, just one month before the 2019 general election.


What’s he been up to these days, I hear you ask? Well, six years after being elevated to the House of Lords by Keir Starmer, further congratulations are in order. Watson’s just been appointed as

Palantir’s newest senior vice-president

, working closely with Louis Mosley (grandson of Oswald, and the second-worst Mitford sister). A hero of the working man, a Labour titan, through and through.


Watson’s new job is more of a promotion than a big move: the Baron of Wyre Forest had been a member of Palantir’s advisory board since 2024. According to the company – named, reassuringly, after the evil and corrupting magic seeing stones from The Lord of the Rings – Watson’s role will be to increase the “social and economic value” of its work through public services, jobs and skills. Translation: this former minister will help grease our way to the government teat.


The assistance of an ex-Westminster big dog couldn’t come a moment too soon for Palantir. The company is facing pressure on PM Andy Burnham to cancel its £330m NHS contract, and is in a legal dispute with London mayor Sadiq Khan over his blocking of a £50m Metropolitan police AI contract. Palantir’s involvement with

US immigration enforcement

 (ICE) and work with the Israel Defence Force 

during the genocide

 has made the tech giant a flashpoint for protesters.


What’s more, polling shows that the

overwhelming majority of Brits

 are in favour of regulating AI more tightly. There’s a growing sense that AI has 

more risks than benefits

, and more than three-quarters of people cite the use of personal data without consent as a negative impact of the technology on their lives.


The task for Watson, then, is to convince the prime minister and his cabinet to ignore campaigners and voters alike, and hand over lucrative government contracts to Palantir with as little fuss as possible. If Palantir was after a man who’s had practice going to bat for morally-compromised causes, they could have chosen no better: since stepping down as an MP, Tom Watson went onto advise

Flutter Entertainment

, which owns Paddy Power, Betfair and SkyBet. Steel-trap memories may recall Watson once having been an ardent voice for betting regulation in the House of Commons.


To be fair to Watson, he’s hardly the first man through the revolving door. Nick Clegg, another former deputy prime minister, headed for the sunshine of Silicon Valley after leaving government, taking a job with Meta (then-Facebook). Ex-PM Rishi Sunak has taken roles with Anthropic and Microsoft since leaving government, and former chancellor George Osborne leapt into bed with

OpenAI

.


And hey, maybe these guys are just fabulous workers: diligent, industrious, indefatigable. Or maybe, just maybe, it’s not their character that’s valuable, so much as their contact books. The point of hiring politicians, from a tech-oligarch’s point of view, is to wear away at political resistance. Why persuade voters, when you can just buy democracy out from under them?

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Truth be Told (Again) | To make a dictator (un)necessary
content:
By Ernesto Stephen C. Gordovez


On September 23, 1972, the day Martial Law was announced, Ferdinand Marcos was certain — or, at the very least, he was determined to sound like it.


In

 Proclamation No. 1081

, the intelligence had been “carefully evaluated and verified.” The conspiracy was “definitely established.” The enemies had been identified, the danger had been mapped, and the contours of the crisis had been drawn.


In this world the would-be dictator painted, the Philippines was a country riddled with communist infiltration and armed separatist insurgencies, where seemingly innocent organizations allegedly served secret revolutionary ends, recruiting intellectuals and students into subversion and waging “propaganda assaults” against a government besieged on all sides by chaos. Dramatically, by Marcos’s telling, it had all the makings of a paranoid Cold War thriller.


Marcos says he tried.


I have already utilized the first two courses of action, first, by calling upon the armed forces to suppress the aforesaid lawless violence, committing to that specific job almost 50% of the entire armed forces of the country. . . and, second, by suspending the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus on August 21, 1971 up to January 11, 1972. . .


Marcos says he failed.


In spite of all that, both courses of action were found inadequate and ineffective to contain, much less solve, the present rebellion and lawlessness in the country . . .


the rebellion and armed action undertaken by these lawless elements . . . have assumed the magnitude of an actual state of war against our people and the Republic of the Philippines;


Whether every threat was quite as Marcos described it was almost beside the point. What ultimately mattered was what the would-be dictator made them mean. Each failure narrowed the field. Each danger pointed toward the same conclusion.


To say: I have no choice.


And so, on September 23, 1972, Ferdinand Marcos announced the only conclusion his proclamation had left standing: Martial Law, imposed supposedly

“to save the Republic and reform society.”

 


Never mind that this “last resort” had apparently been years in the making.


Never mind that, as written in his very own diary more than two years earlier on

January 28, 1970,

 Marcos had already considered allowing the crisis to “develop naturally,” until terrorism, killings, an assassination attempt, or a coup could make Martial Law acceptable to the public. And lest his ambitions be mistaken for mere concern for the Republic, in the very same entry Marcos contemplated another route and wrote: “If I want to be perpetuated in power, this is the easier way to it.”


Never mind that, as Juan Ponce Enrile admits in his memoir, Marcos had already ordered a confidential legal study on the nature and extent of Martial Law, which Enrile’s group submitted by the end of that very same January. 


Never mind that, on

February 11, 1971

, Marcos himself wrote of a growing opinion that “what the Philippines needs is a benevolent dictator,” before adding: “Some day soon I must make a decision on this.”


Never mind that, on

September 21, 1972

 itself, Marcos privately admitted to U.S. Ambassador Byroade that plans for Martial Law were already at an advanced state — and, in the same conversation, conceded that he did not consider the government to be in significant danger of being toppled at the time.


Never mind, too, that September 21 was itself part of the story. The proclamation that would forever fix that date in history was not put into effect until the night of the 22nd — and historical accounts indicate that Marcos backdated it to the 21st, reportedly because of his superstition about the number seven.


Never mind these facts inconvenient to the story the dictator wanted — needed — to tell. 


By September 23, 1972, Marcos had his story straight: the crisis was intolerable, every measure thus far had failed, and, if he were to be believed, he had no choice.


And that was the sleight of hand.


Marcos did not need to invent every threat. He only had to arrange them into a world in which his dictatorship appeared to be the only reasonable response. The lie of Martial Law was not simply that there was no crisis, nor that every danger was invented. 


Rather, the damning lie was that the crisis could mean only one thing: Marcos.


The dictatorship that followed is rightly remembered and denounced for the countless terrors and abuses it inflicted …
